Chapter I General Provisions

(Purpose)

Article 1The purpose of this Act is to protect the rights and interests of individuals while ensuring the smooth and proper management of the processes or services of administrative entities as well as ensuring due consideration of the value of personal information and the fact that the proper and effective application of personal information contributes to the creation of new industries and the realization of a vibrant economic society and an enriched quality life of the Japanese public; by setting forth the basic principles for the proper handling of personal information, creating a governmental basic policy with regard to this, establishing other matters to serve as a basis for measures to protect personal information, and clarifying the responsibilities of the national and local governments and establishing obligations that businesses and administrative entities that handle personal information are required to fulfill in accordance with their circumstances, as well as establishing the Personal Information Protection Commission, in light of the significantly expanding utilization of personal information as digital society evolves.

(Definitions)

Article 2(1)"Personal information" in this Act means information relating to a living individual which falls under any of the following items:

(i)information containing a name, date of birth, or other identifier or the equivalent (meaning all items (excluding individual identification codes) made by writing, recording, sound or motion, or other means, in a document, drawing, or electronic or magnetic record (this includes a record created in electronic or magnetic form (meaning electronic form, magnetic form, or any other form that cannot be perceived with the human senses; the same applies in item (ii) of the following paragraph); hereinafter the same); hereinafter the same) which can be used to identify a specific individual (this includes any information that can be easily collated with other information and thereby used to identify that specific individual);

(ii)those containing an individual identification code.

(2)"Individual identification code" in this Act means one prescribed by Cabinet Order which consists of any character, letter, number, symbol or other codes falling under any of the following items:

(i)characters, letters, numbers, symbols or other codes converted in order to be provided for use by computers, used to identify a specific individual by a distinguishing physical feature of theirs;

(ii)characters, letters, numbers, symbols or other codes used to identify a specific user, purchaser, or recipient, which are assigned differently for each of them regarding the use of services for an individual or the purchase of goods for an individual, or which are stated or recorded in an electronic or magnetic means differently for each of them in a card or other document issued to an individual.

(3)"Sensitive personal information" in this Act means personal information as to an identifiable person's race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, the fact of having suffered damage by a crime, or other identifiers or their equivalent prescribed by Cabinet Order as those of requiring special care so as not to cause unjust discrimination, prejudice or other disadvantages to that person.

(4)"Identifiable person" in relation to personal information in this Act means a specific individual identifiable by personal information.

(5)"Pseudonymized personal information" in this Act means information relating to an individual that can be prepared in a way that makes it not possible to identify a specific individual unless collated with other information by taking any of the measures prescribed in each following item in accordance with the divisions of personal information set forth in those items:

(i)personal information falling under paragraph (1), item (i): deleting a part of the identifiers or their equivalent contained in the personal information (including replacing the part of the identifiers or their equivalent with other identifiers or their equivalent without following patterns that enable its restoration);

(ii)personal information falling under paragraph (1), item (ii): deleting all individual identification codes contained in the personal information (including replacing the individual identification codes with other identifiers or their equivalent without following patterns that enable restoration of the individual identification codes).

(6)"Anonymized personal information" in this Act means information relating to an individual that can be prepared in a way that makes it not possible to identify a specific individual by taking any of the measures prescribed in each following item in accordance with the divisions of personal information set forth in those items; and also make it not possible to restore that personal information:

(i)personal information falling under paragraph (1), item (i): deleting a part of the identifiers or their equivalent contained in the personal information (including replacing the part of the identifiers or their equivalent with other identifiers or their equivalent without following patterns that enable its restoration);

(ii)personal information falling under paragraph (1), item (ii): deleting all individual identification codes contained in the personal information (including replacing the individual identification codes with other identifiers or their equivalent without following patterns that enable restoration of the individual identification codes).

(7)"Information related to personal information" in this Act means information relating to a living individual which doesn't fall under personal information, pseudonymized personal information and anonymized personal information.

(8)"Administrative organ" in this Act means the following:

(i)organs within the Cabinet (excluding the Cabinet Office) or under the jurisdiction of the Cabinet which are established pursuant to the provisions of laws;

(ii)the Cabinet Office, the Imperial Household Agency, and organs prescribed in Article 49, paragraphs (1) and (2) of the [Act for Establishment of the Cabinet Office](/en/laws/link/1369) (Act No. 89 of 1999) (if, under these organs, an organ designated by Cabinet Order as prescribed in item (iv) is established, that organ designated by Cabinet Order is excluded);

(iii)organs prescribed in Article 3, paragraph (2) of the [National Government Organization Act](/en/laws/link/3766) (Act No. 120 of 1948) (if, under these organs, an organ designated by Cabinet Order as prescribed in item (v) is established, that organ designated by Cabinet Order is excluded);

(iv)organs referred to in Articles 39 and 55 of the [Act for Establishment of the Cabinet Office](/en/laws/link/1369) and in Article 16, paragraph (2) of the [Imperial Household Agency Act](/en/laws/link/282) (Act No. 70 of 1947), and extraordinary organs referred to in Articles 40 and 56 of the [Act for Establishment of the Cabinet Office](/en/laws/link/1369) (including as applied mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 18, paragraph (1) of the [Imperial Household Agency Act](/en/laws/link/282)), that are designated by Cabinet Order;

(v)facilities and other organs referred to in Article 8-2 of the [National Government Organization Act](/en/laws/link/3766), and extraordinary organs referred to in Article 8-3 of that Act, that are designated by Cabinet Order;

(vi)the Board of Audit.

(9)"Incorporated administrative agency or other prescribed corporation" in this Act means an incorporated administrative agency as prescribed in Article 2, paragraph (1) of the Act on General Rules for Incorporated Administrative Agency (Act No. 103 of 1999) and the corporation listed in the Appended Table 1.

(10)"Local incorporated administrative agency" in this Act means a local incorporated administrative agency as prescribed in Article 2, paragraph (1) of the Local Incorporated Administrative Agency Act (Act No. 118 of 2003).

(11)"Administrative entity" in this Act means the following organs:

(i)administrative organs;

(ii)local government organs (excluding assemblies; the same applies hereinafter except the following Chapter, Chapter III and Article 69, paragraph (2), item (iii));

(iii)incorporated administrative agencies or other prescribed corporations (excluding corporations listed in the Appended Table 2; the same applies in Article 16, paragraph (2), item (iii), Article 63, Article 78, paragraph (1), item (vii), (a) and (b), Article 89, paragraphs (4) through (6), Article 119, paragraphs (5) through (7), and Article 125, paragraph (2));

(iv)local incorporated administrative agencies (excluding those whose main purpose is providing the service listed in Article 21, item (i) of the Local Incorporated Administrative Agency Act, or those whose purpose is providing the service listed in item (ii) or (iii) of that Article (limited to the part relating to (h)); the same applies in Article 16, paragraph (2), item (iv), Article 63, Article 78, paragraph (1), item (vii), (a) and (b), Article 89, paragraphs (7) through (9), Article 119, paragraphs (8) through (10), and Article 125, paragraph (2)).

(Basic Principles)

Article 3The proper handling of personal information must be pursued in view of the fact that it should be handled prudently in line with the philosophy of respecting the autonomy of the individual.

Chapter II Responsibilities of the National and the Local Governments

(Responsibilities of the National Government)

Article 4The national government is responsible for comprehensively developing and implementing the necessary measures to ensure the proper handling of personal information by national government organs, local government organs, incorporated administrative agencies or other prescribed corporations, local incorporated administrative agencies, and businesses in conformity with the purport of this Act.

(Responsibilities of the Local Governments)

Article 5Local governments are responsible for developing and implementing necessary measures to ensure the proper handling of personal information by local government organs, local incorporated administrative agencies, and businesses within their territory based on its characteristics in conformity with the purport of this Act while considering the consistency with the measures taken by the national government.

(Legislative Measures)

Article 6The government is to take necessary legislative and other measures to ensure that there are special measures in place to protect personal information whose strict proper handling it is necessary to ensure in order to further protect the rights and interests of individuals, and also take necessary measures in collaboration with the governments of other countries to establish an internationally harmonized system for personal information through cooperation with international organizations and other international frameworks, in view of the nature of the personal information and the way in which it is used.

Chapter III Measures to Protect Personal Information

Section 1 Basic Policy on the Protection of Personal Information

Article 7(1)The government must establish a basic policy on the protection of personal information (hereinafter referred to as a "basic policy") in order to further comprehensive and integrated measures to protect personal information.

(2)The basic policy is to provide for the following details:

(i)the basic course of action for furthering measures to protect personal information;

(ii)the details of the measures to protect personal information that are to be taken by the national government;

(iii)the basic details of the measures to protect personal information that are to be taken by local governments;

(iv)the basic details of the measures to protect personal information that are to be taken by incorporated administrative agencies or other prescribed corporations;

(v)the basic details of the measures to protect personal information that are to be taken by local incorporated administrative agencies;

(vi)the basic details of the measures to protect personal information to be taken by businesses handling personal information prescribed in Article 16, paragraph (2), businesses handling pseudonymized personal information prescribed in paragraph (5) of that Article, businesses handling anonymized personal information prescribed in paragraph (6) of that Article, and certified personal information protection organizations prescribed in Article 51, paragraph (1);

(vii)information about the smooth processing of complaints about the handling of personal information;

(viii)other material information for furthering measures to protect personal information.

(3)The Prime Minister must call for a cabinet decision on the basic policy developed by the Personal Information Protection Commission.

(4)Following a cabinet decision made under the preceding paragraph, the Prime Minister must disclose the basic policy to the public without delay.

(5)The provisions of the preceding two paragraphs apply mutatis mutandis to amendments to the basic policy.

Section 2 Measures Taken by the National Government

(Protection of Personal Information Held by a National Government Organ)

Article 8(1)The national government is to take necessary measures so as to ensure the proper handling of personal information held by its organs.

(2)The national government is to take necessary measures so as to ensure the proper handling of personal information held by incorporated administrative agencies or other prescribed corporations.

(Support for Local Governments)

Article 9The national government is to take the necessary measures, such as providing information and formulating guidelines to ensure that local governments and businesses properly and effectively implement the measures that they are required to take, in order to support measures to protect personal information which local governments formulate and implement, and in order to support actions that the people or businesses take to ensure the proper handling of personal information.

(Complaint Processing Measures)

Article 10The national government is to take the necessary measures to ensure the appropriate and prompt processing of complaints arising between businesses and identifiable persons regarding the handling of personal information.

(Measures to Ensure the Proper Handling of Personal Information)

Article 11(1)The national government is to take the necessary measures to ensure that businesses handling personal information as prescribed in the following Chapter properly do so, by effecting an appropriate division of roles between the national and local governments.

(2)The national government is to take the necessary measures to ensure the proper handling of personal information by local governments and local incorporated administrative agencies prescribed in Chapter V.

Section 3 Measures Taken by the Local Government

(Protection of Personal Information Held by Local Government Organs)

Article 12(1)Local governments are to take the necessary measures in order to ensure the proper handling of personal information their organs hold.

(2)Local governments are to take the necessary measures in order to ensure the proper handling of personal information held by local incorporated administrative agencies they establish.

(Support for Local Businesses)

Article 13Local governments must endeavor to take the necessary measures to support businesses and residents within their territory so as to ensure the proper handling of personal information.

(Mediation for Complaint Processing)

Article 14Local governments must endeavor to provide mediation for complaint processing and take other necessary measures to ensure that any complaint arising between a business and an identifiable person regarding the handling of personal information is processed appropriately and promptly.

Section 4 Cooperation between the National and the Local Governments

Article 15The national and the local governments are to cooperate with one another in taking measures to protect personal information.

Chapter IV Obligations of Businesses Handling Personal Information

Section 1 General Provisions

(Definitions)

Article 16(1)"Personal information database or the equivalent" in this Chapter and Chapter VIII means a collective body of information comprised of personal information, as set forth in the following (excluding those prescribed by Cabinet Order as having little possibility of harming individual rights and interests in consideration of how the information is used):

(i)those systematically organized so as to be searchable for particular personal information using a computer;

(ii)beyond what is set forth in the preceding item, those prescribed by Cabinet Order as having been systematically organized so as to be easily searchable for particular personal information.

(2)"Business handling personal information" in this Chapter and Chapters VI through VIII means a person that uses a personal information database or the equivalent for business; provided, however, that this excludes persons set forth as follows:

(i)national government organs;

(ii)local governments;

(iii)incorporated administrative agencies or other prescribed corporations;

(iv)local incorporated administrative agencies.

(3)"Personal data" in this Chapter means personal information compiled in a personal information database or the equivalent.

(4)"Personal data the business holds" in this Chapter means personal data which a business handling personal information has the authority to disclose; to correct, add or delete content from; to cease to use; to erase; or to cease to provide to a third party, other than what Cabinet Order provides for as data which is likely to harm the public interest or other interests if its existence or non-existence is made clear.

(5)"Business handling pseudonymized personal information" in this Chapter and Chapters VI and VII means a person that uses a collective body of information consisting of pseudonymized personal information for business, which has been systematically organized to be searchable using a computer or is the equivalent as prescribed by Cabinet Order as systematically organized in order to be easily searchable for particular pseudonymized personal information (referred to as a "pseudonymized personal information database or the equivalent" in Article 41, paragraph (1)); provided, however, that this excludes persons set forth in each item of paragraph (2).

(6)"Business handling anonymized personal information" in this Chapter and Chapters VI and VII means a person that uses collective body of information consisting of anonymized personal information for business, which has been systematically organized to be searchable using a computer or is the equivalent prescribed by Cabinet Order as systematically organized in order to be easily searchable for particular anonymized personal information (referred to as an "anonymized personal information database or the equivalent" in Article 43, paragraph (1)); provided, however, that this excludes persons set forth in each item of paragraph (2).

(7)"Business handling information related to personal information" in this Chapter and Chapters VI and VII means a person that uses collective body of information consisting of information related to personal information for business, which has been systematically organized to be searchable using a computer or is the equivalent as prescribed by Cabinet Order as systematically organized in order to be easily searchable for particular information related to personal information (referred to as an "database or the equivalent of information related to personal information" in Article 31, paragraph (1)); provided, however, that this excludes persons set forth in each item of paragraph (2).

(8)"Academic research institution or the equivalent" in this Chapter means a university or other organization or group associated with academic studies, or a person belonging to it.

Section 2 Obligations of Businesses Handling Personal Information and Businesses handling Information Related to Personal Information

(Specifying the Purpose of Use)

Article 17(1)In handling personal information, the business handling personal information must specify as much as possible the purpose for which it uses that information (hereinafter referred to as the "purpose of use").

(2)When altering the purpose of use, businesses handling personal information must not alter it beyond the extent that can be appreciably linked to what it was before the alteration.

(Restriction Due to Purpose of use)

Article 18(1)A business handling personal information must not handle personal information beyond the scope necessary for achieving the purpose of use specified pursuant to the provisions of the preceding Article without obtaining the identifiable person's consent to do so in advance.

(2)If, due to a merger or other such circumstances, a business handling personal information acquires personal information when succeeding to the business of another business handling personal information, it must not handle that personal information beyond the scope necessary for achieving the pre-succession purpose of use for that personal information without obtaining the identifiable person's consent to do so in advance.

(3)The provisions of the preceding two paragraphs do not apply in the following cases:

(i)cases based on laws and regulations (including local ordinances; hereinafter the same applies in this Chapter);

(ii)cases in which there is a need to protect the life, wellbeing, or property of an individual, and it is difficult to obtain the consent of the identifiable person;

(iii)cases in which there is a special need to improve public wellbeing or promote healthy child development, and it is difficult to obtain the consent of the identifiable person;

(iv)cases in which there is a need to cooperate with a national government organ, local government, or person entrusted thereby with performing the functions prescribed by laws and regulations, and obtaining the consent of the identifiable person is likely to interfere with the performance of those functions;

(v)cases in which the business handling personal information is an academic research institution or the equivalent, and needs to handle the personal information for the purpose of using it in academic research (hereinafter referred to as "academic research purposes" in this Chapter) (including cases in which a part of the purpose of handling the personal information is for academic research purposes, and excluding cases in which there is a risk of unjustly infringing on individual rights and interests);

(vi)cases in which personal data is provided to an academic research institution or the equivalent, and they need to handle the personal data for academic research purposes (including cases in which a part of the purpose of handling the personal data is for academic research purposes, and excluding cases in which there is a risk of unjustly infringing on individual rights and interests).

(Prohibition of Inappropriate Use)

Article 19A business handling personal information must not utilize personal information in a way that there is a possibility of fomenting or inducing unlawful or unjust act.

(Proper Acquisition)

Article 20(1)A business handling personal information must not acquire personal information by deception or other wrongful means.

(2)A business handling personal information must not acquire sensitive personal information without obtaining the identifiable person's consent in advance, except cases set forth in the following:

(i)cases based on laws and regulations;

(ii)cases in which there is a need to protect the life, wellbeing, or property of an individual, and it is difficult to obtain the consent of the identifiable person;

(iii)cases in which there is a special need to improve public wellbeing or promote healthy child development, and it is difficult to obtain the consent of the identifiable person;

(iv)cases in which there is a need to cooperate with a national government organ, local government, or person entrusted thereby with performing the functions prescribed by laws and regulations, and the consent of the identifiable person is likely to interfere with the performance of those functions;

(v)cases in which the business handling personal information is an academic research institution or the equivalent, and needs to handle the sensitive personal information for academic research purposes (including cases in which a part of the purpose of handling the sensitive personal information is for academic research purposes, and excluding cases in which there is a risk of unjustly infringing on individual rights and interests);

(vi)cases of acquiring the sensitive personal information from an academic research institution or the equivalent and it is necessary to acquire that information for academic research purpose (including cases in which a part of the purpose of acquiring the sensitive personal information is for academic research purposes, excluding cases in which there is a risk of unjustly infringing on individual rights and interests) (limited to cases in which the business handling personal information and the academic research institution or the equivalent jointly conduct academic research);

(vii)cases in which the sensitive personal information is open to the public by a person identifiable by that information, a national government organ, a local government, an academic research institution or the equivalent, a person set forth in each item of Article 57, paragraph (1), or other person prescribed by Order of the Personal Information Protection Commission;

(viii)other cases prescribed by Cabinet Order as equivalent to the cases set forth in each preceding item.

(Notification of a Purpose of Use when Acquiring Personal Information)

Article 21(1)Unless the purpose of use has already been disclosed to the public, a business handling personal information must promptly notify the identifiable person of that purpose of use or disclose this to the public once it has acquired personal information.

(2)Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding paragraph, a business handling personal information must explicitly specify the purpose of use to the identifiable person, before acquiring their personal information which appears in a written agreement or other document (this includes an electronic or magnetic record; hereinafter the same applies in this paragraph) as a result of concluding an agreement with that person; or acquiring their personal information which appears in a document, directly from the person in question; provided, however, that this does not apply if there is an urgent necessity to dispense with this requirement in order to protect the life, wellbeing, or property of an individual.

(3)If a business handling personal information alters the purpose of use, it must notify identifiable persons of the altered purpose of use or disclose this to the public.

(4)The provisions of the preceding three paragraphs do not apply in the following cases:

(i)notifying the identifiable person of the purpose of use or disclosing this to the public is likely to harm the life, wellbeing, property, or other rights or interests of the identifiable person or a third party;

(ii)notifying the identifiable person of the purpose of use or disclosing this to the public is likely to harm the rights or legitimate interests of the business handling personal information;

(iii)it is necessary for the business to cooperate with a national government organ or a local government in performing the functions prescribed by laws and regulations, and notifying the identifiable person of the purpose of use or disclosing this to the public is likely to interfere with the performance of those functions;

(iv)the purpose of use is considered to be clear, in light of the circumstances in which the personal information is acquired.

(Maintaining the Accuracy of Data)

Article 22Businesses handling personal information must endeavor to keep the content of personal data accurate and up to date, within the scope necessary for achieving the purpose of use, and delete the personal data without delay if they no longer require it.

(Measures for Managing the Security of Personal Data)

Article 23Businesses handling personal information must take the necessary and appropriate measures for managing the security of personal data including preventing the leaking, loss or damage of the personal data they handle.

This webpage contains the full English-language text of Japan's "Act on the Protection of Personal Information" (Act No. 57 of 2003), with the last version amended by Act No. 37 of 2021. The Act is Japan's primary data protection legislation, designed to protect individual rights and interests while ensuring proper management of personal information in light of the expanding utilization of personal information as the digital society evolves.

The Act is organized into 8 chapters and 185 articles:

**Chapter I (Articles 1-3): General Provisions** — Establishes the purpose of the Act and key definitions, including "personal information" (information relating to a living individual that can identify a specific person, including individual identification codes), "sensitive personal information" (race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, crime victim status), "pseudonymized personal information" (information prepared so a specific individual cannot be identified unless collated with other information), "anonymized personal information" (information where re-identification and restoration are impossible), and "information related to personal information."

**Chapter II (Articles 4-6): Responsibilities of National and Local Governments** — The national government is responsible for developing and implementing comprehensive measures; local governments handle measures within their territory; the government must take legislative measures and collaborate internationally.

**Chapter III (Articles 7-15): Measures to Protect Personal Information** — Requires the government to establish a basic policy on personal information protection (approved by cabinet and disclosed publicly), and outlines measures taken by national and local governments, including complaint processing and cooperation between levels of government.

**Chapter IV (Articles 16-59): Obligations of Businesses Handling Personal Information** — This is the core chapter governing private-sector obligations. Key requirements include:
- Specifying the purpose of use (Article 17) and not handling information beyond that purpose without consent (Article 18)
- Prohibiting inappropriate use and improper acquisition (Articles 19-20), including requiring consent for sensitive personal information except in specified circumstances
- Notifying identifiable persons of the purpose of use (Article 21)
- Maintaining data accuracy, security management, and supervising employees and entrusted persons (Articles 22-25)
- Reporting leaks (Article 26)
- Restrictions on providing personal data to third parties (Article 27) and to third parties in foreign countries (Article 28)
- Preparing records of third-party provision (Article 29) and confirming receipt from third parties (Article 30)
- Individual rights to disclosure, correction, and cessation of use or deletion (Articles 32-39)
- Complaint processing (Article 40)
- Specific obligations for pseudonymized and anonymized personal information (Articles 41-46)
- Certification of Personal Information Protection Organizations (Articles 47-56)
- Exclusions and exceptions, including for academic research institutions (Articles 57-59)

**Chapter V (Articles 60-129): Obligations of Administrative Entities** — Covers obligations for government organs (national and local administrative organs, incorporated administrative agencies, and local incorporated administrative agencies). This includes restrictions on holding personal information, clear indication of purpose of use, proper acquisition, security measures, employee obligations, leak reporting, restrictions on use/provision (including to third parties in foreign countries), personal information file registers, individual rights to disclosure (Articles 76-89), correction (Articles 90-97), ceasing use (Articles 98-103), appeals for review (Articles 104-107), and provisions for anonymized personal information held by administrative entities (Articles 109-123).

**Chapter VI (Articles 130-170): The Personal Information Protection Commission** — Establishes the Commission as the independent supervisory authority, covering its organization, duties, independence in exercising authority, supervision and monitoring powers over businesses (including reports, on-site inspections, guidance, advice, recommendations, and orders), supervision of certified organizations, and monitoring of administrative entities.

**Chapter VII (Articles 171-175): Miscellaneous Provisions** — Covers scope of application, information provision to foreign enforcement authorities, international cooperation, and delegation to Cabinet Order.

**Chapter VIII (Articles 176-185): Penal Provisions** — Sets out criminal penalties for violations.

The Act reflects a comprehensive, unified framework consolidating both private-sector and public-sector data protection under one law, administered by the Personal Information Protection Commission.

--- SOURCE 4: Third-Party Access Cybersecurity Threats and Precautions ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12575072

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article (published in 2025, Appl Clin Inform 16(5):1518–1530, PMCID: PMC12575072) presenting the results of a multinational survey on third-party access cybersecurity threats and precautions in healthcare delivery organizations (HDOs). The study was conducted by George A Gellert, Daniel Borgasano, Robert Palermo, Gabriel L Gellert, and Sean P Kelly, and the survey was created and pretested by Ponemon Institute and Imprivata.

METHODS: An online, anonymous survey was deployed to IT and IT cybersecurity personnel in HDOs across four nations (Australia, Germany, UK, and US). Data was extracted from a larger 2024 multisector survey of 1,942 respondents; a delimited analysis of 209 respondents (10.8%) who had IT cybersecurity management/leadership roles was completed. Respondent distribution was 12% Australia, 30% Germany, 20% UK, 38% US. Survey data was analyzed using stratified contingency tables. IRB approval was not needed as the study involved no patient data.

KEY RESULTS:
- Only 51.1% of HDOs had a comprehensive inventory of all third parties accessing their network. Reasons for lack included insufficient resources (48%), no centralized control over third-party relationships (36%), complexity (28%), and frequent third-party turnover (22%).
- 60% reported third-party access to sensitive/confidential information was not routinely monitored; of those who do monitor, 53% do so manually.
- 19% of HDOs had more than 40 third parties with network access, 31% had 21–40, and on average 22 third parties had HDO network access.
- More than half (56.4%) reported a breach involving a third party in the last 12 months; 48% believe third-party remote access is becoming their weakest attack surface.
- Two-thirds of HDOs anticipate third-party breaches increasing in the next 12–24 months.
- 55% ranked VPAM effectiveness at ≤6 on a 10-point scale; 49% ranked PAM effectiveness at ≤6. Only 36% applied their privileged access risk strategy consistently.
- Barriers to reducing access risks: lack of oversight/governance (53%) and insufficient resources (45%).
- Breach consequences include loss/theft of sensitive information (60%), regulatory fines (49%), severed third-party relationships (47%), loss of revenue (42%) and business partners (38%).
- HDOs expend an average of 129 hours per week investigating third-party and privileged access security issues.
- Mean cost of restoring access to third-party/privileged access users over the prior 12 months was US $86,550.
- Common actions taken include network segmentation/isolation (69%), removing access credentials when appropriate (66%), and verification of third-party need for network access (56%).
- Key challenges: taking too long to grant access to privileged users (61%), too expensive to monitor/control privileged access (60%), and inability to apply access policy controls at the point of a change request (70%).

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: The article cites that the global mean cost of a data breach is US $4.45 million, healthcare data breaches cost an average of US $7.42 million (highest of any industry for 14 consecutive years), and healthcare breaches take a mean of 279 days to identify and contain. Notable breaches referenced include the 2021 Broward Health breach (1.35 million patients affected via a third-party medical provider) and the 2023 Advanced Medical Management breach (~320,000 individuals affected). The article also discusses VPAM/PAM features including zero trust enforcement, credential vaulting, employment verification, session monitoring, and support for OCR audit readiness, GDPR compliance, NIST SP 800-207, and ISO 27001. Recent regulatory context includes the FTC Health Breach Rule.

CONCLUSION: HDOs recognize the increasing threat of third-party cyber breaches but are struggling to address them effectively due to budget constraints, lack of expert resources, complexity, and third-party turnover. There is a demonstrated need for automated, cost-effective solutions with a consistent strategy that minimizes breach risk by securing remote access to privileged assets, accounts, and data.
</summary>

Ransomware attacks against financial sector increased 9x between Feb-April 2020, increased 520% between March-June 2020, and rose 151% in the first 6 months of 2021. Finance is among the top three most targeted sectors for DDoS attacks. Multi-vector DDoS attacks rose 80% in 2021. Recommended defense controls: Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM), Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), regular firewall updates, Attack Surface Management, learning threat actor TTPs (Tactics, Techniques & Procedures), security ratings, regular data backups, and a documented cyber threat detection and response strategy.

<summary>
The Black Kite Third-Party Breach Report 2025, the 6th annual installment in Black Kite's research series, analyzes the most significant third-party cyber incidents of 2024. The central theme is that major cyber incidents followed a common pattern: attackers exploited trusted third-party vendors, and the initial target was rarely the organization that suffered the most damage. These were systematic exploitations of vendor ecosystem blind spots, described as "silent breaches" with cascading damage.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Ransomware accounted for 51.7% of known third-party attack methods in 2024, the dominant threat vector across every industry analyzed.
- The Cencora breach resulted in a $75M ransom payment—the largest ever recorded in a third-party breach—highlighting concentration risk in pharmaceutical distribution.
- The CrowdStrike outage reached 8.5 million devices and caused an estimated $5B in damages, demonstrating that third-party failures don't require malicious intent to produce catastrophic impact.
- HealthEC LLC exposed sensitive data for 45 million patients, cascading to patient records across dozens of downstream hospital systems.
- Unauthorized network access was the most commonly cited attack method, though the figure often masks root causes like unpatched systems, compromised credentials, and misconfigured access controls.
- Healthcare, retail and logistics, manufacturing, and finance faced the most severe cross-industry impact.

EIGHT INCIDENTS DOCUMENTED IN DEPTH: Cencora, Change Healthcare, Snowflake, CrowdStrike, CDK Global, HealthEC, BlueYonder, and Cleo. Notable details include: the Cleo file transfer attack (by ClOp group) cascaded across retail and logistics supply chains; Change Healthcare (by ALPHV/BlackCat) paralyzed US healthcare billing and claims processing for weeks; CDK Global suffered a $25M ransom and disrupted car dealerships; Snowflake demonstrated credential misuse on a shared cloud platform; and fourth-party exposure amplified damage in the Cleo, Snowflake, and CrowdStrike incidents—the most affected organizations had no direct relationship with the compromised vendor.

RECOMMENDATIONS FOR TPRM PROGRAMS: (1) Enforce continuous monitoring across every vendor tier, not just tier-1 suppliers; (2) replace questionnaire-based evidence with intelligence-driven vendor engagement (self-reported questionnaires produced no useful signal in the Cencora, Cleo, or HealthEC incidents); (3) map concentration risk before attackers exploit it using tools like the Ransomware Susceptibility Index® (RSI™); and (4) build incident response protocols that account for vendor-originated operational disruption, not just data breaches.

METHODOLOGY: Built from public breach disclosures, regulatory filings, and confirmed incident reports (representing a lower bound of actual incidents), supplemented by FocusTags® intelligence data and Supply Chain Module findings. Findings were validated against industry research including Google's Threat Analysis Group reporting, which tracked 97 zero-day vulnerabilities exploited in 2023 (a 56% increase over the prior year). GDPR, HIPAA, and DORA drove measurable improvements in incident response times among regulated organizations in 2024, though compliance was described as a baseline, not a ceiling.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive legal guide on Data Protection & Privacy in Japan for 2026, authored by Mori Hamada & Matsumoto (Tokyo) and Oh-Ebashi LPC & Partners. It covers Japan's principal data protection law, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI), its regulatory framework, and recent reform discussions.

**Key Regulatory Framework:**
- The APPI is Japan's primary data protection law, applying to private business operators handling personal information. Since April 2022, national administrative bodies were integrated into the APPI. Local governments are regulated under local regulations (*jourei*), with standardized nationwide principles introduced in April 2023.
- The APPI has extraterritorial application (Article 171) for foreign operators handling personal data of individuals in Japan in connection with providing goods/services to them. Operators in Japan providing personal data abroad generally need prior data subject consent (Article 28.1).
- The My Number Act governs Japan's 12-digit individual identification numbers. The Telecommunications Business Act (TBA) regulates cookies and imposes obligations on large telecom service providers (5M+ paid or 10M+ free users).
- Japan has mutual "adequacy" recognition with the EU and UK (renewed March/April 2023).
- On 9 January 2026, a draft policy outlining APPI reforms was released with four themes: promotion of appropriate data utilisation, regulation tailored to risk, prevention of improper use, and measures ensuring regulatory compliance effectiveness.

**Rights and Obligations:**
- Handling operators have obligations regarding entrustment (Article 25), joint use (Article 27.5(iii)), business succession (Article 27.5(ii)), and opt-out consent mechanisms (Article 27.2).
- No mandatory data protection officers under APPI, though PPC Guidelines recommend related measures. No mandatory PIAs, privacy by design/default obligations.
- Data subjects may request disclosure (Article 33), correction/deletion (Article 34), and discontinuation of use (Article 35) of retained personal data.

**Special Categories:**
- "Special care-required personal information" (race, creed, medical history, criminal record, crime victim status) requires prior consent for acquisition and third-party provision; no opt-out mechanism available.
- The APPI recognizes "anonymously processed information" (Article 2.6) and "pseudonymously processed information" (Article 2.5, introduced by 2020 amendment). The Next-Generation Medical Infrastructure Act (promulgated May 2023) creates a framework for "pseudonymously processed medical information" for medical research and pharmaceutical approval support.

**AI Developments:**
- The AI Act took effect on 1 September 2025, establishing an AI Strategy Headquarters and basic government policies, but contains no specific compliance obligations or penalties.
- PPC published its interpretation of the APPI for generative AI (June 2023). MIC and METI published AI Business Guidelines (April 2024).
- The PPC considers AI learned-model parameters not to be personal data if no correspondence to specific individuals exists, but AI developers can only use personal data without consent within the scope of outsourced work. The PPC is considering a system allowing legitimate provision of personal data for statistical creation including "AI development."

**Data Breach Requirements:**
- Breaches must be reported to the PPC (preliminary report within 3-5 days, final report within 30 days, or 60 days for unlawful-purpose incidents) under Article 26.1, with specific reporting items required. Data subjects must be notified regarding certain breach details (Article 26.2).

**Regulators and Enforcement:**
- The PPC is the primary regulator. FSA oversees banks; MIC oversees telecom providers. The PPC cannot conduct criminal investigations and the APPI imposes no administrative fines (though introduction is under discussion). Criminal sanctions possible in limited circumstances.

**Enforcement Trends:**
- In June 2024, a major case involved non-life insurance agents sharing policyholder personal data without consent. The FSA issued a business improvement order (24 March 2025) and the PPC issued administrative guidance (30 April 2025), highlighting the need for compliance over industry custom.

**Privacy Litigation:**
- Data subjects can seek damages in court. A key 2017 Supreme Court decision (correspondence education case) held that mental distress from privacy invasion itself can support damages claims even without other harm. Consumer class actions are limited to property damage and emotional distress under the Collective Redress Act.

**Non-Personal Data:**
- No specific IoT laws; MIC published IoT security guidelines (July 2016); JC-STAR labelling system for IoT security launched March 2025. METI published big data sharing contract guidelines.

**Cookies and Advertising:**
- Cookies aren't directly regulated under APPI but become personal information if collatable with individuals. "Personally referable information" concept introduced April 2022. TBA obligations (June 2023) require TSPs to notify/obtain consent regarding sending user information to external parties.

**Employment Privacy:**
- MHLW issued notices on employee health information handling. Employers may monitor workplace communications with appropriate internal rules and disclosure.

**M&A:**
- Business succession transfers don't require consent. Post-integration, personal data can't be used for purposes not originally contemplated without obtaining consent or properly classifying/managing data.

**International Transfers:**
- Prior consent generally required for overseas transfers (Article 28). Since April 2022, additional requirements include providing data subjects with foreign country name, information about its protection system, and recipient measures. "Appropriate and reasonable methodologies" include agreements between data importer/exporter and intergroup privacy rules. APEC CBPR is recognized. No data localisation requirements or blocking statutes in Japan.

**Reform Discussions (January 2026):**
- PPC's "Policy on Institutional Amendments" (January 2026) outlines four pillars: promoting proper data utilisation, addressing risks, preventing improper use, and ensuring regulatory effectiveness.
- Proposals include: easing consent requirements for AI development (statistical creation), allowing processing without consent where it clearly doesn't contradict data subject's will (e.g., hotel booking data to hotels, bank data sharing for remittances), easing consent for life/health protection purposes, new regulations on children's personal data (including consent from legal representatives for under-12s), new regulations on biological data (e.g., facial features), and adjustment of the entrustment regulatory framework (e.g., cloud services). No clear implementation timeline exists; specific amendments may be published as early as spring 2026.

This is a Global Law Experts guide titled "How to Report a Data Breach in Japan Online (2026 APPI & PPC Guidance)." It provides a comprehensive, practice-ready playbook for compliance teams, in-house counsel, and CSIRT leaders on reporting data breaches under Japanese law following the 2026 amendments to the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) and guidance from the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC).

KEY LEGAL FRAMEWORK: Japan's data breach notification law is codified in Article 26 of the APPI, first enacted in 2003, substantially reformed in 2020, with mandatory breach notification taking effect April 1, 2022. The PPC is the sole national regulator. The 2026 PPC updates clarified thresholds, refined "likely to have occurred" trigger, added encryption exemptions, and streamlined online submission.

FOUR MANDATORY REPORTING CATEGORIES (Article 26): (1) leakage of sensitive personal information (race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record); (2) leakage involving property damage risk (credit card numbers, bank accounts); (3) leakage likely caused by wrongful intent (unauthorized access, ransomware, insider theft); (4) leakage affecting 1,000 or more individuals.

WHO TO NOTIFY: (a) PPC - when any of the four categories apply, via online reporting page at ppc.go.jp/en/contactus; (b) affected data subjects - direct individual notice when risk to rights/interests exists; (c) NPA/Prefectural Police - when criminal conduct involved; (d) JC3 (Japan Cybercrime Control Center) - for large-scale coordinated incidents; (e) sector-specific regulators when applicable. These obligations run simultaneously and are separate.

REPORTING PROCESS: Two-stage filing. Preliminary report filed promptly after discovery (recommended internal SLA: within ~72 hours; triage within 24-48 hours). Supplementary report within 30 days (60 days for wrongful-intent breaches). Official submissions generally use Japanese despite English guidance being available.

TIMELINES: Unlike GDPR's fixed 72-hour window, APPI uses "promptly" standard. Recommended: detection to escalation 0-24 hours; legal assessment 24-48 hours; preliminary PPC report within 48-72 hours (internal SLA); supplementary report within 30/60 days.

PENALTIES: PPC corrective orders (zesei meirei) - non-compliance punishable by up to 1 year imprisonment or fines up to ¥1,000,000 for individuals and ¥100,000,000 for legal entities. Criminal penalties for intentional misuse: up to 1 year imprisonment or ¥500,000 fine for individuals, corporate ceiling ¥100,000,000. PPC enforcement actions are publicly published.

CROSS-BORDER: Multinationals face overlapping duties (GDPR, PIPEDA, PDPA). File in jurisdiction with shortest deadline first. Must disclose cross-border transfers under APPI Article 28 in PPC report.

The article was authored by Global Law Experts, with the featured expert being Noboru Kitayama of Mori Hamada & Matsumoto in Japan. It includes templates for PPC reports, data-subject notices, police escalation emails, a decision tree, and a 7-step incident response checklist, plus an FAQ section covering hashed password exemptions, English filing, and separate notification obligations.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from DLA Piper provides a comprehensive overview of data protection laws in Japan, primarily governed by the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) and overseen by the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). Key points include:

**Legal Framework:** The APPI was originally enacted in 2003, amended effective 30 May 2017, and further amended (Amended APPI) effective April 1, 2022. The separate public sector data protection law was integrated into the APPI on April 1, 2022 (local government laws after April 1, 2023). Discussions are underway for further amendments from 2025 onward, including introduction of an administrative monetary penalty system and injunction/damages systems for qualified consumer organizations, though timing remains unclear.

**Key Definitions:**
- Personal Information: Information about a living individual that can identify a specific individual (including Personal Identifier Codes such as passport/driver's license numbers).
- Sensitive Information: Race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, etc.; requires consent to obtain and no opt-out option for third-party transfer.
- Anonymously Processed Information: Personal identifiers removed such that individuals cannot be restored; can be used/disclosed without consent but has high compliance hurdles.
- Pseudonymously Processed Information (new under Amended APPI): Processed so it cannot identify a specific individual but can be decrypted by referencing other info; purpose of use can be changed without consent.
- Personally Referable Information: Related to personal matters but not Personal Information (e.g., cookies, age, gender, location data); transfer requires prior consent in certain circumstances.

**Authority:** The PPC issues guidelines, is neutral and independent, and has power to perform audits and issue cease and desist orders, but lacks power to impose administrative fines or criminal penalties. Contact: Kasumigaseki Common Gate West Tower, 32nd Floor, Chiyoda-ku Tokyo; ppc.go.jp.

**Registration & DPO:** No central registration system exists in Japan. There is no legal requirement to appoint a data protection officer, though guidelines suggest assigning specific directors/employees (e.g., Chief Privacy Officer) to control personal information.

**Collection & Processing:** Business operators must specify the purpose of use to the fullest extent possible, publicly announce it (one-click access on homepage recommended for websites), and not handle information beyond the scope necessary for the stated purpose without prior consent.

**Transfer of Data:** Personal data generally requires prior consent for third-party disclosure unless opt-out method is adopted (not available for sensitive data or data obtained illegally), joint use notice is provided, or merger/entrustment applies. For cross-border transfers, prior consent specifying the receiving country is required unless the country is white-listed (currently UK and EU based on adequacy decision of January 23, 2019) or the receiving party has "similarly adequate standards" (including APEC CBPR recognition). Consent disclosures must include the receiving country's name, data protection law system, and receiving party's measures.

**Security:** APPI requires business operators to prevent personal information leakage; PPC guidelines recommend Systematic, Human, Physical, and Technical Security Control Measures.

**Breach Notification:** Business operators must report breaches to the PPC and affected individuals when: (i) sensitive personal information is leaked, (ii) information could cause financial damage from unauthorized use, (iii) leakage by wrongful purpose, or (iv) breach involves more than 1,000 data subjects. Notification may be unnecessary if data was encrypted or otherwise made useless to third parties.

**Enforcement:** PPC may request reports, conduct on-site inspections, and issue remedial orders. Failure to submit reports: fine up to JPY 500,000. Failure to follow PPC orders: up to 1 year imprisonment or fine up to JPY 1,000,000 (entity fine up to JPY 100,000,000). Unauthorized disclosure: up to 1 year imprisonment or fine up to JPY 500,000 (entity fine up to JPY 100,000,000).

**Electronic Marketing:** Regulated by the Act on Specified Commercial Transactions (ASCT) and the Anti-Spam Act. ASCT requires opt-in consent for email/fax ads to consumers with record retention of 3 years (email) and 1 year (fax). Anti-Spam Act requires consent records (1 month retention), opt-out mechanisms, and prohibits sending to randomly generated addresses. Violations can result in fines up to JPY 30,000,000 for entities.

**Online Privacy:** No specific cookie law; cookies generally fall under Personally Referable Information. Under the Telecommunications Business Act, service providers transmitting third-party cookies must notify users, obtain consent, or take opt-out measures.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 20: Act on the Protection of Personal Information - English - Japanese Law Translation ---
URL: https://www.japaneselawtranslation.go.jp/en/laws/view/4241/en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains the full English-language text of Japan's "Act on the Protection of Personal Information" (Act No. 57 of 2003), with the last version amended by Act No. 37 of 2021. The Act is Japan's primary data protection legislation, designed to protect individual rights and interests while ensuring proper management of personal information in light of the expanding utilization of personal information as the digital society evolves.

The Act is organized into 8 chapters and 185 articles:

**Chapter I (Articles 1-3): General Provisions** — Establishes the purpose of the Act and key definitions, including "personal information" (information relating to a living individual that can identify a specific person, including individual identification codes), "sensitive personal information" (race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, crime victim status), "pseudonymized personal information" (information prepared so a specific individual cannot be identified unless collated with other information), "anonymized personal information" (information where re-identification and restoration are impossible), and "information related to personal information."

**Chapter II (Articles 4-6): Responsibilities of National and Local Governments** — The national government is responsible for developing and implementing comprehensive measures; local governments handle measures within their territory; the government must take legislative measures and collaborate internationally.

**Chapter III (Articles 7-15): Measures to Protect Personal Information** — Requires the government to establish a basic policy on personal information protection (approved by cabinet and disclosed publicly), and outlines measures taken by national and local governments, including complaint processing and cooperation between levels of government.

**Chapter IV (Articles 16-59): Obligations of Businesses Handling Personal Information** — This is the core chapter governing private-sector obligations. Key requirements include:
- Specifying the purpose of use (Article 17) and not handling information beyond that purpose without consent (Article 18)
- Prohibiting inappropriate use and improper acquisition (Articles 19-20), including requiring consent for sensitive personal information except in specified circumstances
- Notifying identifiable persons of the purpose of use (Article 21)
- Maintaining data accuracy, security management, and supervising employees and entrusted persons (Articles 22-25)
- Reporting leaks (Article 26)
- Restrictions on providing personal data to third parties (Article 27) and to third parties in foreign countries (Article 28)
- Preparing records of third-party provision (Article 29) and confirming receipt from third parties (Article 30)
- Individual rights to disclosure, correction, and cessation of use or deletion (Articles 32-39)
- Complaint processing (Article 40)
- Specific obligations for pseudonymized and anonymized personal information (Articles 41-46)
- Certification of Personal Information Protection Organizations (Articles 47-56)
- Exclusions and exceptions, including for academic research institutions (Articles 57-59)

**Chapter V (Articles 60-129): Obligations of Administrative Entities** — Covers obligations for government organs (national and local administrative organs, incorporated administrative agencies, and local incorporated administrative agencies). This includes restrictions on holding personal information, clear indication of purpose of use, proper acquisition, security measures, employee obligations, leak reporting, restrictions on use/provision (including to third parties in foreign countries), personal information file registers, individual rights to disclosure (Articles 76-89), correction (Articles 90-97), ceasing use (Articles 98-103), appeals for review (Articles 104-107), and provisions for anonymized personal information held by administrative entities (Articles 109-123).

**Chapter VI (Articles 130-170): The Personal Information Protection Commission** — Establishes the Commission as the independent supervisory authority, covering its organization, duties, independence in exercising authority, supervision and monitoring powers over businesses (including reports, on-site inspections, guidance, advice, recommendations, and orders), supervision of certified organizations, and monitoring of administrative entities.

**Chapter VII (Articles 171-175): Miscellaneous Provisions** — Covers scope of application, information provision to foreign enforcement authorities, international cooperation, and delegation to Cabinet Order.

**Chapter VIII (Articles 176-185): Penal Provisions** — Sets out criminal penalties for violations.

The Act reflects a comprehensive, unified framework consolidating both private-sector and public-sector data protection under one law, administered by the Personal Information Protection Commission.
</summary>

args.summary:
This cybersecurity deep-dive episode (published June 20, 2025) analyzes the Chain IQ supply chain breach and provides a comprehensive framework for defending against supply chain attacks.

## The Chain IQ Breach
Chain IQ, a Swiss procurement and service provider, suffered a massive data breach in early June 2025 perpetrated by the group "World Leaks" (formerly known as Hunters International), a group focused on data theft and public extortion rather than encryption. Key impacts included:
- **UBS**: Personal data of 137,000 employees stolen, including names, emails, phone numbers, job roles, office locations, and even the internal direct phone number of UBS CEO Sergio Armati.
- **Pictet**: 230,000 lines of internal billing data exposed, including highly detailed expenses (grocery shopping, hotel stays, pottery purchases).
- **Other exposed clients**: World Leaks exposed lists of hundreds of companies linked to Chain IQ, including FedEx, IBM, Swiss Life, AXA, Swisscom, and KPMG.
- Client financial data reportedly remained untouched, but employee and operational data exposure was severe.

## Attacker Tactics (World Leaks)
- Operates primarily as an extortion platform (data theft + public leak threats, not encryption), though some victims experienced actual ransomware deployment, suggesting collaboration with groups like the SEC ransomware group.
- Uses a sophisticated multiplatform setup: a main leak site (trophy wall), negotiation site, an insider platform offering journalists 24-hour advanced access to impending leaks, and an affiliate panel.
- Victim site includes countdown timers to public disclosure, direct chat, and a storage page allowing victims to browse their own stolen data (validation + psychological leverage).
- Initial operations faced bugs and fluctuating data size claims (one victim's leak claimed at 7TB, then 700GB, then 1.5TB), raising doubts about their accuracy.

## Key Statistics
- 62% of supply chain attacks exploit trust in third-party providers.
- 66% of suppliers don't even know how they were compromised.
- Organizations have a 27.7% chance of suffering a data breach; almost 60% of these breaches are directly linked to third parties.
- MFA can block up to 99.9% of automated cybercrime attempts.
- MFA can block up to 99.9% of automated cyber crime attempts.
- SolarWinds Orion breach: compromised software updates installed backdoors in ~18,000 customers (including US government agencies and Fortune 500s), undetected for at least 9 months, perpetrated by APT29/Cozy Bear (Russian SVR) primarily for espionage.

## ENISA Survey Findings (April–June 2022)
- 86% of surveyed organizations reported having ICT supply chain cybersecurity policies, but 53% have no dedicated budget for these issues.
- Banking sector most mature: 98% have policies, 43% have dedicated budgets.
- Digital infrastructure: 60% with policies but only 2% with dedicated budgets; online search engines: 47% with policies, 6% with budgets.
- 52% have rigid patching policies covering only 0-20% of assets; 13.5% lack visibility over patching for 50%+ of assets.
- 46% patch critical vulnerabilities within one month; another 46% within six months.
- Only 48% have fully implemented risk-based vulnerability management; 15% have no process at all.
- Supplier risk evaluation criteria: product/service type (59%), spending amount (47%), regulatory status (42%).

## Expert Quote
- Steven Meyer, co-CEO of Zenata Cybersecurity, stated that trust placed in supplier certifications or compliance audits is "dangerously overestimated" — compliance through paperwork can create an "illusion of security."

## Defense Frameworks
1. **Assume Breach Mentality**: Assume a breach is inevitable; focus on three attack surfaces — people, processes, and technologies.
   - People: Comprehensive ongoing cybercrime awareness training (phishing, spear phishing, social engineering, DDoS, ransomware, malware, clickjacking); distinguish innocent users from hostile insider threats.
   - Processes: Robust information security policies (ISPs) plus least privilege principle (PLP).
   - Technologies: Multi-layered defenses including updated antivirus, MFA (blocks up to 99.9% of automated attacks), and attack surface monitoring (including vendor technologies).

2. **Privileged Access Management (PAM)**: Protect the "vault of master keys" and protect the PAM itself. External defenses include detecting third-party data leaks; internal defenses include Identity Access Management (IAM) with centralized account management and encryption using AES (used by US government for classified data).

3. **Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA)**: "Never trust, always verify" — assumes all network activity is malicious by default. Powered by three components: policy engine (trust algorithm), policy administrator (communicates decisions), and policy enforcement point (final gatekeeper). Critical for securing remote endpoints.

4. **Top-Down Strategic Approach**: Assign clear responsibility; create collaborative roles across supply chain, cybersecurity, product security, physical security; increase board involvement; adopt risk-based approach; form multi-dimensional teams (security, procurement, legal).

5. **Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) Cycle**:
   - Plan: ICT supply chain risk management (identify all suppliers and risks).
   - Do: Supplier relationship management (policies, procedures, contractual agreements, performance monitoring).
   - Check: Vulnerability handling (monitor assets, assess risks, deploy patches).
   - Act: Quality of products/services (secure practices built in, transparency for customers).

## Supply Chain Risk Assessment Good Practices (aligned with ISO 31000, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 9000)
- Define scope and context; identify all suppliers and service providers.
- Assess risks for impact on business continuity.
- Implement risk mitigation using international standards.
- Continuous monitoring via internal logs and global threat intelligence feeds.
- Prioritize suppliers with security-enforcing functions, privileged access, or sensitive information handling.
- Consider country-specific intelligence, national authority restrictions, known incidents, threat intelligence, supplier security maturity, and transparency.
- Continuously monitor changes in supplier risk profiles (acquisitions, personnel shifts, new operating models).

## Systemic Challenges
- Terminology confusion over "supply chain" and "managed service provider" definitions hampers NIS-2 implementation.
- State-sponsored attacks with unlimited resources require national-level management and intelligence service involvement.
- Need for shared testing platforms for ICT security, requiring private investment for sustainability.

# Chain IQ data breach affects major banks and companies in Switzerland

Posted date 31/07/2025

Chain IQ, a large company dedicated to procurement and indirect purchasing services, was the target of a cyber-attack affecting the data of 19 other companies. Among the affected companies, the media highlighted names such as UBS, Pictet, Manor, Implenia, KPMG or Mizuho.

The attack was claimed on June 11, 2025 by the ransomware group Worldleaks, which published the breach of Chain IQ's systems on its Tor-based leak website. It announced the theft of about 910 GB of data and more than 1.9 million files. The stolen information is related to the purchases of some customers who contract Chain IQ's services. The company itself claimed that the attackers managed to extract data containing business contact details of employees of selected customers, including the employees' phone numbers.

Following the release of the data, Chain IQ notified law enforcement authorities and began reviewing all of its systems, strengthening protective measures and cutting off the attackers' access to the affected environment. In fact, it also managed to restore software introduced by the attackers during the attack for further analysis. Chain IQ is working with InfoGuard and Kyndryl to maintain the security of its systems.

args.summary:
Chain IQ, a major procurement and indirect purchasing services company, was the target of a cyber-attack affecting the data of 19 other companies, including major Swiss and international firms such as UBS, Pictet, Manor, Implenia, KPMG, and Mizuho. The ransomware group Worldleaks claimed the attack on June 11, 2025, publishing the breach on its Tor-based leak website. The attackers stole approximately 910 GB of data and more than 1.9 million files related to the purchases of Chain IQ's customers. The stolen information included business contact details of employees of selected customers, including phone numbers.

Following the data release, Chain IQ notified law enforcement authorities, reviewed all of its systems, strengthened protective measures, and cut off attackers' access to the affected environment. The company also managed to restore software introduced by the attackers during the attack for further analysis. Chain IQ is working with InfoGuard and Kyndryl to maintain the security of its systems.

Key developments reported in references (June 2025): Over 100,000 UBS employees were affected by the massive theft of sensitive data, which also impacted Pictet; security firm reports confirmed Chain IQ and UBS data were stolen in the ransomware attack; Chain IQ officially acknowledged the cyber-attack in a statement on chainiq.com; and Reuters reported that UBS and Pictet confirmed data leaks but stated that client data was unaffected. The article is tagged with: security breach, intrusion, ransomware, and data theft. Published by Spain's INCIBE-CERT (Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad) on July 31, 2025.

# The Chain IQ Cybersecurity Incident: A Case Study in Supply Chain Risk

* June 20, 2025
* [Uncategorized](https://xenexsoc.com/category/uncategorized/)

In today’s interconnected business landscape, procurement management software has become the digital backbone of organizational supply chains. But as the recent Chain IQ ransomware attack demonstrates, these systems also represent one of the most vulnerable entry points for cybercriminals looking to maximize their impact across multiple organizations simultaneously.

## **When One Attack Becomes Many: The Chain IQ Incident**

Chain IQ, a global procurement services firm trusted by major financial institutions and corporations, recently fell victim to a devastating ransomware attack orchestrated by the cybercrime group “World Leaks.” The breach didn’t just impact Chain IQ—it created a domino effect that exposed sensitive data from multiple high-profile clients, including UBS (affecting over 130,000 employees), Pictet, and construction giant Implenia.

This wasn’t an isolated incident. The attackers targeted Chain IQ alongside 19 other companies, demonstrating a sophisticated understanding of how to leverage supply chain vulnerabilities for maximum impact. In a single coordinated attack, cybercriminals gained access to employee business contact details, names, emails, phone numbers, job roles, office locations, and preferred languages across multiple organizations.

## **The Procurement Security Paradox**

Procurement management systems create an inherent security paradox. By design, these platforms must be deeply integrated with organizational processes and contain vast amounts of sensitive information, including:

* Vendor relationships and contractual details
* Financial transaction histories
* Supply chain dependencies and vulnerabilities
* Strategic sourcing intelligence
* Business partnership structures

This rich data environment makes procurement platforms attractive targets for cybercriminals, who understand that compromising a single provider can unlock access to dozens of client organizations. The Chain IQ attack perfectly illustrates this multiplier effect—one successful breach exposed sensitive information across major financial institutions and corporations simultaneously.

## **Beyond Data Theft: The Real Impact of Procurement Breaches**

The Chain IQ incident exposes risks that extend far beyond simple data theft. The compromised information provides attackers with detailed intelligence for launching sophisticated social engineering campaigns, targeted phishing attacks, and further supply chain compromises. When cybercriminals possess employee contact details, organizational structures, and business relationships, they can craft highly convincing attacks that bypass traditional security measures.

Moreover, procurement data reveals the intricate web of business dependencies that modern organizations rely on. This intelligence allows attackers to identify the most critical suppliers and partners, potentially enabling them to target the entire supply chain ecosystem systematically.

**Building Resilient Procurement Security** The Chain IQ incident serves as a stark reminder that procurement management software represents a critical attack surface requiring dedicated security attention. # Chain IQ, UBS Data Stolen in Ransomware Attack

A ransomware group has claimed the theft of millions of files from procurement service provider Chain IQ and 19 other companies.

![](https://www.securityweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Iounut-SecurityWeek.jpg)

By

[Ionut Arghire](https://www.securityweek.com/contributors/ionut-arghire/)

|

* [+ Flipboard](# "Share on Flipboard") [+ Reddit](# "Share on Reddit") [+ Whatsapp](https://web.whatsapp.com/send?text=Chain IQ, UBS Data Stolen in Ransomware Attack https://www.securityweek.com/chain-iq-ubs-data-stolen-in-ransomware-attack/) [+ Whatsapp](whatsapp://send?text=Chain IQ, UBS Data Stolen in Ransomware Attack https://www.securityweek.com/chain-iq-ubs-data-stolen-in-ransomware-attack/) [+ Email](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#)

**Swiss procurement service provider Chain IQ has confirmed falling victim to a cyberattack that led to the theft of customer data.**

The Zug, Switzerland-based firm says it learned of the incident after a threat actor published data allegedly stolen from its systems on the dark web.

“On June 12, 2025, Chain IQ, along with 19 other companies, was the target of a cyberattack that had never before been seen on a global scale. This cyberattack resulted in data theft. Data from some Chain IQ customers was published on the dark web,” the company says in an incident [notice](https://chainiq.com/news/cyber-attack-chain-iq-group-ag/).

Chain IQ says it immediately activated its response plan and checked all relevant systems, and notified customers, employees, and partner companies, as well as the relevant authorities.

“The incident was contained after 8 hours and 45 minutes by revoking the attackers’ access to the affected environment,” the company says.

Chain IQ said no bank customer data was compromised in the incident, but confirmed that the attackers exfiltrated “data containing employee business contact details of selected clients”, including client employees’ phone numbers.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to local [media](https://www.letemps.ch/cyber/plus-de-100-000-employes-d-ubs-touches-par-un-vol-massif-de-donnees-sensibles-affectant-aussi-pictet?srsltid=AfmBOopj_kt0nNdS32W18PJZxduTFjb5EcKaPSNl22CXYiRiUEOTHbUw), Swiss financial groups UBS and Pictet, as well as Manor, and real estate and construction services company Implenia were impacted.

Responding to a *SecurityWeek* inquiry, UBS confirmed the impact from the incident, but said that no client data was stolen in the attack.

“A cyber-attack at an external supplier has led to information about UBS and several other companies being stolen. No client data has been affected. As soon as UBS became aware of the incident, it took swift and decisive action to avoid any impact on its operations,” UBS said.

The attack on Chain IQ was claimed by the ransomware group Worldleaks, which added the company to its Tor-based leak site on June 11, claiming the theft of roughly 910 GB of data, or more than 1.9 million files.

“External suppliers have become one of the most readily attacked, compromised, and exploited organizations that we deal with,” Neovera VP Paul Underwood said in an emailed comment.

“Although in a statement it was reported that no client data was involved in the cyberattack, it does not mean that the cyberattack does not have value to not only the attacker but to what potentially could happen in the future to these organizations that were affected,” Underwood continued.
