Recognizing its importance, the ESAs and, in particular, EBA have integrated DORA into their 2025 supervisory priorities and strategic plans ESAs 2025 Working Program1 Sustainable Finance Consumer Protection and Financial Innovation Other Cross-Sectorial matters 1For a complete analysis, we suggest: B.Ghilardi, T.Travezzoli, A.Proietti; ESAs: The Work Programme 2025; JIT; November 2024 Digital Operational Resilience In 2025, the ESAs will continue working on supervisory convergence to facilitate a harmonized implementation of the DORA framework. They will also start supervisory activities on critical third-party ICT providers (CTPPs) under the new EU-wide Oversight Framework. Additionally, the ESAs completed a feasibility study in January 2025 on the further centralization of major ICT-related incident reporting EBA 2025 Priorities P4 - Starting oversight and Supervisory activities for DORA and MiCAR2 In 2025, the EBA will start to take over its supervisory responsibilities regarding DORA and MiCAR, such as the oversight of ICT-third-party service providers, as well as for the supervision of issuers of ART and EMT P5 - Developing Consumer-Oriented mandates and ensuring a Smooth transition to the new AML/CFT framework P3 - Enhancing Data Infrastructure and launching the data portal P2 - Enhancing risk-based and forward-looking financial stability for a Sustainable economy P1 - Implementing the EU banking package and enhancing the Single Rulebook 2For a complete analysis, we suggest: N.Mazzoni, M.Ranieri, J.Figuriello; MiCAR The EU Approach to Crypto-Asset Regulation; JiT; March 2025 DORA as ESAs and, in particular, EBA Priority in 2025 Introduction 1/4 Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 6 6 C o p y r i g h t © In January 2025, the ESAs published a joint report, under DORA Art. 21, evaluating the feasibility of further centralizing the reporting of major ICT-related incidents. In collaboration with NCAs, the ECB, and ENISA, the report assessed three possible models of increasing centralization, including a fully centralized EU Hub Baseline Data Sharing Centralizied (EU Centrlized HUB) The Baseline Scenario, mandated by DORA from January 2025, is a decentralized model in which FEs report major ICT incidents to their NCAs, who then forward the information to EU-level bodies via a shared platform (ESAs System ) FEs notify NCAs as outlined in the Baseline Scenario, but instead of directly sharing data with stakeholders, NCAs forward the relevant information to a centralized hub that acts as a coordination mechanism, distributing data to all stakeholders FEs report directly to a centralized hub, which will ensure the distribution and availability of data to all relevant stakeholders. The tool will embed advanced analytical features to support supervisory analysis and follow-ups Pro Cons Feasibility The baseline scenario is already under development and should be considered the starting point if any further process implementations is being defined The study has confirmed the feasibility of the Data Sharing model with an elapsed time for its development, if chosen to proceed further, defined in no less than 3 years The study has confirmed the feasibility of the Centralized model with an elapsed time for its development, if chosen to proceed further, defined in no less than 5 years • No DORA amendment required • Low single-point of failure risk due to the distribution of data across multiple nodes (FE, NCA, Eu-Bodies) • Proliferation of data flow • Potential slow response time • Limited aggregate analytical capacity at the EU level • Higher long-term maintenance costs • Enhance the baseline scenario structure without modifying the core architecture (FE-NCA-UE Bodies) • Minimum adjustment required to DORA Art.19 • Presents the same cons and risks of the baseline scenario but on a lower level • Do not represent a full centralized HUB • Enhanced EU-level cybersecurity coordination and response • High standardization and limited data collection delays and inconsistency • Low incident response rate • Requires amendment to DORA Art.19 and to ICT forms, templates, and procedures • Requires commitment of all the stakeholders to be developed • High risk of data concentration Focus - Feasibility on Further Centralization of Major ICT-Related Incident Reporting Introduction 2/4 Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 7 7 C o p y r i g h t © 2 0 2 4 -A l l r i g h t s r e s e r v e d The relevance of DORA implementation to the EU’s plans for developing innovative and resilient financial markets is also reflected in the EBA and ECB (SSM) strategic priorities for 2025–2027, as outlined in its latest Single Programming Document (SPD) Finalise and implement an effective and proportionate Single Rulebook 01 Foster financial stability in an economy transitioning towards sustainability 02 05 Enable an integrated reporting system for enhanced assessment and disclosure 03 The ECB’s strategic plan for the next three years regarding DORA includes the following goals: • Collecting data on third-party ICT providers to identify links between supervised entities and third-party providers, potential concentration risks, and weaknesses in banks’ outsourcing arrangements • Conducting targeted reviews of risk management frameworks for outsourcing risks, as well as of cyber resilience frameworks and risk controls • Following up on findings from the cyber resilience stress test • Carrying out targeted OSIs on operational risk and IT resilience frameworks • Integrating the implementation of DORA into the supervisory framework Implement DORA oversight and MiCAR supervision 04 Focus on innovation for the benefit of consumers, and ensure a smooth transition to the new AML/CFT framework EBA & ECB Priorities 2025-2027 Introduction 3/4 Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 8 The Regulatory Timeline Introduction 4/4 As of January 2025, the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) is fully applicable across the EU, establishing harmonized requirements for managing ICT risks, reporting incidents, and ensuring operational continuity. DORA was first introduced in 2020 as part of the Digital Finance Package and was formally adopted in 2022, with two key RTS and ITS packages published in 2024 Sept 2020 Dec 2022 Jan 2023 Sept 2023 July 2024 Jan 2025 The European Commission proposed DORA as part of the Digital Finance Package, aiming to create a harmonized regulatory framework for ICT risk management in the financial sector The European Parliament and the Council formally adopt Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, establishing DORA The regulation goes into effect, initiating a two-year transition period for financial entities to adjust to the new requirements The first package of technical specifications (RTS and ITS) from the DORA regulation is published by ESAs The second package of technical specifications (RTS and ITS) from the DORA regulation is published by ESAs DORA becomes fully applicable. As of this date, all subject entities must comply with the regulatory requirements Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 02 Key Areas DORA – Five Keys Area ICT Risk Management ICT-related Incident Management, Classification and Reporting Digital Operational Resilience Testing Managing of ICT Third-party Risk Information-sharing Arrangements Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 10 DORA - Five Key Areas Key Areas 1/6 DORA is built around five key areas that form the foundation of a harmonized regulatory framework for managing ICT and cyber risk within the EU financial sector. It sets out comprehensive rules for ICT risk management, requiring financial entities and critical third-party ICT service providers to adopt robust cybersecurity measures, implement structured incident reporting processes, conduct regular resilience testing, and ensure effective third-party risk management ICT Risk Management ICT-related Incident Management, Classification, Reporting Digital Operational Resilience Testing Managing of ICT Third-party Risk (TPR) Information Sharing Arrangements • Financial institutions will be required to set up and maintain resilient ICT systems and implement comprehensive business continuity policies • Institutions will need to ensure they are monitoring risks emanating from the reliance on critical providers Financial institutions will be required to establish and implement a management process to monitor and log ICT-related incidents, be able to classify the incident according to the criteria detailed, and ensure reporting of incidents to the relevant authorities Elements within the ICT risk management framework should be periodically tested for preparedness. Any weaknesses, deficiencies, or gaps must be identified and promptly eliminated Financial institutions will be required to demonstrate robust controls around TPR management: o Defining a strategy and associated policy o Conducting due diligence and risk assessments on critical providers o Creating a mapping between critical providers and the business functions that they support • Financial institutions should conduct information sharing with regulators and other financial institutions • This will support early identification of new threats across the industry, allow financial institutions to implement mitigating controls, and help reduce the impact of threats to all financial institutions Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 11 ICT Risk Management Key Areas 2/6 DORA Regulation Technical Standards (EBA) Under DORA, financial entities are required to establish an internal governance and control framework that ensures the effective management of ICT risk, to achieve a high level of digital operational resilience In the context of increasing digitalization, financial entities are expected to uphold high standards of digital operational resilience. This involves not only protecting their ICT infrastructure but also ensuring continuity and trust in their services, as cited in the regulations in Art. 5 to 11. The key areas of focus can be summarized as follows: • Governance and Responsibility: Institutions must establish solid internal governance for ICT risk. The management body is responsible for setting strategies, approving policies, and coordinating ICT functions • ICT Risk Management: A complete and up-to-date risk management framework is essential, with clearly defined roles and continuous monitoring of ICT risks and assets • Operational Resilience: Entities must detect anomalies quickly, maintain business continuity through backup and recovery plans, monitor systems constantly, and communicate clearly during ICT incidents The RTS, formally adopted by the European Commission in January 2024, provides a framework to ensure that all financial entities can effectively manage ICT risks and maintain operational resilience. They establish detailed requirements for financial entities in order to develop the ICT Risk Management Framework and the Simplified ICT Risk Management Framework.
• ICT Risk Management Framework: o ICT Security Policies and Controls: Financial institutions are required to establish robust policies and procedures to ensure the security and resilience of their ICT systems o Human Resources and Access Management: It is needed to define roles and responsibilities related to ICT security and to manage user identities and access rights o Incident Detection and Response: Institutions must be able to detect anomalous activities and potential threats and to define clear criteria for triggering incident response processes o Business Continuity and Recovery: The RTS requires a comprehensive ICT business continuity policy and recovery plans to ensure operational resilience o Reporting and Review: periodically review their ICTRMF and submit reports to the proper authorities • Simplified ICT Risk Management Framework (SICTRMF): o Governance and Risk Management: Focus on assigning responsibilities, defining a security policy, and managing ICT risks based on the entity’s size and complexity o Systems, protocols, and tools to minimize the impact of ICT risk: Include implementing basic access controls, monitoring systems, protecting data, and ensuring secure operations o Business continuity management: Simplified business continuity plan tailored to the entity’s size and risk profile o Reporting: Financial entities must produce a concise report on the review of the process application Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 12 ICT-related Incident Management, Classification, Reporting Key Areas 3/6 Financial institutions are required to define, establish, and implement an ICT incident management process to ensure the timely detection, effective handling, and appropriate reporting of ICT-related incidents DORA Regulation Technical Standards (EBA) Financial institutions must implement a clear and structured ICT incident management process to detect, handle, and report incidents effectively, as cited in the regulations in articles 12-16-23-24. This includes defining roles, responsibilities, and procedures to minimize impact, ensure service continuity, and protect customer trust.
Incidents must be classified based on factors such as customer impact, duration, data loss, and financial consequences. Significant incidents must be reported to the relevant authorities, and they must be informed promptly along with the mitigation measures taken.
Authorities are expected to provide timely feedback or guidance to help institutions strengthen their response capabilities. However, financial entities remain fully accountable for managing and reporting ICT incidents. European supervisory bodies may also issue alerts and compile statistics to support broader risk and vulnerability assessments across the industry Through the adoption of RTS and ITS (July 2024), a clear structure has been defined to support financial institutions in ensuring consistency in how ICT-related incidents are identified, documented, and communicated, so that responses are timely and coordinated across the sector.
The RTS had defined: • What kind of incidents must be reported, focusing on those that are significant in terms of impact on operations, data integrity, or customer trust • When these incidents must be reported, set clear timelines for: o Initial Notification: Within 4 hours from the incident classification, but no later than 24 hours after the incident occurred o Intermediate Report: Within, and no later than, 72 hours from the initial notification. Financial entities must update the report once normal operations are restored o Final Reports: Within 1 month of the last intermediate report On the other hand, the ITS provided the templates and procedures that financial entities must use when submitting their reports. A major focus of the ITS is usability, clarifying also how to submit reports, including through which channels and in what structure, making the process more streamlined and less prone to errors. Together, the RTS and ITS create a harmonized framework that improves the EU’s ability to monitor and respond to digital threats in the financial sector. They also help financial entities by providing clear expectations and reducing uncertainty about compliance Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 13 Digital Operational Resilience Testing Key Areas 4/6 Under DORA, financial entities must define and implement a structured Digital Operational Resilience Testing program that includes a comprehensive set of assessments, tests, methodologies, practices, and tools DORA Regulation Technical Standards (EBA) Financial institutions are required to implement a structured Digital Operational Resilience Testing program to assess their ICT systems, as per DORA Art. 25, 26, 43, 44. Testing must be conducted by independent parties following defined procedures to classify and address identified vulnerabilities. Internal validation processes are necessary to ensure that all weaknesses are effectively remediated. The testing program must encompass a variety of assessments, including vulnerability scans, penetration tests, and performance evaluations, all tailored to the institution’s specific risk profile. For systemically important institutions, TLPT is mandatory at least once every three years. These advanced tests simulate real-world cyberattacks on live systems and require validation by the relevant supervisory authorities.
TLPT must be performed by independent, highly qualified, ethically responsible, and insured testers. When external providers are engaged, institutions must ensure that data security is maintained throughout the testing process The primary goal of the RTS for Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT), adopted by the European Commission in July 2024, is to define a harmonized methodology and set of requirements for TLPT. Unlike routine security assessments, TLPT involves intelligence-driven simulations that replicate the tactics of real-world cyber attacks. The objective is to rigorously assess an institution’s ability to detect, respond to, and recover from sophisticated attacks that could compromise critical systems or data. These extensive TLPTs are required only for financial entities classified as significant by their NCA. The framework requires the simulation of real-world attacks on an institution's live production systems, involving not only technology but also people and processes, and follows a three-phase approach: • Preparation Phase: The scope and critical functions to be tested are defined. The financial entity must submit the scope to its NCA for approval before the test can begin • Test Phase: The test is executed on live systems. Different teams with different scopes are involved (attackers, defenders, and controllers) • Closure Phase: The results are analyzed, and a recovery plan is prepared based on the findings. Both the plan and a test summary must be submitted to the NCA The RTS also sets conditions for the testers, who must be independent, technically skilled, and bound by strict confidentiality obligations. If a critical function relies on third-party services (e.g. cloud or SaaS providers), then that third-party service must be included in the scope of the TLPT.
The RTS establishes that a TLPT conducted by a cross-border financial entity under the supervision of one EU authority must be recognized as valid by authorities in all other EU member states where it operates Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 14 Managing of ICT Third-party Risk Key Areas 5/6 The management of third-party risk under DORA requires the establishment of a comprehensive system to anticipate, respond to, and recover from ICT-related incidents. This system aims to ensure the operational resilience of financial institutions, safeguard them against cyber threats, and guarantee compliance with regulatory requirements. Aligned to DORA’s principles, ESMA published in June 2025 a cross-sectoral third-party risk management framework DORA Regulation Technical Standards (EBA) Financial entities must maintain and update a record of information relating to all contractual arrangements, distinguishing those that cover ICT services supporting critical functions from those that do not. Financial entities shall communicate to competent authorities at least annually the number, categories, type of contractual arrangements, and ICT services and functions provided.
Before entering into a contractual agreement on the use of ICT services, financial entities must: • Identify and assess conflicts of interest that the contractual agreement may cause, as cited in Chapter V, Art. 28 • Undertake all due diligence on potential third-party ICT service providers (Chapter V, Art. 28-29) • Identify and assess all relevant risks in relation to the contractual agreement, as regulated in Chapter V, Art. 28-30 • Assess whether the contractual agreement covers the use of ICT services in support of a critical or important function (Chapter V, Art. 31) The Regulatory Technical Standards, approved by the European Commission in January 2024, define specific parameters for ICT risk management, incident communication, digital operational resilience, and the management of ICT third-party vendors.
Specifically, the main DORA RTS regarding third-party ICT risk management focuses on: • Contractual agreements: Establishing clear contractual arrangements with external ICT service providers that define responsibilities and security requirements • Control: Continuously monitoring the performance of external suppliers and their capability to manage risks effectively • Monitoring and supervision: Implementing systems to supervise external suppliers and ensure their compliance with applicable regulations A key requirement introduced by the RTS is the maintenance and regular updating of a Register of information related to contracts for ICT services provided by third parties. This register must include: • Relevant details on all ICT services supplied by direct third-party providers • Information on all subcontractors significantly involved in delivering ICT services • Specifics of the contractual agreements governing the use of these services On 21 January 2025, the European Commission informed the European Supervisory Authorities that it had rejected the initial proposal for RTS concerning the procurement and subcontracting of external suppliers providing critical ICT services. The proposal has since been updated and is currently under review by the European Commission Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 15 Information-Sharing Arrangements Key Areas 6/6 The information sharing arrangements in the DORA regulation are essential tools for strengthening the financial sector's resilience to cyber risks. These agreements allow financial institutions to share information about cyber threats, increasing awareness and preparedness of all actors in the sector DORA Regulation Technical Standards Financial entities may exchange amongst themselves cyber threat information and intelligence, including indicators of compromise, procedures, cybersecurity alerts, and configuration tools, as defined under DORA’s Chapter VI, Art. 45. The Arrangements for the exchange of information and experience relating to ICT security must: • Take place within trusted communities of FEs • Enhance the digital operational resilience by reducing threat spread capacity, increasing threat identification methodologies • Be implemented through information-sharing arrangements that protect the potentially sensitive nature of the information shared Financial entities shall notify NCAs of their participation in the information-sharing arrangements upon validation of their membership. The intent is to create networks for sharing details on threats and vulnerabilities to organize collective exercises and simulations, and use shared information to enhance security protocols The ESAs have not issued specific Regulatory Technical Standards regarding Information Sharing Arrangements, as the DORA Regulation already outlines the core principles governing the exchange of information between financial entities and ICT service providers. Art. 45 of DORA sets out detailed guidelines for the proper management and sharing of information related to ICT risks.
Key aspects of Information Sharing Arrangements include: • Notification to Authorities: Financial entities are mandated to notify their competent authorities of their participation in any such agreement • Exchange of threat intelligence: Agreements may involve the exchange of cyber threat intelligence, including indicators of compromise (IOCs), tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), early warning signals, and secure configuration tools • Involvement of third-party providers: The agreements may include the involvement of ICT) service providers and how public authorities are involved • Data protection measures: Financial entities must implement measures to protect data during its transmission, ensuring its availability, authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality These Information Sharing Arrangements, as established by DORA, serve as a strategic tool to enhance the cybersecurity posture of the financial sector. They enable institutions to share relevant threat intelligence and provide a structured framework for managing ICT risks collectively Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 03 Regulatory Enforcement Supervisory Framework The Lead Overseer Enforcement Regime & Italian law DORA and AI Act Considerations Conclusions Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 17 Regulatory Enforcement 1/4 Supervisory Framework The DORA supervisory framework is structured to ensure a complementary division of responsibilities between the ESAs and the NCAs. The ESAs are responsible for overseeing the consistent application of DORA by NCAs, directly supervising CTPPs, and developing and implementing regulatory and technical standards. Meanwhile, NCAs are in charge of supervising financial entities’ compliance with DORA’s requirements on risk management, ICT-related incident reporting, and digital operational resilience at the national level Entities Roles ESAs NCAs Oversight Forum • EBA - European Banking Authority • ESMA -European Securities and Markets Authority • EIOPA - European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority National Competent Authorities are the designated regulators in each EU member state responsible for enforcing the regulation and ensuring compliance within their jurisdiction.
Italian designated NCAs: • Bank of Italy • CONSOB • IVASS • COVIP Defined under DORA’s Art.32, as a subcommittee of the ESAs Joint Committee, it comprises: • ESAs Chairpersons • One senior representative from each NCA • ESAs Executive Directors • Observers from the European Commission, ESRB, ECB, and ENISA • If needed, Independent experts may be invited • Develop RTS and ITS jointly with the European Commission • Direct oversight of Critical Third-Party ICT Providers (CTPPs) through the Lead Overseer mechanism • Coordinate and oversee consistent application of DORA across NCAs • Define criteria for advanced TLPT • Issue guidelines and recommendations to promote supervisory convergence • Supervise financial entities with the ability to impose corrective measures and fees on financial entities • Review and assess ICT third-party risk management strategies • Oversight of TLPT • ICT Incident reporting assessment, classification, and information sharing with ESA • Facilitate regulatory coordination among supervisory bodies • Conducts an annual collective assessment of the outcomes and findings from the supervisory activities on all CTPPs • Provide information or advice in the context of the exercise of the LO’s powers or about opinions to NCAs where a CTPP refuses to endorse recommendations Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 18 Under DORA, the Lead Overseer is a designated authority from one of the three ESAs that may be appointed as the Lead Overseer for specific Critical ICT Third-Party Providers (CTPPs) that are external technology providers whose services are essential to the functioning of financial institutions across the EU Regulatory Enforcement 2/4 The Lead Overseer The Lead Overseer is not a traditional supervisory body. Instead, it acts as a centralized EU-level authority responsible for: • Monitoring systemic ICT risks posed by CTPPs to the financial sector • Ensuring harmonized oversight across all EU member states • Acting as the single point of contact for the oversight of each designated CTPP This role is crucial because many financial institutions rely on the same few large ICT providers (e.g. cloud platforms), which creates concentration risk. A failure in one provider could impact multiple institutions simultaneously Oversight Planning and Execution Develop an annual oversight plan for each CTPP, tailored to the provider’s risk profile and service criticality. Define supervisory priorities, including areas of concern such as cybersecurity, data integrity, and operational continuity Risk Assessment Evaluate whether the provider has robust, effective, and sound mechanisms to manage ICT risks. Focus on services that support critical functions of financial entities. Extend the assessment to non-critical services if necessary to address broader risks On-site and Off-site Inspections Perform off-site reviews of documentation and systems. Conduct on-site inspections at data centers or operational hubs, often in collaboration with NCAs and the EU cybersecurity agency (ENISA) Coordination with National Supervisors Work closely with NCAs, who are responsible for ensuring that financial entities respond appropriately to the Lead Overseer’s findings. Facilitate cross-border cooperation and information sharing to ensure consistent application of DORA across the EU The Lead Overseer Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 19 Unlike other EU regulatory frameworks that provide for specific and harmonised sanction regimes, DORA employs a two-tiered approach: it sets out common principles and guiding directives at the EU level but delegates the responsibility of defining the precise thresholds and specifications of penalties to the individual Member States and their National Competent Authorities Regulatory Enforcement 3/4 Enforcement Regime & Italian law DORA Common Principles Under Art.50, 51, 52, 53, 54, DORA requires Member States to empower NCAs with at least the following enforcement powers: • Have access to any document or data held in any form that the competent authority considers relevant for the performance of its duties, and receive or take a copy of it • Carry out on-site inspections or investigations, which shall include but shall not be limited to • Require corrective and remedial measures for breaches of the requirements of this Regulation • Lay down rules establishing appropriate administrative penalties and remedial measures for breaches (that shall be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive) Member States may choose not to establish administrative penalties for breaches already subject to criminal sanctions under national law. However, if they decide to define such sanctions, they must ensure that competent authorities have the necessary powers to cooperate with judicial and criminal justice bodies Italian Enforcement Regime Under D.Lgs. 23/2025 (March 2025), Italy aligned with DORA regulations and established the sanctioning regime, which distinguishing between severe (e.g., missing ICT risk management) and less severe (e.g. misclassified incidents) violations (the sanctions also apply to ICT providers, depending on the type of financial entities they serve): • Sever violations: o Banks: from 30K€ to 10% of the annual turnover o Other non-banking intermediary: from 30K€ to 5 Mln€ or 10% of annual turnover if > 5 Mln o CSD: from 30K€ to 20Mln€ or 10% of annual turnover if > 20€Mln o Benchmark Administrators: from 10k€ to 1Mln€ or 10% of annual turnover if > 1Mln€ o Crowdfunding providers: from 500€ to 500k€ or 5% of annual turnover if > 500K€ • Less severe violations: o Banks: from 30K€ to 7% of the annual turnover o Other non-banking intermediary: from 30K€ to 3,5Mln€ or 7% of annual turnover if > 3,5Mln€ o CSD: from 30K€ to 14Mln€ or 7% of annual turnover if > 14€Mln o Benchmark Administrators: from 10k€ to 700k€ or 7% of annual turnover if > 700K€ o Crowdfunding providers: from 500€ to 350k€ or 3,5% of annual turnover if > 350K€ Copyright © 2025 - All rights reserved 20 Regulatory Enforcement 4/4 DORA and AI Act1 Considerations To foster an environment that promotes innovation2 while safeguarding European ethical values, the European Union has enacted the AI Act (in force since August 2024, with the prohibition of “unacceptable risk” systems effective from February 2025). In this context, FIs that deploy or rely on AI systems within their IT architecture must ensure compliance with both the AI Act and the DORA Mapping When developing or acquiring an AI system that qualifies as “high-risk” under the AI Act (Art. 6), or one supporting a critical business function (DORA Art. 3), financial entities must classify it within the scope of ICT critical functions, as defined by DORA under Art. 5 and 8 Risk Management Procedures High-risk AI systems must be integrated into the financial entity’s ICT Risk Management (ICT RM) framework, as defined by DORA under Chapter 2. This includes identifying, evaluating, and mitigating not only general ICT risks, but also the specific risks posed by AI systems (AI Act Chapter 2) Incident Reporting AI-related incidents must be detected and managed within the ICT incident framework and reported to NCAs and ESAs under DORA if they qualify as major ICT-related incidents (DORA Chapter 3). If the incident concerns an in-house application developed by the financial institution, it must also be reported to the AI Market Surveillance Authority under AI Act Art. 73 Third-Party Risk Management AI providers whose systems qualify as high-risk must undergo comprehensive ICT third-party risk assessments under DORA Chapter 4 and must also comply with the obligations set out in the AI Act Chapter 3, Section 3 Testing and Auditability DORA and the AI Act both require robust testing and transparency. DORA mandates resilience testing, including TLPT for critical entities (Chapter 5), while the AI Act requires pre-deployment checks, ongoing performance monitoring, and logging for high-risk AI systems (Chapter 2). args.summary:
This presentation from iason (an international consulting firm) provides a comprehensive analysis of the EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), which came fully into effect on January 17, 2025. The document covers DORA's regulatory framework, key implementation areas, and enforcement mechanisms.

**Regulatory Context and Timeline:**
- DORA, alongside MiCAR, is a key component of the EU's Digital Finance Package aimed at harmonizing ICT risk management and strengthening EU financial market resilience
- DORA was first proposed in September 2020, formally adopted in December 2022 (Regulation EU 2022/2554), with a two-year transition period. The first package of RTS/ITS technical standards was published in January 2023, the second in July 2024, and DORA became fully applicable in January 2025
- The ESAs completed a feasibility study in January 2025 on further centralizing major ICT-related incident reporting, evaluating three models: the Baseline (decentralized, already in development), a Data Sharing model (feasible, 3+ years to develop), and a fully Centralized EU Hub (feasible, 5+ years to develop, would require amending DORA Art. 19)

**The Five Key Areas of DORA:**
1. **ICT Risk Management** (Art. 5-11): Requires internal governance frameworks, comprehensive ICT risk management frameworks, and operational resilience. The RTS adopted January 2024 establishes requirements for both the ICT Risk Management Framework and a Simplified ICT Risk Management Framework (SICTRMF)
2. **Incident Management, Classification & Reporting**: Significant incidents must be reported with specific timelines - initial notification within 4 hours of classification (no later than 24 hours after incident), intermediate report within 72 hours, and final report within 1 month
3. **Digital Operational Resilience Testing**: Includes vulnerability scans, penetration tests, and TLPT (Threat-Led Penetration Testing) for systemically important institutions at least every three years. TLPT follows a three-phase approach (Preparation, Test, Closure) and must be validated by supervisory authorities
4. **Third-Party Risk Management**: Requires due diligence on ICT providers, maintaining a register of all ICT contracts (including subcontractors), and annual communication to authorities. ESMA published a cross-sectoral third-party risk framework in June 2025. Notably, the European Commission rejected the initial RTS proposal on procurement of critical ICT services on January 21, 2025
5. **Information-Sharing Arrangements** (Art. 45): Financial entities may exchange threat intelligence within trusted communities, must notify NCAs of participation, and must protect data availability, authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality

**Regulatory Enforcement:**
- The supervisory framework divides responsibilities between ESAs (overseeing CTPPs, developing technical standards) and NCAs (national supervision). An Oversight Forum (Art. 32) coordinates among ESAs, NCAs, and EU bodies
- The Lead Overseer is a centralized EU authority monitoring systemic ICT risks posed by Critical Third-Party ICT Providers (CTPPs), addressing concentration risk from large providers like cloud platforms
- DORA uses a two-tiered enforcement approach: common principles at EU level (Art. 50-54), with Member States defining specific penalties. Italy aligned through D.Lgs. 23/2025 (March 2025), distinguishing severe violations (e.g., banks: €30K to 10% of annual turnover) and less severe violations (e.g., banks: €30K to 7% of turnover)

**DORA and AI Act Considerations:**
- Financial entities using AI systems must ensure compliance with both the AI Act and DORA. High-risk AI systems must be integrated into the ICT Risk Management framework, AI-related incidents reported under DORA, and AI providers subject to third-party risk assessments. Both regulations require robust testing and auditability (TLPT under DORA; pre-deployment checks and monitoring under AI Act Art. 73)

**Final Remarks:** DORA aims to harmonize ICT risk management across EU states, strengthen digital resilience, and safeguard customer trust. Compliance requires establishing strong ICT governance, developing comprehensive risk management frameworks, ensuring incident detection and reporting capabilities, conducting regular resilience testing, and managing third-party risks through contractual safeguards and continuous oversight.

# NHS patients notified 18 months after ransomware exposed medical test data

Lusanda Molefe

November 18, 2025

![blood test tube ](https://www.paubox.com/hubfs/NHS%20patients%20notified%2018%20months%20after%20ransomware%20exposed%20medical%20test%20data.jpg)

NHS pathology provider Synnovis has finally begun notifying healthcare organizations about a data breach that exposed sensitive patient information, including sexually transmitted infection and cancer test results, 18 months after a Qilin ransomware attack crippled London hospitals in June 2024. 

### What happened

On June 3, 2024, Synnovis, a pathology partnership between Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, and international diagnostics provider SYNLAB, suffered a [ransomware attack](https://www.theregister.com/2025/11/13/synnovis_qilin_investigation/) that impacted nearly all of its IT systems. The attack, attributed to the Qilin ransomware gang, severely disrupted pathology services across London and forced the cancellation of more than 10,000 acute outpatient appointments and over 1,700 elective operations.

The incident created critical blood supply shortages as hospitals could not process urgent blood tests, and King's College Hospital NHS Trust confirmed in June 2025 that the disruption contributed to at least one patient death, marking one of the rare documented cases where ransomware has been directly linked to a fatality.

On June 20, 2024, Qilin published approximately 400GB of stolen data on its dark web leak site after Synnovis refused ransom demands. Security firm CaseMatrix analyzed the published material and estimated that data relating to more than 900,000 NHS patients was exposed, though Synnovis has neither confirmed nor disputed that figure.

The compromised information includes patient names, NHS identification numbers, dates of birth, and in some cases, detailed test results that could be matched to specific individuals. The most sensitive information identified by analysts includes pathology and histology forms describing symptoms of intimate medical conditions, including sexually transmitted infections and cancer diagnoses.

On November 10, 2025, more than 17 months after the initial attack, Synnovis [announced](https://synnoviscyberupdate.co.uk/) it had completed its forensic investigation and begun notifying affected NHS organizations. Under UK data protection law, Synnovis acts as a data processor while the individual NHS hospitals and clinics function as data controllers, meaning the healthcare providers themselves must determine whether patient notification is necessary and carry out those notifications directly.

### Why it matters

Synnovis attributed the prolonged investigation timeline to "exceptional scale and complexity," explaining that "the compromised data was unstructured, incomplete and fragmented, and often very difficult to understand." The company [stated](https://www.synnovis.co.uk/news-and-press/synnovis-completes-forensic-review-following-2024-cyberattack) that forensic experts "had to use highly specialized platforms and bespoke processes to piece it together" after attackers stole data "in haste and in a random manner from Synnovis' working drives."

However, cybersecurity experts have sharply criticized the delay. "The human impact, including a patient death and severe service interruptions, far surpasses the complexities of the forensic investigation," [said](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/synnovis-breach-notification-2024/) Damon Small, a board member at security firm Xcape. "When a vendor fails, the clock on patient safety and privacy must start immediately, not 17 months later."

Denis Calderone, COO at security company Suzu, [argued](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/synnovis-breach-notification-2024/) that data management failures, not investigation complexity, drove the delay, "Unstructured and fragmented data isn't a valid excuse; it's evidence of inadequate data management. If you can't quickly identify compromised information, you've fundamentally failed basic data governance."

The breach also illustrates vulnerabilities in healthcare supply chain relationships. Synnovis functions similarly to a HIPAA business associate in the US context, a third-party service provider that processes protected health information on behalf of covered entities. When business associates suffer breaches, the regulatory and notification obligations flow back to the covered entities, but patients remain vulnerable throughout the investigation period.

### The big picture

The Qilin ransomware operation has established itself as a significant threat to healthcare organizations globally. Operating as a Ransomware-as-a-Service platform, Qilin has claimed responsibility for more than 300 victims since emerging in August 2022. The group employs double-extortion tactics, stealing data before encrypting systems, then threatening to publish stolen information if ransom demands are not met.

Synnovis's forensic investigation revealed that attackers did not breach the company's primary laboratory database. Instead, they grabbed whatever files they could access during the intrusion from working drives. This opportunistic approach resulted in the "unstructured, incomplete and fragmented" dataset that Synnovis says required specialized reconstruction efforts.

The company emphasized that stolen data "has never been available in a form that could easily be used by anyone with ill intent," though cybersecurity experts note that even partial medical information becomes valuable when combined with data from other breaches. Foreign intelligence services and sophisticated criminal operations routinely aggregate information from multiple sources to build comprehensive profiles for espionage, fraud, or targeted attacks.

Synnovis secured a legal injunction prohibiting further publication or use of the stolen data, though such orders provide limited practical protection once information circulates in criminal forums. The company stated there is "no evidence that Qilin's interest in its business, or the stolen data, was ongoing" and claimed no evidence suggests the compromised data has been misused against individuals, though proving a negative remains difficult when stolen data trades hands in underground markets.

### FAQs

#### What is the difference between a data processor and a data controller?

Under UK data protection law (and similarly under GDPR), a data controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data, while a data processor handles data on the controller's behalf. In the Synnovis case, NHS hospitals and clinics are data controllers because they decide how patient data is used for healthcare delivery, while Synnovis is a data processor that runs laboratory tests according to the hospitals' instructions. This distinction matters for breach notification because controllers, not processors, must decide whether to notify affected individuals.

#### What does Ransomware-as-a-Service mean?

Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) is a business model where ransomware developers create the malicious software and provide it to affiliates who conduct the actual attacks, with profits split between developers and affiliates. This model, used by groups like Qilin, lowers barriers to entry for cybercriminals who lack the technical skills to develop ransomware themselves. RaaS operations often include customer support, negotiation services, and payment infrastructure, functioning like legitimate software companies but for criminal purposes.

#### What is double-extortion ransomware?

Double-extortion ransomware involves two threats: attackers encrypt victims' systems (preventing access to data) and separately threaten to publish stolen data online if ransom demands aren't met.

# NHS Pathology Provider Synnovis Notifies Organizations Affected by June 2024 Ransomware Attack

Posted By [Steve Alder](https://www.hipaajournal.com/author/hipaajournal/ "Posts by Steve Alder") on Nov 12, 2025

The UK pathology lab Synnovis suffered a ransomware attack last year. It has taken 17 months to complete the highly complex data review and notify the affected healthcare provider clients.

Synnovis provides blood, urine, and specimen testing for many healthcare organizations in the United Kingdom and has a pathology partnership with Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust and King’s College Hospitals NHS Trust in London, and SYNLANB, a provider of laboratory, diagnostic, and advisory services.

The ransomware attack occurred on June 3, 2024, when the Qilin ransomware group encrypted files on its network. Prior to encrypting files from its network, data was exfiltrated from its network. The ransomware attack caused massive disruption to business operations at Synnovis, interrupting many of its pathology services. Synnovis said that almost all of its IT systems were affected.

NHS trusts that relied on Synnovis for blood testing and other services were forced to cancel appointments, and the lack of blood testing led to a shortage of O-negative blood. The shortage continued for months, with stocks depleted across the country. Disruption to patient services was extensive, with more than 10,000 appointments cancelled in the wake of the attack.

Synnovis immediately launched an investigation and assembled a task force of experts from Synnovis, the affected NHS Trusts, NHS England, and third-party specialists to restore systems and data as quickly as possible. The UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA), the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), and the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) were notified, and Synnovis has been working closely with those agencies throughout the recovery process.

It took until late autumn 2024 to replace all of the affected IT infrastructure and restore systems and services to pre-attack operational levels. “By month four immediately after the cyberattack, we had rebuilt a new blood transfusion platform, by month five we had completed a substantial cloud migration of our core systems, and by November 2024 we had rebuilt over 75 applications and reconnected a vast pathology estate spanning seven locations from the ground up, including over 65 scientific analyzers and more than 120 individual connections”, explained Synnovis.

Determining which organizations and individuals had been affected and the data types involved has taken considerably longer. Synnovis explained that the ransomware group stole data in haste in a random manner from its working drives, and due to the exceptional scale and complexity of the data review, it has taken more than a year to complete. That process required bespoke systems and processes to be created to reconstruct the affected data.

Synnovis said the forensic analysis confirmed that no data was taken from its primary lab databases, and the data exfiltrated in the attack was not in a form that could easily be used by anyone with ill intent”. Despite an extensive forensic investigation, it was not possible to determine how the ransomware group gained access to its network. All IT infrastructure impacted by the attack was completely replaced.

Synnovis said it consulted with its affected NHS trust partners, and the decision was taken not to pay the ransom. Doing so would have gone against its ethical principles, and the ransom would undoubtedly have been used to fund further attacks on other critical infrastructure entities, potentially threatening national security. The amount demanded by the ransomware group was not disclosed.

Synnovis has recently completed the data analysis and restoration, and the affected organizations are now being notified. Notifications will be completed by November 21, 2025, after which the affected organizations will decide whether notifications need to be issued to the affected patients under UK data protection laws. Synnovis stressed that the company will not be contacting any of the affected patients directly. Under UK data protection laws, it is down to the data controller to conduct their own legal and risk assessments to determine whether notifications are required. Any individual receiving a communication about the data breach that purports to have come directly from Synnovis rather than one of the affected organizations should assume it is a scam.

The incident clearly demonstrates the massive impact ransomware attacks can have on critical infrastructure. In this case, this was a calculated attack designed to cause as much damage and disruption as possible for financial gain.

## June 22, 2024: Ransomware Group Leaks Data from 300 Million Patient Interactions with NHS

The Russian ransomware and extortion group Qilin has added the data stolen in the attack on Synnovis to its dark web data leak site after the deadline for paying the $50 million ransom demand expired.

Synovis, a provider of pathology services to the UK’s National Health Service (NHS), was attacked by the Qilin ransomware group on June 3, 2024, resulting in disruption to many of its services. Multiple NHS trusts in London continue to be affected by the attack, with the recovery expected to take several weeks. Synnovis does not anticipate fully recovering from the attack for several months.

Two of the worst-affected NHS trusts were the King’s College Hospital Foundation Trust and Guy’s and St Thomas’ Foundation Trust, two of the busiest NHS trusts in the country. The attack affected 7 hospitals operated by those trusts, forcing them to cancel 1,134 planned operations and 2,194 outpatient appointments in the first 13 days following the attack. Blood tests in the capital are operating at around 10% of normal levels.

As is typical in ransomware attacks, Qilin exfiltrated data before encrypting files. In the early hours of Friday morning, Qilin uploaded 400 GB of confidential data to its dark web data leak site, where it can be freely downloaded by cybercriminals. The uploaded data includes information from more than 300 million patient interactions with the NHS. The data upload is currently being verified but it appears to be genuine.

The data contains personally identifying information and blood test results, including highly sensitive test results for HIV, sexually transmitted infections, and cancer. It is likely to take several weeks before the exact types of data and the number of affected individuals are known due to the scale of the data theft. The data breach does not appear to be limited to NHS patients. Synnovis also provides pathology services to private healthcare providers, and some of the stolen data is understood to include private healthcare records.

The affected patients may now be subjected to extortion attempts due to the sensitivity of some of the stolen data. For instance, cybercriminals could threaten patients who tested positive for HIV by making that information public if they do not pay to have their data deleted.

The UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) and the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) are currently considering taking retaliatory action against the hacking group. Since this was an attack that affected the NHS and included the theft of NHS data, the attack is effectively an attack on the state. One of the main priorities is to try to take down as much of the uploaded data as possible.

The NCA recently headed an international law enforcement operation against the LockBit ransomware group that resulted in the seizure of its command and control infrastructure in February 2024. While the operation was a success, it was short-lived. The LockBit infrastructure was rapidly rebuilt, and the group was able to continue its operations. According to a recent report from NCC Group, LockBit was the most active ransomware group in May 2024.

## June 18, 2024: More Than 1,500 Appointments Cancelled Following Ransomware Attack on NHS Pathology Vendor

At least 1,500 operations and outpatient appointments had to be canceled at two NHS trusts – King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust – following the ransomware attack on Synnovis. The affected NHS hospitals remain open and are continuing to provide care as normal; however, appointments have been postponed that rely heavily on pathology services, and blood testing is being prioritized for the most serious cases. For instance, many individuals have had phlebotomy appointments canceled. The canceled appointments included more than 100 cancer treatments and 18 organ transplants.

That number is likely to grow considerably as other NHS trusts were also affected by the attack, and the 1,500 canceled appointments were only for the period from 3-9 June.Synnovis is expecting to be able to restore some of its IT functionality in the coming weeks but anticipates that disruption will likely continue to be experienced for several months.

The attack is continuing to disrupt blood-matching tests, which has forced the affected hospitals to use O Negative and O Positive blood for patients who can’t wait for alternative matching methods. That has led to a shortage of O-type blood, with the NHS responding to the shortage by calling for the public to urgently arrange blood donation appointments across the country, with the high demand likely to continue for several weeks.

The Qilin ransomware group behind the attack told Bloomberg that they demanded a $50 million ransom payment and required payment to be made within 120 hours. They also claimed to have gained access to the Synnovis network by exploiting a zero-day vulnerability, although they did not state what vulnerability they exploited. The Qilin group has yet to add Synnovis to its data leak site, which could indicate Synnovis is negotiating with the group.

## June 5, 2024: Care Disrupted at London Hospitals Due to Ransomware Attack on Pathology Vendor

A ransomware attack on a UK-based provider of medical laboratory services is disrupting patient services at multiple NHS hospitals in London, including Guy’s Hospital, St Thomas’ Hospital, King’s College Hospital, Royal Brompton Hospital, Evelina London Children’s Hospital, and other care sites in six London boroughs – Bexley, Greenwich, Lewisham, Bromley, Southwark, and Lambeth. The attack has had a much wider impact than initially thought, with the South London and the Maudsley (Slam) trust also affected, the largest provider of mental health services in the country, and GP surgeries throughout South London.

Synnovis, a provider of diagnostic and pathology services, published an alert on its customer service portal on Monday, warning that all of its systems are currently unavailable. An investigation has been launched, and its IT team is trying to determine the cause of the outage. The attack has now been linked to a Russian cybercriminal group called Qilin, which is known for using ransomware to encrypt files on victims’ networks and demanding ransom payments to decrypt files and prevent the release of stolen data. The attack appears to be confined to Synnovis. Hospitals connected to the IT systems of Synnovis do not appear to have had their own systems infiltrated.

On Monday, Synnovis notified the affected NHS Trusts that it had experienced a malware attack, and later confirmed in email messages that it was a ransomware attack. A critical incident emergency status has been declared in the region. Synnovis is working with the National Cyber Security Centre and the Cyber Operations Team to investigate and recover from the attack, but cannot yet say how long its systems will be offline.

The affected hospitals have tried and tested business continuity plans for critical incidents such as ransomware attacks, and they are continuing to provide care for patients, although the attack is having a significant impact on the delivery of services at the affected hospitals. Emergency services are still available, but the hospitals have lost pathology services, cannot perform quick-turnaround blood tests, and blood transfusions are particularly affected, so much so that a nationwide appeal has been launched by the NHS for O blood-type donors.

As a result, all non-emergency pathology appointments have been canceled or redirected to other hospitals, and hospital staff have been instructed only to request emergency blood samples. Synnovis can still conduct blood tests, but the results are being printed out when obtained from its laboratories, and they are being hand-delivered, as the lack of access to computer systems is preventing electronic transmission.

One of the problems with an attack such as this is that until it can be determined exactly what the hackers have done while inside the compromised systems, data cannot be trusted. The hackers could have manipulated test results on which decisions about patient care are made. As a result, test results need to be re-run and results re-recorded due to the risk of data manipulation.

According to data from the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), there have been 215 ransomware attacks on hospitals in the United Kingdom since 2019. Last year, ransomware attacks reached record levels, with at least 1,231 attacks conducted across all industry sectors in the UK. Government officials are concerned that many attacks are not being reported.

This is also not the first ransomware attack to affect Synnovis in 2024. The BlackBasta ransomware group attacked Synnovis in April this year and published all the data stolen in the attack on its leak site when the ransom was not paid. Cybercriminal groups are known to work together and provide access to compromised networks to other groups. It is unclear if the BlackBasta attack is linked to the Qilin attack.

The Administrative Requirements of the Privacy Rule (§164.530) requires covered entities to train all members of their workforces on the policies and procedures developed to comply with the Privacy and Breach Notification Rules. Naturally, the sooner training is provided, the less chance there is of an inadvertent impermissible disclosure due to a lack of knowledge. It is important to note that training must be provided even if a new member of the workforce has held a similar role in a previous position and that some states have mandatory time frames within which training must be provided (for example, in Texas, training must be provided within 90 days).

 × 

 Why is it necessary to prove the breach notification requirements are complied with? 

It is necessary to prove the breach notification requirements are complied with to ensure covered entities and business associates do not overlook notifying individuals in the required timeframe when submitting an annual breach report to HHS’ Office for Civil Rights for breaches affecting fewer than 500 individuals. Some organizations have delayed notifying individuals about data breaches, increasing the risk of individuals’ data being used to commit identity theft or fraud before individuals have the opportunity to protect themselves from such events. The burden of proof standard mitigates the likelihood of individuals being overlooked.

 Why calculate the likelihood of a notifiable breach? 

While many types of impermissible uses and disclosures, data thefts, and unauthorized access events are clearly notifiable breaches, there are also many types that are not. If it can be determined that an impermissible use or disclosure does not qualify as a notifiable breach by using the exclusion criteria in §164.402, it will not be necessary to comply with the breach notification requirements – saving organizations time and money, and a potential compliance review by HHS’ Office for Civil Rights.

 Why is it important to have an anonymous reporting channel? 

Although it is not a requirement of HIPAA to provide an anonymous reporting channel, members of the workforce should be encouraged to speak out when they believe a violation of HIPAA has occurred in order that the incident can be investigated and corrected if necessary. It is felt (although cannot not proven) that anonymous reporting channels generate more reports because members of the workforce feel protected against retaliation. However, if an anonymous reporting channel is provided, it needs to be used in compliance with HIPAA, and any PHI contained within the anonymous report has to be safeguarded against unauthorized access, loss, and theft.

 Why is it necessary to monitor business associate compliance? 

It is necessary to monitor business associate compliance because a covered entity can be held liable for a violation of HIPAA by a business associate if the covered entity “knew, or by exercising reasonable diligence, should have known” of a pattern of activity or practice of the business associate that constituted a material breach or violation of the business associate’s obligations under the HIPAA Business Associate Agreement.

 × 

 Why is it important to execute HIPAA-compliant Agreements with business associates? 

It is important to execute HIPAA-compliant Agreements with business associates because if an Agreement does not comply with the relevant standards it is invalid. If an Agreement is invalid, covered entities are not permitted to disclose PHI to the business associate, and any disclosure of this nature would represent a violation of HIPAA.

 Why is it important to identify partners and vendors that qualify as business associates? 

It is important to identify partners and vendors that qualify as business associates because when a service is provided for or on behalf of a covered entity that involves the creation, receipt, maintenance, or transmission of PHI, a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement has to be entered into which stipulates the permitted uses and disclosures of PHI by the business associate, both parties’ compliance obligations, and other terms that may apply.

 × 

 Why is it important to be able to quickly retrieve documentation? 

There are many examples of when it may be necessary to retrieve documentation within a specific timeframe to comply with HIPAA. The most common is when an individual requests access to their PHI maintained in a designated record set. Less common examples include when an individual wishes to revoke an authorization or when HHS’ Office for Civil Rights requests documentation to resolve a HIPAA complaint. In most cases, the documentation has to be provided within 30 days.

 × 

 Why is the application of sanctions important? 

The application of sanctions is important to ensure members of the workforce do not take compliance shortcuts “to get the job done”, and the shortcuts deteriorate into a culture of non-compliance. The sanctions applied should be relevant to the nature of the violation. For example, a verbal warning and/or refresher training may be appropriate for a minor violation, while repeated or more serious violations should attract harsher sanctions. The application of sanctions must be documented and records stored for at least 6 years, either physically in paper records or with HIPAA compliance software.

 × 

 Why is it important we monitor changes to transaction code systems? 

It is important for organizations to monitor changes to transaction code systems for two reasons. The first is that using out-of-date transaction codes can result in delays to (for example) authorizations and payments. The second reason is that organizations who persistently use out-of-date transaction codes can be reported to CMS – which has the authority to enforce Part 162 of HIPAA via corrective action plans and financial penalties.

 Why is it important NPIs are used correctly in Part 162 transactions? 

The National Provider Identifier identifies your organization or subparts of your organization in Part 162 transactions. It is important that NPIs are used correctly in (for example) eligibility checks and authorization requests to prevent delays in responses to requests for treatment. It is also important that NPIs are used correctly in claims and billing transactions to make sure payments are received on time.

 Why are automatic logoff capabilities important? 

Automatic logoff capabilities are important to prevent unauthorized users from accessing ePHI when a device is unattended. Additionally, if a device is lost or stolen, the device cannot be used to access ePHI without the login credentials being known and used.

 Why is it important that login credentials and passwords are not shared? 

It is important that login credentials and passwords are not shared for systems that contain ePHI because, if multiple users are using the same access credentials, it will be impossible to determine when specific users access ePHI. As well as eliminating the usefulness of audit logs and access reports, if a system has been configured to reject multiple logins using the same credentials, it could result in users being blocked from accessing ePHI when necessary, or the system being corrupted.

 Why are data backup, emergency mode, and disaster recovery plans important? 

The requirements to implement and test a data backup plan, an emergency mode operations plan, and a disaster recovery plan fall within the contingency plan standard of the Security Rule (§164.308). These requirements are designed to ensure the integrity and availability of ePHI in the event of a natural or manmade disaster.

 Why is it important that information access policies cater to changing roles and terminations? 

Information access policies should make sure that the right people have access to the right level of ePHI at the right time. This means the policies have to be sufficiently flexible to support changing roles, promotions, and time off due to (for example) a suspension or maternity leave. The policies should also include procedures for terminating access to ePHI when a member of the workforce leaves so the departing individual cannot access the organization’s ePHI remotely.

 Why is it important to have a documented security management process? 

The requirement to have a security management process is the first standard in the HIPAA Security Rule’s Administrative Safeguards. The process must consist of at least a risk analysis, an actioned remediation plan, a sanctions policy, and procedures to regularly review information system activity. All analyses, remediation plans, sanctions, and reviews must be documented. Documentation must be stored for at least 6 years, either physically on paper on via HIPAA compliance software.

 × 

 Why is it important that HIPAA Authorization Forms comply with §164.508 of the Privacy Rule? 

HIPAA Authorization Forms have to comply with §164.508 in order to be valid. If a HIPAA Authorization Form lacks the core elements or required statements, if it is difficult for the individual to understand, or if it is completed incorrectly, the authorization will be invalid and any subsequent use or disclosure of PHI made on the reliance of the authorization will be impermissible. For this reason, members of the workforce responsible for obtaining valid authorizations must be trained on the implementation specifications of this standard. HIPAA Authorization Forms must be stored for a minimum of 6 years.

 × 

 Why is it important to keep Notices of Privacy Practices compliant with §164.520? 

A HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices advises patients and plan members of their privacy rights, how the organization can use or disclose PHI, and how an individual can complain if they believe their privacy rights have been violated or their PHI has been used or disclosed impermissibly. Notices must be reviewed and amended as necessary whenever a material change affects either an individual’s rights or how PHI can be used or disclosed. They must then be re-distributed and/or re-displayed in accordance with §164.520.

 × 

 Why must members of the workforce be trained in responding to patient access and accounting requests? 

Members of the workforce must know how to respond to patient access and accounting requests – even if it is to direct the request to the HIPAA Privacy Officer – because the primary reason for complaints to HHS’ Office for Civil Rights in recent years has been the failure to respond in the time allowed with the information requested. At present, the majority of HIPAA enforcement activities focus on non-compliance with the patients’ rights standards of the HIPAA Privacy Rule.

 × 

 Why is it necessary to have procedures in place to respond to patients exercising their HIPAA rights? 

The reason it is necessary to have procedures in place to respond to patients exercising their HIPAA rights is that some rights are susceptible to exploitation. For example, procedures should be in place to verify the identity of patients, review confidentiality requests, and determine if a request is being made to support an abusive, deceptive, or harmful activity.

 Why is compliance with the minimum necessary standard important? 

The minimum necessary standard (§164.502(b) and §164.512(d)) requires that only the minimum necessary information is used or disclosed to achieve the purpose of the use or disclosure. This is to better protect the privacy of individually identifiable health information. However, the standard does not apply in every circumstance, and covered entities that apply the standard too rigidly could encounter communication challenges or, in some cases, be in violation of other HIPAA regulations.

 Why is it important that users detect and report malicious software and phishing emails when software can do this? 

The healthcare sector and healthcare records in particular is often targeted by hackers due to the billing details contained in medical records and ransomware value of the personal information in Protected Health Information. Email is one of the most common attack vectors. It is important healthcare staff know how to identify malicious software and phishing emails because the detection capabilities of security software are often limited to how the software is configured and how frequently it is updated. Even the best security software can allow threats to evade detection and, when this happens, users need to be able to identify the threat and report it so other users do not (for example) open a malicious attachment or interact with a phishing email.

 × 

 Why is it important that all members of the workforce receive ongoing security awareness training? 

It is important that all members of the workforce receive ongoing security awareness training for two reasons. The first reason – that training is provided to all members of the workforce – is because an attacker can infiltrate a network via a device that does not have access to electronic PHI, and then move laterally through the network until they find a healthcare database to attack. The second reason – that training must be ongoing – is due to the evolving nature of cyberthreats. Members of the workforce must be informed about the latest threats, how to recognize them, and how to report them.

 × 

 Why is the documentation of every training session - and workforce attestation where required - important? 

The documentation and record keeping of every HIPAA training session is important for two reasons – so that covered entities can keep up to date with which members of the workforce have received what training in the event of transfers or promotions, and so that covered entities can demonstrate the training has been provided in the event of an OCR compliance investigation. Workforce attestation is also required by some state laws with more stringent privacy protections than HIPAA.

 × 

 Why is it necessary to schedule refresher training when there is a change to a policy or procedure? 

The provision of refresher training when there is a material change to policies and procedures is necessary to ensure all members of the workforce affected by the change are made aware of it. Refresher training only has to be provided to those the change affects; but, if the training relates to a change in HIPAA policies and procedures, the training must be documented and – where required by state law – attested to by those who attend. In addition, it is a best practice to provide annual refresher training to all members of the workforce so that those not directly affected by material changes to policies and procedures are made aware of them.

 × 

 What difference does it make if I am a covered entity or business associate? 

Although covered entities and business associates have many similar HIPAA compliance obligations, some regulations apply differently to each type of organization depending on the nature of their activities. If you qualify as a covered entity, and you also provide services to other covered entities as a business associate, it will be necessary for you to complete the assessment twice.

args.summary:
This is a news article from The HIPAA Journal (posted November 12, 2025, by editor-in-chief Steve Alder) reporting on the Synnovis ransomware attack and its fallout. The main story covers the June 3, 2024, ransomware attack on Synnovis, a UK pathology lab providing blood, urine, and specimen testing services to numerous UK healthcare organizations, including partnerships with Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust and King's College Hospitals NHS Trust in London, plus SYNLAB (a provider of laboratory, diagnostic, and advisory services).

The Qilin ransomware group encrypted files on Synnovis's network after exfiltrating data. The attack caused massive disruption, forcing NHS trusts to cancel appointments, leading to a nationwide shortage of O-negative blood that lasted months, with more than 10,000 appointments canceled. It took until late autumn 2024 to fully restore systems to pre-attack operational levels.

It took 17 months to complete the highly complex data review and notify affected healthcare provider clients. Synnovis confirmed no data was taken from its primary lab databases, and that the exfiltrated data was "not in a form that could easily be used by anyone with ill intent." The company decided not to pay the ransom (amount not disclosed) as doing so would have gone against its ethical principles and could fund further attacks on critical infrastructure. Notifications were to be completed by November 21, 2025, after which affected organizations (data controllers) will decide whether to notify patients under UK data protection laws. Synnovis stressed it will not contact patients directly, and warned that any communication purporting to come directly from Synnovis should be assumed to be a scam.

The article also includes backdated coverage of earlier events:
- June 22, 2024: Qilin leaked 400GB of data (including info from more than 300 million patient interactions with the NHS) on its dark web leak site after the $50 million ransom deadline expired. Data included sensitive test results for HIV, STIs, and cancer, plus some private healthcare records. The NCA and NCSC considered retaliatory action.
- June 18, 2024: At least 1,500 operations and outpatient appointments were canceled (including more than 100 cancer treatments and 18 organ transplants) across two NHS trusts. A zero-day vulnerability was claimed by the attackers, who demanded a $50 million ransom payable within 120 hours.
- June 5, 2024: Initial attack affected multiple hospitals in six London boroughs (Bexley, Greenwich, Lewisham, Bromley, Southwark, and Lambeth), including Guy's Hospital, St Thomas' Hospital, King's College Hospital, Royal Brompton Hospital, and Evelina London Children's Hospital, plus the South London and the Maudsley (Slam) mental health trust and GP surgeries. Test results needed to be re-run due to the risk of data manipulation. According to the ICO, there have been 215 ransomware attacks on UK hospitals since 2019, with at least 1,231 attacks across all UK industry sectors last year. This was the second ransomware attack on Synnovis in 2024—BlackBasta had attacked in April 2024 and published stolen data when the ransom wasn't paid.

The article demonstrates the massive impact ransomware attacks can have on critical infrastructure, describing it as a calculated attack designed to cause as much damage and disruption as possible for financial gain.
