  Cyber Update: 29th September 2025 [Volvo Group](https://se.linkedin.com/company/volvo-group?trk=public_post-text) has confirmed a data breach impacting employee information after a ransomware attack on its HR software supplier, Miljdata. The incident compromised personal details including names and Social Security numbers. The DataCarry ransomware group has claimed responsibility, publishing the stolen data on its leak site. This breach highlights the widespread risk of supply chain vulnerabilities. The incident not only affected Volvo but also impacted 25 private companies, 200 Swedish councils, and several educational institutions. args.summary:
Volvo Group North America has confirmed a data breach that exposed sensitive employee personal information, including names and Social Security numbers. The breach did NOT originate from Volvo's own internal networks; instead, it resulted from a ransomware attack on Miljdata, one of Volvo's third-party HR software suppliers — highlighting the growing risks of supply chain vulnerabilities.

Timeline of events:
- August 20, 2025: The initial ransomware attack targeting Miljdata occurred.
- August 23, 2025: The HR software provider became aware of the ransomware attack (three days later).
- September 2, 2025: Miljdata confirmed that Volvo Group personnel data had been compromised and informed Volvo Group the same day.

Volvo has assured that its internal systems were not compromised during this event and that the breach was contained within the supplier's environment. Affected employees were reportedly offered 18 months of free identity protection.

The DataCarry ransomware group claimed responsibility and published the stolen data on its leak site. The incident had cascading effects beyond Volvo, impacting approximately 25 private companies, 200 Swedish councils, and several educational institutions.

Cybersecurity professionals commenting on the incident emphasized that supply chain vulnerabilities remain one of the biggest blind spots in cybersecurity, noting that even well-protected enterprises face risk when third-party vendors fail to meet the same security standards. Commentators stressed that the delays in detection (attack on August 20, discovery on August 23, Volvo informed nearly two weeks later) increased exposure and amplified damage, underscoring the need for stronger third-party risk management, vendor assessments, and data protection measures.

# Volvo Employee SSNs Stolen in Supplier Ransomware Attack

Three international vehicle manufacturers have fallen to supply chain cyberattacks in the past month alone.

![Picture of Nate Nelson](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt8edb70f1c73f8a5a/6978c3c26fdea754c9f2e2e9/Nate_Nelson_bio_pic_2-crop_2.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Nate Nelson")

September 26, 2025

![A Volvo sign](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt3469a00cd75eaafe/68d6df00615dc380b562df70/Volvo-Heidi_Besen-Alamy.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "A Volvo sign")

Volvo Group North America (Volvo NA) has been breached via a third-party human resources (HR) software provider.

At the root of the story is Miljödata, a Swedish company specializing in occupational software-as-a-service (SaaS), whose cloud infrastructure was breached in August. Thanks to its centralized, multi-tenant arrangement, hundreds of customers and millions of individuals have been affected. In a recent letter to its staff, Volvo NA, whose parent company is based in Sweden, revealed itself to be one such victim.

Like other Miljödata customers, Volvo NA's systems were untouched by the attack. Still, its employees' names and [Social Security numbers (SSNs)](/threat-intelligence/international-crime-rings-defraud-us-govt-billions) were stolen, and potentially published to the Dark Web. According to its website, Volvo NA employs just shy of 20,000 people.

"For municipalities, universities, and even big corporations like Volvo, this isn't just a security issue, it's an integrity issue," says Anders Askasen, vice president of product marketing at Radiant Logic. "People suddenly wonder whether the systems handling their most sensitive data are fit for the purpose, and with good reason. That loss of confidence is as damaging as the leak itself."

Related:[Scottish Govt Suffers Potentially Widening Data Breach at Prosecutor's Office](/cyberattacks-data-breaches/scottish-govt-data-breach-prosecutors-office)

## The Miljödata Incident

Miljödata is widely spread across Sweden. For example, it's a supplier to around 80% of the country's municipal governments. Among its offerings is "Adato," a platform for documenting and managing employee sick leave and rehabilitation processes.

On Aug. 20, the so-called "DataCarry" ransomware group breached Miljödata's cloud infrastructure. The company discovered the attack three days later. The threat actors demanded a ransom of 1.5 Bitcoins, equaling around $165,000 at the time of writing. On Sept. 12 they warned that they'd publish the stolen data to the Dark Web, and in the hours that followed [they carried out that threat](https://databreach.com/breach/miljodata-2025).

The attack didn't just affect Miljödata. Because customers tend to deploy platforms like Adato in the cloud, all of their data is stewarded by Miljödata. According to local media, several universities, at least [25 companies](https://www.svt.se/nyheter/inrikes/forsvarsforetag-och-sas-med-i-datalackan-kan-exploateras-av-frammande-makt), [164 municipalities](https://swedenherald.com/article/cyberattack-hits-250-miljodata-customers-including-164-municipalities), and more than [1.5 million individuals](https://swedenherald.com/article/miljodata-data-breach-exposes-sas-pilots-and-major-companies) were impacted as a result.

The leak was bad enough that, in the grand scheme of things, Volvo NA employees might even consider themselves relatively lucky. Employees of [other affected organizations](https://www.slu.se/en/news/2025/09/adato-0908/) lost their names and personal identity numbers — Sweden's equivalent to SSNs — but also a variety of other personally identifying information (PII) such as their gender, dates of birth, details of their employment, and contact information including phone numbers, home addresses, and [870,100 email addresses](https://haveibeenpwned.com/Breach/Miljodata).

Related:[Long-running Data Theft Campaign Targeting Salesforce, ServiceNow](/cyberattacks-data-breaches/long-running-data-theft-campaign-salesforce-servicenow)

On the ground in Sweden, Askasen reports that "this breach is among the most disruptive to strike Sweden’s public sector in years. When over a million citizens discover that personal identity numbers, contact details, and employment records are circulating on criminal forums, it delivers a direct blow to the social contract that underpins digital government, particularly in a high-tax society like Sweden, where trust in public institutions ought to be non-negotiable."

## Stellantis, Jaguar Also Attacked

Within weeks of the Adato incident that impacted Volvo NA, two other vehicle manufacturing giants fell to their own, rather similar, supply chain cyberattacks.

On Sep. 21 [the ShinyHunters group](/cyberattacks-data-breaches/payback-shinyhunters-google-salesforce) breached Stellantis, parent company to consumer vehicle brands like Chrysler, Dodge, and Jeep, and luxury brands like Alfa Romeo and Maserati. They claimed to have [stolen customer names and contact details](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/automaker-giant-stellantis-confirms-data-breach-after-salesforce-hack/) from the company's Salesforce instance.

On Aug. 31, "Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters" — a collaboration between hackers from ShinyHunters, Scattered Spider, and the Lapsus$ group — attacked Jaguar Land Rover (JLR). They forced the company to pause production the following day. In fact, its factory lines remained halted and employees were instructed to stay home for weeks thereafter. Finally, toward the end of the month, the company indicated that it was beginning a [phased restoration](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/jaguar-land-rover-restoration-cyberattack/761251/) of its operations.

Related:[Ransomware Hits Colombian Justice Ministry Days Before Presidential Transition](/cyberattacks-data-breaches/ransomware-hits-colombian-justice-ministry-presidential-transition)

JLR's case best demonstrated the kinds of consequences that can result from attacks against vehicle manufacturers. The British company's government got involved — UK prime minister Keir Starmer [told the BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c0q75q4l87no) it was "working 24/7" to support the many suppliers that rely on JLR for their own survival. "I am acutely aware of the urgency of the situation and the difficulties that many of these companies are inevitably finding themselves [in]," he said.

In Volvo's case, though there was no impact to operations, Askasen says the consequences to the company, its employees, and even Sweden as a whole could be serious.

"For Volvo, this isn't only about employee privacy — it's about national competitiveness," he says. "Exposure of employee identity data creates fraud risks, but exposure of operational or HR systems also erodes confidence in the resilience of Swedish industry. Car manufacturing is deeply tied to national supply chains and the broader economy."

# Volvo Group Employee Data Breach Notice

by [CertPro Digest](https://certpro.com/author/certpro-digest/ "Posts by CertPro Digest") | Sep 25, 2025 | [Data](https://certpro.com/category/data/) | [0 comments](https://certpro.com/volvo-group-data-breach/#respond)

![“DoorDash data breach security update”](https://certpro.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/data-breach.webp)

Excerpt from SecurityWeek Article, Published on September 25, 2025

The Volvo Group is currently notifying its current and former employees of a serious data breach triggered by a ransomware attack on its third-party supplier, Miljödata, in August 2025. Miljödata provides critical HR and rehabilitation support systems — named Adato and Novi — used by Volvo’s workforce. The attack was orchestrated by the DataCarry ransomware group.

The breach spread widely, impacting not only Volvo but approximately 25 private companies, multiple educational institutions, and nearly 200 Swedish municipalities, including Sweden’s capital, Stockholm. Data stolen in the attack was made public on September 14 after being posted on the hacker group’s dark web leak site.

The compromised information includes roughly 870,000 unique email addresses as well as names, physical addresses, phone numbers, government-issued IDs, birthdates, and gender details. For some users, employment records such as employee IDs and sick leave data were also exposed. Specifically, Volvo disclosed that some employees’ Social Security numbers and names were struck in the breach.

Following detection of the incident on August 20 and notification by Miljödata on September 2, Volvo began notifying affected individuals in September and also reported the breach to the Massachusetts Attorney General’s office on September 24. To protect impacted employees, Volvo is providing 18 months of free identity theft protection and credit monitoring services, including dark web monitoring and real-time threat alerts.

This incident underscores the risks companies face through vulnerabilities in their third-party vendors, especially with ransomware attacks aimed at holding sensitive corporate data hostage. Volvo’s transparent response and protective measures align with best practices in cybersecurity breach management to mitigate harm and rebuild trust.

To delve deeper into this topic, visit the [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/volvo-group-employee-data-stolen-in-ransomware-attack/) article.

Volvo

[Volvo Group North America](https://www.volvogroup.com/en/) recently experienced a data breach impacting current and former employees.

The cybersecurity incident involved Miljödata, a third-party supplier of human resources software used by Volvo. On Aug. 23, 2025, Miljödata discovered it had suffered a suffered a ransomware attack on Aug. 20, 2025.

An investigation took place and on Sept. 2, 2025, it was determined that data related to Volvo Group North America personnel may have been compromised. Miljödata notified Volvo the same day. Exposed information included first and last names in combination with Social Security numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, and medical records.

A total number of 16,991 impacted current and former Volvo personnel were impacted, including three from Maine and 15 from Massachusetts.

Volvo Group North America began notifying affected individuals by mail in Sept. 2025. The data breach was also disclosed to the [Indiana Attorney General](https://www.in.gov/attorneygeneral/consumer-protection-division/id-theft-prevention/files/DB-YeartoDate-Report-3_2026.pdf), the [Massachusetts Attorney General](https://www.mass.gov/doc/2025-1648-volvo-group-north-america-llc/download), [Maine Attorney General](https://www.maine.gov/agviewer/content/ag/985235c7-cb95-4be2-8792-a1252b4f8318/5f8e9d3f-dfdb-4be0-8826-d7fe9d27a328.html), and the [Vermont Attorney General](https://ago.vermont.gov/document/2026-02-05-volvo-group-north-america-data-breach-notice-consumers).

## Volvo Group North America's response

In response to the incident, Miljödata launched an investigation with cybersecurity experts and began implementing enhanced security measures.

In addition to required state and federal disclosures, Volvo is offering impacted individuals a free 18-month subscription to Allstate’s Identity Protection Pro+ service. Services include three-bureau credit monitoring, annual credit reports, monthly credit score tracking, full-service identity restoration, dark web monitoring, high-risk transaction monitoring, financial transaction monitoring and real-time threat alerts.

If you receive a notice from Volvo about this breach, you may want to:

* Sign up for the free credit monitoring and identity protection services, offered by the company.
* Monitor your credit reports and financial accounts for any unusual activity.
* Be alert for phishing emails or phone calls that may use your exposed information.
* Consider placing a fraud alert or credit freeze with major credit bureaus.

Volvo North America hit via third-party breach: a wake-up call for all orgs Volvo has confirmed a ransomware attack on its third-party supplier Miljödata, which exposed sensitive employee data such as names, SSNs, DOBs, contact info, government IDs across ~870,000 accounts. The attacker group DataCarry claimed responsibility and dumped the stolen data on the dark web. The attack didn’t target Volvo directly but instead went through their supply chain. How they got in: Via vulnerabilities in a supplier’s systems. They targeted systems handling medical, injury, rehab records; all high value and sensitive data. Once inside, they exfiltrated data and then leaked to pressure for ransom. What to do to stop this: Supply chain security audits: Treat your vendors as part of your attack surface Zero Trust & least privilege access: Even trusted partners should have limited, tiered access Continuous monitoring & anomaly detection: Detect lateral movement early Data segmentation & encryption at rest/in transit: If breached, damage is contained Incident response & tabletop drills: Simulate supplier-driven attacks

  💀 Ransomware Evolved: The Rise of Double Extortion 💀 Traditional ransomware was bad enough — attackers encrypted data and demanded payment for the decryption key. But now, the game has changed. 🚨 Double extortion is becoming the new norm: Attackers first steal sensitive data before encrypting it. Even if victims restore from backups, criminals threaten to leak or sell the data unless a ransom is paid. This puts organizations at risk of regulatory penalties, reputational damage, and loss of customer trust. Why this matters: 🔒 Backups alone are no longer enough. 🔍 Organizations need robust incident response, threat intelligence, data loss prevention, and network segmentation to minimize impact. 👥 Employee awareness & phishing resilience remain critical since many ransomware attacks start with a single compromised account. args.summary:
This LinkedIn post by cybersecurity professional Vincent Gaudemard reports on a ransomware attack on Volvo North America that occurred via a third-party supplier breach. Volvo confirmed that its third-party supplier Miljödata was hit by ransomware, exposing sensitive employee data (names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, contact info, and government IDs) across approximately 870,000 accounts. The attacker group DataCarry claimed responsibility and dumped the stolen data on the dark web.

Key details of the attack:
- The attack did not target Volvo directly but went through their supply chain
- Attackers exploited vulnerabilities in the supplier's systems, targeting high-value systems handling medical, injury, and rehab records
- Once inside, they exfiltrated data and leaked it to pressure payment of a ransom

The post outlines recommended security measures to prevent such attacks:
1. Supply chain security audits - treat vendors as part of your attack surface
2. Zero Trust & least privilege access - even trusted partners should have limited, tiered access
3. Continuous monitoring & anomaly detection - detect lateral movement early
4. Data segmentation & encryption at rest/in transit - contain damage if breached
5. Incident response & tabletop drills - simulate supplier-driven attacks

The post also includes a comment from Michael Kimes emphasizing that cybersecurity is only as strong as the entire supply chain, highlighting the importance of continuous vendor risk assessments, zero trust principles, and robust incident response plans.

The page also contains "More Relevant Posts" listing other recent cybersecurity incidents, including: Jaguar Land Rover (4+ week production halt from ransomware with 350GB exfiltrated, likely via compromised credentials), Asahi (30 worldwide factories shuttered), the rise of double extortion tactics in ransomware, KNP Logistics Group collapse (158-year-old UK company ended by a single guessed password exploited by Akira ransomware group, leaving 700 employees without jobs), Red Hat security breach (sophisticated supply chain attack on production system secrets), Envoy Air/American Airlines (Clop ransomware exploiting Oracle E-Business Suite zero-day CVE-2025-61882), and Volkswagen (8Base ransomware group allegedly leaking sensitive data via third-party).

METHODS: An online, anonymous survey was deployed to IT and IT cybersecurity personnel in HDOs across four nations (Australia, Germany, UK, and US). Respondent distribution was 12% Australia, 30% Germany, 20% UK, 38% US. Survey data was analyzed using stratified contingency tables. IRB approval was not needed as the study involved no patient data.

KEY RESULTS:
- Only 51.1% of HDOs had a comprehensive inventory of all third parties accessing their network. Reasons for lack included insufficient resources (48%), no centralized control over third-party relationships (36%), complexity (28%), and frequent third-party turnover (22%).
- 60% reported third-party access to sensitive/confidential information was not routinely monitored; of those who do monitor, 53% do so manually.
- 19% of HDOs had more than 40 third parties with network access, 31% had 21–40, and on average 22 third parties had HDO network access.
- More than half (56.4%) reported a breach involving a third party in the last 12 months; 48% believe third-party remote access is becoming their weakest attack surface.
- Two-thirds of HDOs anticipate third-party breaches increasing in the next 12–24 months.
- 55% ranked VPAM effectiveness at ≤6 on a 10-point scale; 49% ranked PAM effectiveness at ≤6. Only 36% applied their privileged access risk strategy consistently.
- Barriers to reducing access risks: lack of oversight/governance (53%) and insufficient resources (45%).
- Breach consequences include loss/theft of sensitive information (60%), regulatory fines (49%), severed third-party relationships (47%), loss of revenue (42%) and business partners (38%).
- HDOs expend an average of 129 hours per week investigating third-party and privileged access security issues.
- Mean cost of restoring access to third-party/privileged access users over the prior 12 months was US $86,550.
- Common actions taken include network segmentation/isolation (69%), removing access credentials when appropriate (66%), and verification of third-party need for network access (56%).
- Key challenges: taking too long to grant access to privileged users (61%), too expensive to monitor/control privileged access (60%), and inability to apply access policy controls at the point of a change request (70%).

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: The article cites that the global mean cost of a data breach is US $4.45 million, healthcare data breaches cost an average of US $7.42 million (highest of any industry for 14 consecutive years), and healthcare breaches take a mean of 279 days to identify and contain. Notable breaches referenced include the 2021 Broward Health breach (1.35 million patients affected via a third-party medical provider) and the 2023 Advanced Medical Management breach (~320,000 individuals affected). The article also discusses VPAM/PAM features including zero trust enforcement, credential vaulting, employment verification, session monitoring, and support for OCR audit readiness, GDPR compliance, NIST SP 800-207, and ISO 27001. Recent regulatory context includes the FTC Health Breach Rule.

CONCLUSION: HDOs recognize the increasing threat of third-party cyber breaches but are struggling to address them effectively due to budget constraints, lack of expert resources, complexity, and third-party turnover. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a cybersecurity blog post published by Conscia (a European IT infrastructure and cybersecurity provider) on the CEVA Logistics cyberattack, written by David Kasabji, Head of Threat Intelligence at Conscia Group. The article analyzes how a cyber intrusion at CEVA Logistics (a global logistics provider operating 1,000+ warehouses with approximately $18.3 billion in 2025 revenue) became a multi-company disclosure event across Europe.

Key facts about the incident:
- The attack affected CEVA between 29 July and 1 August 2026, affecting part of its European contract logistics operation
- Eight warehouses were disrupted, while air, ocean, ground and rail transportation operations continued normally
- Affected organizations include Valve, Bol, De Bijenkorf, Ajax, ING and Ace & Tate — though none of these organizations were themselves breached

- No payment credentials or banking data were compromised, according to affected companies

Main arguments covered:
1. **Third-party cyber risk**: The incident demonstrates that the organization suffering the original breach and the organization carrying the customer relationship are not the same. The disclosure burden fell on CEVA's customers (Valve provided the clearest timeline and data categories; Bol suspended data exchange with CEVA). "Contracts can transfer responsibilities, but they cannot transfer reputational impact."

2. **Delivery data still creates security risks**: Even without payment card data, exposed delivery information enables targeted phishing and social engineering because attackers can reference real names, delivery addresses and recent purchases. Valve warned customers to expect fraudulent messages referencing hardware orders. The same principle applies to business relationships — knowledge of suppliers, deliveries and fulfilment processes supports convincing business email compromise, supplier impersonation and invoice fraud.

3. **Supply chain concentration risk**: CEVA's scale means a single compromise can expose data from many organizations simultaneously since "a compromise does not need to penetrate ten separate retailers if the same data from those retailers converges inside one service provider." Beyond logistics, identity providers, payroll processors, MSPs, cloud platforms, payment processors and software supply chains can all become concentration points.

4. **Reducing third-party cyber risk recommendations**: Identify where customer/operational data leaves direct control; define clear incident notification requirements in contracts; use strong authentication, conditional access and least privilege for vendor-held identities; continuously reassess access paths; brief finance/AP teams on logistics breaches; and use Cyber Threat Intelligence to monitor criminal marketplaces and MDR to correlate external signals with internal telemetry.

The article concludes that mature risk management must ask what happens when a supplier is NOT secure and how many parts of the organization fail simultaneously. Finance was the most targeted sector for phishing in Q1 2021, and almost 50% of all phishing attacks in 2019 targeted financial services. Phishing tactics now align with breaking news stories to exploit societal anxieties (e.g., COVID-19 pandemic themes). Tactics include email phishing and email conversation thread hijacking.

2. **Ransomware** - Ransomware-as-a-Service is a critical risk. The FBI strongly advises businesses to never pay ransoms, and according to Sophos' State of Ransomware 2020 report, remediation costs double when a ransom is paid. Ransomware attacks against financial sector increased 9x between Feb-April 2020, increased 520% between March-June 2020, and rose 151% in the first 6 months of 2021. The article lists 11 prevalent ransomware strains: Sodinokibi, Conti V2, Lockbit, Clop, Egregor, Avaddon, Ryuk, Darkside, SunCrypt, Netwalker, and Phobos, each with defense resources.

3. **SQL Injections, Local File Inclusion, Cross-Site Scripting, and OGNL Java Injections** - According to Akamai, 94% of observed cyber attacks in the financial sector were facilitated by these four attack vectors. Notable 2021 vulnerabilities included a WordPress plugin SQLi flaw impacting 600,000 sites, an XSS vulnerability in e-commerce sites, an LFI vulnerability in BIQS invoicing software (CVE-2021-39433), and an OGNL injection flaw in Atlassian Confluence.

4. **DDoS Attacks** - The financial sector experienced the highest number of DDoS attacks in 2020, with a 30% increase between 2019-2020. Finance is among the top three most targeted sectors for DDoS attacks. Multi-vector DDoS attacks rose 80% in 2021. Attackers may use DDoS to distract security teams or demand ransom due to strict SLA agreements.

5. **Supply Chain Attacks** - ENISA found that 66% of compromised suppliers either didn't know or failed to report they were breached. 50% of observed supply chain attacks were linked to APTs (APT29, APT41, Thallium, Lazarus, TA413, TA428). ENISA predicts a 4x increase in supply chain attacks between 2020 and 2021. Recommendations include Zero Trust Architecture and Privileged Access Management.

6. **Bank Drops** - Cybercriminals use stolen customer credentials ("fullz" data) to open fake bank accounts. Fullz data on the dark web sells for $15-$60 per record (generic) and $35-$60 for business fullz data. Fullz data can include names, DOB, addresses, SSN, driver's license details, credit scores, bank account numbers, and EINs.

Recommended defense controls: Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM), Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), regular firewall updates, Attack Surface Management, learning threat actor TTPs (Tactics, Techniques & Procedures), security ratings, regular data backups, and a documented cyber threat detection and response strategy.
</summary>

19. **MoD Afghan relocation dataset** — 18,714 ARAP applicants (up to ~100,000 with family); human error via hidden rows in spreadsheet; superinjunction held for nearly two years; compensation scheme announced.
20. **British Library** — ~490,000 files (~600GB); Rhysida ransomware via compromised terminal services credentials without MFA; ~£6-7M recovery costs; published influential lessons-learned report.

--- SOURCE 1: Chain IQ Breach Exposes UBS & Pictet Employee Data: A Supply Chain Failure ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qJ5A2Nd4Chg

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This cybersecurity deep-dive episode (published June 20, 2025) analyzes the Chain IQ supply chain breach and provides a comprehensive framework for defending against supply chain attacks.

## The Chain IQ Breach
Chain IQ, a Swiss procurement and service provider, suffered a massive data breach in early June 2025 perpetrated by the group "World Leaks" (formerly known as Hunters International), a group focused on data theft and public extortion rather than encryption. Key impacts included:
- **UBS**: Personal data of 137,000 employees stolen, including names, emails, phone numbers, job roles, office locations, and even the internal direct phone number of UBS CEO Sergio Armati.
- **Pictet**: 230,000 lines of internal billing data exposed, including highly detailed expenses (grocery shopping, hotel stays, pottery purchases).
- **Other exposed clients**: World Leaks exposed lists of hundreds of companies linked to Chain IQ, including FedEx, IBM, Swiss Life, AXA, Swisscom, and KPMG.
- Client financial data reportedly remained untouched, but employee and operational data exposure was severe.

## Attacker Tactics (World Leaks)
- Operates primarily as an extortion platform (data theft + public leak threats, not encryption), though some victims experienced actual ransomware deployment, suggesting collaboration with groups like the SEC ransomware group.
- Uses a sophisticated multiplatform setup: a main leak site (trophy wall), negotiation site, an insider platform offering journalists 24-hour advanced access to impending leaks, and an affiliate panel.
- Victim site includes countdown timers to public disclosure, direct chat, and a storage page allowing victims to browse their own stolen data (validation + psychological leverage).
- Initial operations faced bugs and fluctuating data size claims (one victim's leak claimed at 7TB, then 700GB, then 1.5TB), raising doubts about their accuracy.

## Key Statistics
- 62% of supply chain attacks exploit trust in third-party providers.
- 66% of suppliers don't even know how they were compromised.
- Organizations have a 27.7% chance of suffering a data breach; almost 60% of these breaches are directly linked to third parties.
- MFA can block up to 99.9% of automated cybercrime attempts.
- MFA can block up to 99.9% of automated cyber crime attempts.
- SolarWinds Orion breach: compromised software updates installed backdoors in ~18,000 customers (including US government agencies and Fortune 500s), undetected for at least 9 months, perpetrated by APT29/Cozy Bear (Russian SVR) primarily for espionage.

## ENISA Survey Findings (April–June 2022)
- 86% of surveyed organizations reported having ICT supply chain cybersecurity policies, but 53% have no dedicated budget for these issues.
- Banking sector most mature: 98% have policies, 43% have dedicated budgets.
- Digital infrastructure: 60% with policies but only 2% with dedicated budgets; online search engines: 47% with policies, 6% with budgets.
- 52% have rigid patching policies covering only 0-20% of assets; 13.5% lack visibility over patching for 50%+ of assets.
- 46% patch critical vulnerabilities within one month; another 46% within six months.
- Only 48% have fully implemented risk-based vulnerability management; 15% have no process at all.
- Supplier risk evaluation criteria: product/service type (59%), spending amount (47%), regulatory status (42%).

## Expert Quote
- Steven Meyer, co-CEO of Zenata Cybersecurity, stated that trust placed in supplier certifications or compliance audits is "dangerously overestimated" — compliance through paperwork can create an "illusion of security."

## Defense Frameworks
1. **Assume Breach Mentality**: Assume a breach is inevitable; focus on three attack surfaces — people, processes, and technologies.
   - People: Comprehensive ongoing cybercrime awareness training (phishing, spear phishing, social engineering, DDoS, ransomware, malware, clickjacking); distinguish innocent users from hostile insider threats.
   - Processes: Robust information security policies (ISPs) plus least privilege principle (PLP).
   - Technologies: Multi-layered defenses including updated antivirus, MFA (blocks up to 99.9% of automated attacks), and attack surface monitoring (including vendor technologies).

2. **Privileged Access Management (PAM)**: Protect the "vault of master keys" and protect the PAM itself. External defenses include detecting third-party data leaks; internal defenses include Identity Access Management (IAM) with centralized account management and encryption using AES (used by US government for classified data).

3. **Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA)**: "Never trust, always verify" — assumes all network activity is malicious by default. Powered by three components: policy engine (trust algorithm), policy administrator (communicates decisions), and policy enforcement point (final gatekeeper). Critical for securing remote endpoints.

4. **Top-Down Strategic Approach**: Assign clear responsibility; create collaborative roles across supply chain, cybersecurity, product security, physical security; increase board involvement; adopt risk-based approach; form multi-dimensional teams (security, procurement, legal).

5. **Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) Cycle**:
   - Plan: ICT supply chain risk management (identify all suppliers and risks).
   - Do: Supplier relationship management (policies, procedures, contractual agreements, performance monitoring).
   - Check: Vulnerability handling (monitor assets, assess risks, deploy patches).
   - Act: Quality of products/services (secure practices built in, transparency for customers).

## Supply Chain Risk Assessment Good Practices (aligned with ISO 31000, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 9000)
- Define scope and context; identify all suppliers and service providers.
- Assess risks for impact on business continuity.
- Implement risk mitigation using international standards.
- Continuous monitoring via internal logs and global threat intelligence feeds.
- Prioritize suppliers with security-enforcing functions, privileged access, or sensitive information handling.
- Consider country-specific intelligence, national authority restrictions, known incidents, threat intelligence, supplier security maturity, and transparency.
- Continuously monitor changes in supplier risk profiles (acquisitions, personnel shifts, new operating models).

## Systemic Challenges
- Terminology confusion over "supply chain" and "managed service provider" definitions hampers NIS-2 implementation.
- State-sponsored attacks with unlimited resources require national-level management and intelligence service involvement.
- Need for shared testing platforms for ICT security, requiring private investment for sustainability.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Chain IQ breach isn't just a warning — it's a case study in what happens when your cybersecurity depends on someone else's." "The trust placed in supplier certifications or compliance audits is dangerously overestimated. Compliance through paperwork might simply create an illusion of security." — Steven Meyer, co-CEO of Zenata Cybersecurity. "Supply chain attacks can have an incredibly large reach, impacting thousands of organizations, even if they initially target only a few specific entities." "Policies without budget are in essence just words and good intentions, not operational reality." "It's like having a fire extinguisher on the wall that's never been serviced." (referring to the gap between compliance documentation and actual security)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Neotas provides a comprehensive guide to DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act, Regulation EU 2022/2554) compliance, with a focus on third-party risk management (TPRM) for financial services firms in 2026. DORA applies to approximately 22,000 EU financial entities and has been fully in force since 17 January 2025, with no remaining deadlines. It directly supersedes NIS2 for EU financial entities under Article 1(2). Enforcement is active and interventionist in 2026, with regulators examining firms for compliance evidence rather than remediation plans.

**Scope and Penalties:** DORA applies to 20 categories of EU-regulated financial entities (banks, insurers, investment firms, payment institutions, crypto-asset providers, etc.), with proportionality provisions for smaller entities and microenterprises (under 10 employees, turnover below €2m) that still cannot opt out of third-party obligations. Non-EU firms serving EU-regulated clients fall in scope via their clients' Article 28 obligations. Penalties include fines up to 10% of annual global turnover or €10 million for serious breaches; individual senior managers face fines up to €1 million (personal liability); and public disclosure of non-compliance decisions.

**Five Pillars:** (1) ICT risk management (Articles 5-16); (2) Incident management (Articles 17-23) with 4-hour initial, 72-hour intermediate, and 1-month final reporting; (3) Resilience testing (Articles 24-27) with annual basic testing and TLPT every 3 years via TIBER-EU for systemically important firms; (4) ICT third-party risk (Articles 28-30) — carrying the highest compliance gap rate; (5) Information sharing (Articles 45-49).

**Article 28 (TPRM Programme):** Requires a formal ICT TPRM programme embedded in governance with board accountability, pre-contractual due diligence covering substitutability, insolvency risk, data protection and subcontracting chains (Article 28(4)), multi-vendor strategy, continuous monitoring and exit strategies. A standalone vendor questionnaire does not satisfy Article 28. Critical or Important Function (CIF) classification per Article 3(22) is materially important — under-classification creates enforcement risk.

**Register of Information (ROI, Article 28(3)):** Must be built to the ESAs' ITS data model and submitted to national competent authorities at entity, sub-consolidated and consolidated levels. Only 6.5% of nearly 1,000 firms passed all 116 data quality checks in the 2024 ESA dry-run. Common failures: incomplete contract data, missing subcontractor information, incorrect CIF classifications. Spreadsheet-based ROIs fail at scale. The 2026 submission cycle (reference date 31 December 2025) faces higher expectations.

**Article 29 (Concentration Risk):** Requires portfolio-level analysis, not individual vendor scorecards. The ECB found more than 30% of significant banks' outsourcing budgets concentrate on just 10 ICT providers. Firms must assess concentration before new CIF arrangements, develop exit strategies and report to the management body.

**Article 30 (Contractual Requirements):** All ICT contracts must include service description/performance levels, data locations with change notification, audit rights, incident notification, business continuity and termination rights. CIF contracts add exit assistance and full sub-contractor disclosure. No grace period for legacy contracts — gaps must be addressed at next renewal. Regulators sample-check provisions against the mandatory list.

**UK Application:** DORA does not directly bind UK-only firms (which fall under FCA PS21/3, PRA SS1/21, SMCR and UK Critical Third Parties regime PS24/16). But UK firms with EU subsidiaries/branches, UK group IT functions serving EU entities, or UK ICT providers serving EU clients are in scope through those relationships. DORA breaches can trigger personal SMCR liability for UK Senior Managers with EU responsibilities. DORA standards generally satisfy FCA/PRA expectations, but not vice versa.

Regulators examine ROI completeness, CIF classification rationale, Article 30 contract provisions, continuous monitoring records and portfolio-level concentration.

**Standard database checks vs OSINT:** Structured database checks fail to surface non-English adverse media, emerging financial crime indicators, beneficial ownership opacity, hidden subcontractor concentration risk (Article 28(4)(d) fourth-party risk), and ESG violations.

The page concludes with an extensive FAQ section covering definitions, deadlines, penalties, NIS2 differences, and ROI format.

--- SOURCE 25: Preparing for the DORA Oversight Framework: CTPP ... ---
URL: https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-05/Preparing_for_DORA_OVS_framework_CTPP_designation_and_next_steps.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document contains presentation slides from a workshop held on 14 May 2025 by the European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs - EBA, EIOPA, ESMA) for technology service providers preparing for the DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act) Oversight Framework, focusing on CTPP (Critical ICT Third-Party Service Provider) designation and next steps.

**Key Context:**
- DORA is applicable to all European Financial Entities (FEs) from 17 January 2025, establishing a comprehensive framework for digital operational resilience.
- DORA harmonises ICT risk management and resilience rules for 20+ types of financial entities across five areas: ICT risk management, ICT-related incidents, digital operational resilience testing, ICT third-party risk management, and information sharing.
- The oversight framework addresses rising reliance on ICT third-party providers, with more than 30% of significant banks' ICT budgets allocated to just 10 providers, and a 2.1% increase in banks' ICT outsourcing budgets between 2023 and 2024.

**Scope of Oversight:**
- In scope: Designated CTPPs providing ICT services supporting critical or important functions of EU FEs (per Article 31 of DORA and the Commission Delegated Regulation on criticality assessment).
- Out of scope: ICT TPPs already under EU-wide oversight (e.g., SWIFT, Euroclear, TARGET2), FEs providing ICT services to other FEs, intra-group providers, and TPPs active in only one member state.

**Governance Structure:**
- Joint Committee (JC) - Oversight Forum (OF): ESAs' chairs and EDs, CA representatives, and observers from EU COM, ECB, ESRB, ENISA, and NIS2 CAs.
- Joint Oversight Network (JON): coordinates oversight strategies.
- Joint Examination Teams (JETs): composed of ESA staff, DORA CA staff, and NIS2 CA staff (voluntary), carry out oversight tasks under coordination of a Joint Oversight Director (operating under a 'one DORA Oversight team' Target Operating Model organised along technology domains).

**Oversight Activities:**
1. Annual designation of CTPPs (data collection, criticality assessment, notification, designation, appointment of Lead Overseer)
2. Annual risk assessment & planning (via the risk-based Oversight Risk Assessment Process - ORAP)
3. Examinations and ongoing monitoring (requests for information, general investigations, on-site inspections, reports on remedial plans)
4. Recommendations and follow-up (CTPPs must respond within 60 days; possible public disclosure if not followed)

**CTPP Designation Timeline for 2025:**
- April-May: Data collection (FEs submit Registers of Information to CAs, which submit to ESAs)
- June-July: Criticality assessment
- End of July: Notification of potential CTPPs
- August-early September: 6-week period for TPPs' reasoned statements
- October-November: Final designation and publication of CTPP list

**Criticality Assessment:**
- Based on four broad criteria (Article 31 DORA): systemic impact, systemic character/importance of FEs relying on the TPP, reliance on the TPP's services, and substitutability.
- Assessed via 11 sub-criteria in a two-step process: Step 1 (quantitative, automatic assessment of 6 sub-criteria) and Step 2 (qualitative, expert-guided assessment of 5 additional sub-criteria).

**Oversight Fees:**
- For the first year (2025), fees are equally split among CTPPs (total estimated oversight costs ÷ number of designated CTPPs).
- Opt-in fee for TPPs not designated as critical but requesting designation: non-refundable EUR 50,000.

**Expectations for CTPPs:**
- ESAs expect EU and non-EU CTPPs to identify an EU-subsidiary with: access to information, operational/technical resources, financial resources for fee calculation and payment, skilled/senior employees, empowered management, and on-site examination readiness.
- ESAs are committed to transparent and constructive oversight, fostering trust, and protecting CTPP data security.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Marks & Spencer Breach: How A Ransomware Attack ... ---
URL: https://www.blackfog.com/marks-and-spencer-ransomware-attack

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This BlackFog article details the April 2025 ransomware attack on Marks & Spencer (M&S), the UK retail giant with 65,000 staff and over 1,400 stores. The attack, which began over the Easter weekend (Apr 19–21, 2025) with contactless payment and Click & Collect failures, severely disrupted operations and cost the company roughly £300 million in lost operating profit for 2025/26. The breach dragged on through June/July and forced M&S to revert to paper-based tracking for fresh food and clothing, leaving shelves bare.

TIMELINE: Easter weekend glitches (Apr 19–21) → formal stock market statement acknowledging cyber incident (Apr 22) → email from DragonForce hacking group to CEO Stuart Machin (Apr 23) → online shopping suspended (Apr 25) → stolen customer data revealed (May 13), including names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, dates of birth and order histories (no card details or passwords) → £300 million loss quantified and website restored read-only (May 21–22) → online orders resumed for some clothing lines after 46 days (June 10, 2025).

ATTACKERS & METHODS: Classified as ransomware with a double extortion tactic (encryption plus data exfiltration). The Scattered Spider gang claimed the attack. Entry occurred via third-party supplier Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), which ran M&S's IT helpdesk. Attackers used social engineering—posing as internal IT over the phone—to obtain credentials/password resets, then deployed DragonForce ransomware. The group also hit Co-op supermarket and Harrods. CEO Machin called it "unlucky...through human error."

CONSEQUENCES: Weeks of disruption to contactless payments, Click & Collect, gift-card terminals, returns kiosks and the Sparks loyalty program. Deutsche Bank estimated an immediate £30 million profit loss plus ~£15 million weekly until restoration; up to £750 million wiped from market value. Experts warned stolen data could enable targeted fraud/phishing scams. M&S forced password resets for all online accounts.

PREVENTION (5 recommendations): (1) Strong multi-factor authentication, (2) Third-party risk management with least-privilege access and network segmentation, (3) Employee training and verification for social engineering (call-back verification, ticket tracking), (4) Layered email/network defenses and network segmentation, (5) Offline/immutable backups and rehearsed incident response plans.

ADX PITCH: The article argues anti data exfiltration (ADX) solutions like BlackFog, which block unauthorized outbound data flows to C2 infrastructure, anonymizing networks and cloud drives in real time, could have prevented the data exfiltration phase entirely—neutralizing the leverage that made the breach damaging, since most legacy tools only focus on inbound threats, not outbound data theft.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In late April 2025 M&S warned investors that the incident, which it identified as a ransomware breach, would likely drag on through June/July and shave roughly £300 million off its annual profit." "CEO Stuart Machin bluntly told reporters M&S was simply 'unlucky … through human error' – the malicious calls fooled staff despite the company's security investments." "At one point the attack wiped roughly £750 million off M&S's market value." "NCC Group's Matt Hull warned that criminals could use the stolen data to craft 'very convincing scams' posing as M&S."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Marks & Spencer Cyberattack: Scattered Spider Breach & Lessons Learned | Vorboss ---
URL: https://vorboss.com/blog/marks-spencer-cyberattack

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Vorboss blog article (published August 7, 2025) provides a detailed analysis of the Marks & Spencer (M&S) cyberattack perpetrated by the Scattered Spider threat group (also known as UNC3944 or Octo Tempest), which previously targeted major U.S. companies like Caesars Entertainment and MGM Resorts.

**How the attackers gained access:** Scattered Spider used targeted phishing emails and impersonated IT staff to trick employees into surrendering credentials. They employed "MFA fatigue" tactics - spamming employees with repeated login requests until one was mistakenly approved. Threat intelligence researcher Lontz identified suspected Scattered Spider infrastructure using fake domains designed to mimic legitimate login pages.

**What happened after access:** Initial access to M&S systems was believed to have begun as early as February 2025. Attackers used stolen administrative credentials to deploy legitimate remote administration tools (RATs), including:
- Installed remote desktop access tools like AnyDesk and TeamViewer
- Moved through M&S internal systems to gather data
- Targeted critical assets like password databases and user credentials
- Created secret access points, hidden accounts, and scheduled tasks for persistent access

**The attack (April 24, 2025):** Scattered Spider launched the DragonForce ransomware attack on M&S's VMware ESXi servers, encrypting virtual machines powering key systems for e-commerce, payment processing, and logistics. M&S was forced to shut down key systems including online orders and contactless payments, and called in cybersecurity experts from CrowdStrike, Microsoft, and Fenix24 for containment and recovery.

**Key lesson for businesses:** According to the article, "While M&S is a major player, the tactics used in this breach aren't just for corporations, they work just as well against small businesses. Groups like Scattered Spider rely on common tools and stolen identities to gain trust and slip past normal security." The key takeaway is to always verify the people and systems you rely on, whether internal team members or external partners.

**5 quick wins to protect your business:**
1. Train your team to spot dodgy emails, spoofed links, and sketchy login pages
2. Use strong, complex passwords - never reuse passwords across accounts
3. Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA)
4. Stay vigilant - don't open email attachments or click links unless certain of their legitimacy
5. Report suspicious activity fast (unexpected MFA prompts, suspicious login alerts, credential requests)

The article includes additional resources on the M&S breach and Scattered Spider's indicators of compromise (IOCs).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: M&S and Co-op hacks: Scattered Spider is focus of police investigation ---
URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ckgnndrgxv3o

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The National Crime Agency (NCA) has confirmed, in its first interview on the matter, that it is actively investigating the cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider as a key suspect in the wave of ransomware attacks on UK retailers including M&S, Co-op, and Harrods. The attackers are believed to be young (some teenagers) and native English speakers, most likely located in the UK and US—notable because the most high-profile cyber criminals typically come from countries like Russia and North Korea.

Paul Foster, head of the NCA's national cyber-crime unit, stated in a new BBC documentary: "We are looking at the group that is publicly known as Scattered Spider, but we've got a range of different hypotheses and we'll follow the evidence to get to the offenders," adding that catching those responsible is the top priority.

Key facts:
- The hacks were carried out using DragonForce, a ransomware-as-a-service platform; no arrests have been made.
- M&S was hit with ransomware that scrambled its servers, forcing it to halt online shopping for weeks; customer and employee data was stolen.
- Co-op took systems offline to prevent infection but lost a huge amount of customer and staff data now held for ransom; its supermarkets and funeral services were badly affected.
- Harrods pulled systems offline following an attempted cyber-attack.
- When hackers behind the M&S and Co-op attacks anonymously contacted the BBC, they declined to say whether they were Scattered Spider.

About Scattered Spider: The name was coined by CrowdStrike due to the group's sporadic nature; other nicknames include Octo Tempest and Muddled Libra. The group was linked to attacks on two US casinos in 2023 and Transport for London in 2024. In November, the US charged five British and American men and boys (teens and twenties) for alleged Scattered Spider activity, including 23-year-old Scottish man Tyler Buchanan.

Investigators have not revealed how the breaches occurred, but the National Cyber Security Centre earlier urged organizations to review their IT help desk password reset processes—a tactic Scattered Spider favours using social engineering to manipulate staff into resetting accounts or clicking links. A former teen hacker now working in cyber-security from the US said he was unsurprised teenagers could be behind the attacks, noting the tools are "readily available," and warned they are "gonna be arrested 99% of the time."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We are looking at the group that is publicly known as Scattered Spider, but we've got a range of different hypotheses and we'll follow the evidence to get to the offenders," Paul Foster, head of the NCA's national cyber-crime unit, said. "In light of all the damage that we're seeing, catching whoever is behind these attacks is our top priority.", "We know that Scattered Spider are largely English-speaking but that doesn't necessarily mean that they're in the UK - we know that they communicate online amongst themselves in a range of different platforms and channels, which is, I guess, key to their ability to then be able to operate as a collective," Mr Foster said., "Calling up IT help desks is a tactic that Scattered Spider seems to favour and they use social engineering techniques to manipulate someone into doing something like clicking on a link or resetting someone's account to a password they can use," Lisa Forte, from cyber-security firm Red Goat, explained., "It wouldn't surprise me - quite [the] opposite. The tools are readily available and it's very easy to jump online and search straight away. You can feel a bit untouchable but for what end? You're gonna be arrested 99% of the time," a former teen hacker who was arrested nine years ago and now works in cyber-security said.

This article from 1Kosmos discusses the "Scattered Spider" (also known as UNC3944, Octo Tempest, or Muddled Libra) cybercriminal group's attacks on British retail giants Marks & Spencer and Co-op in May 2025, and how organizations can prevent such breaches.

3. Require multi-factor authentication for all users.
4. Train employees to recognize voice phishing; treat unsolicited calls/messages requesting credentials or app approvals as suspicious.
5. Never include passwords, API keys, or access tokens in support tickets.

--- SOURCE 1: Analysis of Enforcement Action by the ICO in 2025 | URM Consulting ---
URL: https://www.urmconsulting.com/blog/analysis-of-enforcement-action-by-the-ico-in-2025-actions-way-down-security-data-breach-fines-way-up

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog by Stuart Skelly, a Senior Consultant at URM, analyzes the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) enforcement activity in the UK for the calendar year 2025, comparing trends against 2024. The central theme is a marked drop-off in the number of enforcement actions combined with a significant increase in the value of fines issued.

Key findings:
- The ICO took only 31 enforcement actions in 2025, half the frequency of 2024 (which saw 62 actions against 47 organisations). Of the 7 public sector organisations, 3 were police forces (with Greater Manchester Police receiving two reprimands in 6 months).
- 17 of the 31 actions were for breaches of the DPA and UK GDPR. Private sector organisations comprised nearly half of those enforced against under UK GDPR/DPA in 2025, versus only about one-eighth in 2024.
- The ICO issued or supported the courts in issuing 15 fines. Only one fine was applied to a public body: an £18,000 penalty against the charity Birthlink for the unnecessary destruction of thousands of adoption records.
- The largest fines of 2025 were security-related breaches following cyber attacks: £14m against Capita plc and Capita Pension Solutions Limited (combined), £3.07m against Advanced Computer Software Group Ltd, £2.31m against 23andMe Inc, and £1.23m against LastPass UK Ltd. A £60,000 fine was also issued to law firm DPP Law for data loss from a cyber attack, plus two smaller court-issued fines against individuals.
- PECR fines totalled only £1.025m in 2025 versus about £20.68m for UK GDPR violations—a reversal from 2024 when PECR breaches dominated.
- The average fine rocketed nearly tenfold from approximately £150K in 2024 to £1.45 million in 2025. The 15 fines brought in around £21.7m to the Treasury, eight times the 2024 yield. Just over half (8) of the fines exceeded £100,000.
- Six of the seven UK GDPR-related reprimands went to public sector bodies, consistent with the ICO's stated policy of not fining public authorities since it is ultimately taxpayers who pay. Two enforcement notices were issued to public bodies for failures in dealing with subject access requests; all other 7 enforcement notices went to private companies for PECR breaches.
- Enforcement activity declined sharply despite, not because of, a drop in complaints—the ICO received over 42,300 data protection complaints in 2024/25, up ~2,500 from the prior year. Civil society groups, academics, and lawyers wrote to the parliamentary Science, Innovation and Technology Committee calling for an inquiry into what they called a 'collapse' in ICO enforcement, prompted in part by the ICO's decision not to investigate the Ministry of Defence after a severe data breach leaking details of over 19,000 Afghans fleeing the Taliban.
- In contrast to earlier concerns, the ICO took no enforcement action in 2025 related to cookies, suggesting its verbal crackdown on top websites' cookie compliance has worked as intended.
- The planned increase of the PECR penalty cap to £17.5 million in 2026 (aligning it with the UK GDPR maximum) is unlikely to have an immediate impact since no PECR fines approached the current £500,000 statutory maximum.

The article concludes with URM's promotional content offering GDPR consultancy services (gap analysis, DSAR support, vDPO, and training courses including BCS CDP certification) to help organisations avoid ICO enforcement action.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

In total, these 15 fines brought in around £21.7m to the Treasury, which is eight times the fine yield for 2024"

--- SOURCE 2: Recent ICO Data Breach Enforcement Emphasizes ... ---
URL: https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/2026/02/recent-ico-data-breach-enforcement

SUMMARY:
<summary>
In the final quarter of 2025, the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) issued GDPR fines totaling £15 million against Capita (including Capita Pension Solutions Limited) and LastPass UK Limited for data breaches resulting from cyberattacks. The fines provide insight into the ICO's current enforcement approach.

Key themes from the decisions:
1. Proactive cybersecurity risk assessment is essential. The ICO fined Capita £14 million on 15 October 2025, finding that inadequate security penetration testing, insufficient security operations center staffing, and poor administrator access controls created a "foreseeable and avoidable risk" exploited by the threat actor. The ICO did not accept cost or time as excuses for security shortcomings and extensively cited UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) guidance in determining "appropriate" security measures.

2. Companies should consider using privilege to protect internal documents. The Capita decision cited internal security documents (e.g., penetration tests) that highlighted weaknesses, so companies should consider conducting testing under privilege where appropriate.

3. There is a high bar for mitigating factors. The ICO fined LastPass £1.2 million on 20 November 2025, noting that despite "good" cooperation, it did not go "beyond what is reasonably to be expected." In Capita, prompt GDPR notification within 14 hours (well before the 72-hour deadline) was not considered a mitigating factor.

4. Fines can be assessed on holding or investment companies' revenue. The ICO based its LastPass fine on the global revenue of its holding company (consistent with EU case law), resulting in a fine of approximately 8.5% of LastPass' turnover. Private equity sponsors and investment companies should note this when budgeting compliance plans and framing corporate "group" entities.

Immediate actions recommended for companies: benchmark cybersecurity against NCSC guidance, review privacy policies/security testing/incident response plans, consider internal records wording and privilege utilization, establish effective ICO engagement models, and conduct tabletop data breach simulations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
These fines underscore the ICO’s emphasis on data breach enforcement and provide insight into the ICO’s approach to investigations and enforcement., "Companies should consider benchmarking cybersecurity against NCSC guidance, reviewing and updating incident response policies, and weighing the use of privilege in internal security documentation.", The ICO based its fine calculation on the global revenue of the holding company (not just the revenue of LastPass), resulting in a significant fine representing approximately 8.5% of LastPass’ turnover.

--- SOURCE 3: The LastPass ICO £1.2M Privacy Fine - Captain Compliance ---
URL: https://captaincompliance.com/education/the-lastpass-ico-1-2m-privacy-fine

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Captain Compliance analyzes the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) £1.2 million fine issued to LastPass for the 2022 data breach that affected 1.6 million British users. The author argues the penalty is inadequate compared to the actual harm, noting cryptocurrency thefts exceeding $438 million directly attributed to cracked LastPass vaults.

The breach unfolded in two stages in August 2022. Stage One involved attackers compromising a LastPass developer's corporate MacBook Pro, gaining access to the development environment and exfiltrating 14 of approximately 200 source code repositories containing production credentials. Stage Two exploited CVE-2020-5741, a known Plex Media Server vulnerability on a senior DevOps engineer's personal laptop. This allowed attackers to install a keylogger, capture the engineer's master password (shared between personal and business vaults), and gain access to AWS keys and decryption keys for LastPass's backup database, stealing encrypted vault data and personal information of millions of users.

Key timeline of cryptocurrency thefts attributed to the breach: October 2023 ($4.4 million), January 2024 ($150 million from Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen), February 2024 ($6.2 million), May 2024 (over $250 million total), December 2024 ($12.38 million), and April 2025 (over $50 million). Blockchain investigator ZachXBT tracked stolen funds; in March 2025, US authorities seized ~$24 million, with the FBI and Secret Service confirming the thefts stem from cracked LastPass vaults.

The article highlights legal failures including inadequate risk assessments, poor third-party risk management, insufficient privileged access controls, and misleading breach communications. Comparative penalties noted: British Airways fined £20 million (400,000 customers), Marriott £18.4 million (339 million customers), versus LastPass's £0.75 per affected user.

For privacy counsel, the article offers eight lessons: security theater kills; privileged access demands special treatment; personal device policies need enforcement; incident communications create legal exposure; "no evidence of decryption" isn't "no risk"; zero-knowledge architecture failed its promise; regulatory penalties don't reflect actual harm; and third-party software on employee devices is organizational risk. The breach continues generating new victims into 2025, creating an unusual situation where harm escalates over time rather than diminishing. LastPass faces ongoing US class action litigation that could dwarf the ICO fine.
</summary>

"Your passwords and notes vault have been copied by hackers in an attempt to decrypt your vault and steal ALL of its contents. It is only a matter of time and effort before they are able to access your data… Even if you do that, if you stored anything of value in there that you can't change, you are still screwed." - Security researcher Taylor Monahan

--- SOURCE 10: The UK’s proposed Cyber Security and Resilience Bill ---
URL: https://www.hlc.com/en/publications/the-uks-proposed-cyber-security-and-resilience-bill

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Hogan Lovells publication analyzes the UK's proposed Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, introduced to Parliament on 12 November 2025. It is the first major overhaul of UK cybersecurity legislation in almost a decade, designed to strengthen essential and digital services against cyber attacks with a strong emphasis on national security. The Bill amends the existing UK NIS Regulations in three primary ways:

**Expanded Scope:** UK NIS currently applies to operators of essential services (utilities, transportation, healthcare) and certain digital services providers (cloud computing, online search, online marketplaces). The Bill extends coverage to data centres, managed service providers, large electrical load controllers, and entities designated as "critical suppliers" — allowing regulators to designate companies in any sector as critical if they supply goods/services to UK NIS organizations where disruption could significantly impact the economy or society.

**Reporting Requirements:** The Bill lowers the threshold for notifiable incidents (now requiring incidents capable of having an adverse effect on network/Information system security). Organisations must make an initial notification within 24 hours of becoming aware of an incident, followed by a full notification within 72 hours, aligning the UK with EU NIS2 requirements. Reportable incidents must also be notified in parallel to the National Cyber Security Centre (part of GCHQ). Regulators can share incident information with relevant international authorities and inform the public when necessary.

**Expanded Regulatory and Government Powers:** Regulators gain power to charge fees (both periodic charges for oversight and specific charges for individual organisations). The maximum financial penalty will change from £17m to the greater of £17m or 4% of an undertaking's global turnover — aligned with UK GDPR. The Bill grants the Secretary of State the discretionary power to direct regulated entities to take steps mitigating imminent/live threats to UK national security, with enforcement fines of 10% of turnover or £17m for contravening such directions, and allows directors to forgo consultation if delay would harm national security.

**Comparison to EU NIS 2:** While the Bill aligns with NIS 2 on expansion of scope and stricter reporting, it diverges by: applying to fewer sectors; not imposing personal liability for management; allowing designation of critical suppliers; providing significant new powers to the SoS; introducing cost recovery through fees; and setting maximum fines at £17m or 4% global turnover (vs. €10M or 2% under NIS 2).

**Timeline:** No public timeline has been set, but the Government is anticipated to pass the legislation by the end of the current Parliamentary session in Spring 2026, with detailed compliance requirements expected via future secondary legislation. Authored by Dan Whitehead, Robert Gardener, Michaela Glass, Edward Roberts, and Jabeen Rizvi.

- The Report covers **3,383 major incidents** reported in 2025 across all EU financial sectors, equating to approximately **0.18 major ICT-related incidents per financial entity** subject to DORA.

--- SOURCE 14: DORA Compliance for Third-Party Risk Management ---
URL: https://www.neotas.com/dora-compliance-for-third-party-risk-management

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Neotas provides a comprehensive guide to DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act, Regulation EU 2022/2554) compliance, with a focus on third-party risk management (TPRM) for financial services firms in 2026. DORA applies to approximately 22,000 EU financial entities and has been fully in force since 17 January 2025, with no remaining deadlines. It directly supersedes NIS2 for EU financial entities under Article 1(2). Enforcement is active and interventionist in 2026, with regulators examining firms for compliance evidence rather than remediation plans.

**Scope and Penalties:** DORA applies to 20 categories of EU-regulated financial entities (banks, insurers, investment firms, payment institutions, crypto-asset providers, etc.), with proportionality provisions for smaller entities and microenterprises (under 10 employees, turnover below €2m) that still cannot opt out of third-party obligations. Non-EU firms serving EU-regulated clients fall in scope via their clients' Article 28 obligations. Penalties include fines up to 10% of annual global turnover or €10 million for serious breaches; individual senior managers face fines up to €1 million (personal liability); and public disclosure of non-compliance decisions.

**Five Pillars:** (1) ICT risk management (Articles 5-16); (2) Incident management (Articles 17-23) with 4-hour initial, 72-hour intermediate, and 1-month final reporting; (3) Resilience testing (Articles 24-27) with annual basic testing and TLPT every 3 years via TIBER-EU for systemically important firms; (4) ICT third-party risk (Articles 28-30) — carrying the highest compliance gap rate; (5) Information sharing (Articles 45-49).

**Article 28 (TPRM Programme):** Requires a formal ICT TPRM programme embedded in governance with board accountability, pre-contractual due diligence covering substitutability, insolvency risk, data protection and subcontracting chains (Article 28(4)), multi-vendor strategy, continuous monitoring and exit strategies. A standalone vendor questionnaire does not satisfy Article 28. Critical or Important Function (CIF) classification per Article 3(22) is materially important — under-classification creates enforcement risk.

**Register of Information (ROI, Article 28(3)):** Must be built to the ESAs' ITS data model and submitted to national competent authorities at entity, sub-consolidated and consolidated levels. Only 6.5% of nearly 1,000 firms passed all 116 data quality checks in the 2024 ESA dry-run. Common failures: incomplete contract data, missing subcontractor information, incorrect CIF classifications. Spreadsheet-based ROIs fail at scale. The 2026 submission cycle (reference date 31 December 2025) faces higher expectations.

**Article 29 (Concentration Risk):** Requires portfolio-level analysis, not individual vendor scorecards. The ECB found more than 30% of significant banks' outsourcing budgets concentrate on just 10 ICT providers. Firms must assess concentration before new CIF arrangements, develop exit strategies and report to the management body.

**Article 30 (Contractual Requirements):** All ICT contracts must include service description/performance levels, data locations with change notification, audit rights, incident notification, business continuity and termination rights. CIF contracts add exit assistance and full sub-contractor disclosure. No grace period for legacy contracts — gaps must be addressed at next renewal. Regulators sample-check provisions against the mandatory list.

**UK Application:** DORA does not directly bind UK-only firms (which fall under FCA PS21/3, PRA SS1/21, SMCR and UK Critical Third Parties regime PS24/16). But UK firms with EU subsidiaries/branches, UK group IT functions serving EU entities, or UK ICT providers serving EU clients are in scope through those relationships. DORA breaches can trigger personal SMCR liability for UK Senior Managers with EU responsibilities. DORA standards generally satisfy FCA/PRA expectations, but not vice versa.

**2026 Enforcement:** First ROI submission cycle is active; 19 ICT providers were designated as Critical ICT Third-Party Providers (CTPPs) in November 2025 facing direct ESA oversight; ECB finalised its Guide on outsourcing cloud services in July 2025. **Regulatory Context and Timeline:**
- DORA, alongside MiCAR, is a key component of the EU's Digital Finance Package aimed at harmonizing ICT risk management and strengthening EU financial market resilience
- DORA was first proposed in September 2020, formally adopted in December 2022 (Regulation EU 2022/2554), with a two-year transition period. The first package of RTS/ITS technical standards was published in January 2023, the second in July 2024, and DORA became fully applicable in January 2025

**The Five Key Areas of DORA:**
1. **ICT Risk Management** (Art. 5-11): Requires internal governance frameworks, comprehensive ICT risk management frameworks, and operational resilience. The RTS adopted January 2024 establishes requirements for both the ICT Risk Management Framework and a Simplified ICT Risk Management Framework (SICTRMF)
2. **Incident Management, Classification & Reporting**: Significant incidents must be reported with specific timelines - initial notification within 4 hours of classification (no later than 24 hours after incident), intermediate report within 72 hours, and final report within 1 month
3. **Digital Operational Resilience Testing**: Includes vulnerability scans, penetration tests, and TLPT (Threat-Led Penetration Testing) for systemically important institutions at least every three years. TLPT follows a three-phase approach (Preparation, Test, Closure) and must be validated by supervisory authorities

Italy aligned through D.Lgs. 23/2025 (March 2025), distinguishing severe violations (e.g., banks: €30K to 10% of annual turnover) and less severe violations (e.g., banks: €30K to 7% of turnover)
