# Fintech Breach Statistics 2025: $7B Lost to Crypto Hacks & 27% of Global Breaches

Fintech now accounts for 27% of all data breaches, averaging $5.9M per incident. Learn the key breach trends, crypto losses, third-party risks, and how penetration testing helps stop attacks before they strike.

![Mohammed Khalil](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2F7df7289653fb2cdfadbec4356da5fc1e947d6c40-1024x1024.jpg&w=64&q=75)

Mohammed Khalil

![Featured Image](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2Fcf1e8188dceea7d315f59f8ed65f04055ec9fb1e-2144x1198.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

* **Fintech breaches are surging, finance** made up **27% of global breaches in 2023**, with an **average cost of $5.90M** per incident.
* **Crypto platforms** have lost over **$7 billion** to hacks: **$3.7B (2022)**, **$1.7B (2023)**, and **$2.2B (2024)**.
* A **SecurityScorecard** study found **41.8% of fintech breaches** originate from **third-party vendors**.
* Commonly exposed data: **customer PII**, including names, addresses, licenses, and **financial transaction data**.
* **Notable cases:** Revolut, Cash App, Ronin, Lemonade, Finastra, and Coinbase.
* **Mitigation:** prioritize [**penetration testing**](https://deepstrike.io/services/penetration-testing-services), **continuous monitoring**, and **anti-phishing programs** to stay ahead of attackers.

## **What are Fintech Breach Statistics?**

![Digital illustration of a holographic data sphere displaying fintech breach metrics ($5.9M cost, 27% global share, $7B crypto losses) surrounded by a glowing DeepStrike shield representing security through analytics.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2F6d57139aee82e9c673d8608565e6d6f08d762591-1536x1024.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

Within [**broader cybersecurity statistics**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/cybersecurity-statistics), fintech breach statistics refer to data on cybersecurity incidents affecting financial technology companies, banks, digital wallets, crypto exchanges, and insurtech companies. These stats include breach frequency, costs, data types exposed, and trends over time. In practical terms, we track how often fintech firms are attacked, what is stolen, and the financial impact. This matters because fintech handles sensitive financial data, so breaches can erode trust and incur huge losses.

Fintech breaches have **spiked** in recent years. For example, Kroll’s 2024 report found the financial sector jumped to [**27% of all breaches handled**](https://www.kroll.com/en/publications/cyber/data-breach-outlook-2024#:~:text=In%202023%2C%20finance%20was%20the,of%20breaches) in 2023 up from 19% in 2022. In other words, **1 in 4 breaches** Kroll dealt with was in finance. This aligns with more publicized hacks crypto thefts, bank hacks, payment app incidents and suggests fintech is now the most attacked industry. As DeepStrike cybersecurity analysts note, attackers see fintech as high value targets rich data and direct money transfers.

These statistics are critical now because fintech is booming. Rapid digital adoption online banking, mobile wallets, crypto expands the attack surface. High profile incidents see below and regulatory fines underscore that breaches aren’t hypothetical they happen frequently and cost millions. Companies like DeepStrike often advise clients that **knowing the stats** helps prioritize security: e.g. focusing on third party risk or insider threats if those drive most breaches.

## **Key Breach Trends & Data 2020- 2025**

![Infographic timeline from 2020 to 2025 showing major fintech breach data — $3.7B stolen in 2022, $1.7B in 2023, $2.2B in 2024 — with DeepStrike’s defense trend rising through the timeline.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2Fefd678a6a96969542ea87df0ccc86774b30565ea-1536x1024.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

### **Year by Year Breakdown**

* **2020- 2021:** Data is scarce, but early crypto hacks like Poly Network’s [**$611M**](https://www.kroll.com/en/publications/cyber/data-breach-outlook-2024#:~:text=In%202023%2C%20finance%20was%20the,of%20breaches) exploit in 2021 hinted at trouble. Pandemic era shifts saw attackers probe banks and neobanks, but fintech wasn’t yet the top breach target. Kroll saw finance at 22% of breaches in 2021.
* **2022:** Crypto platforms **suffered the largest losses**. Chainalysis reports [**$3.7B stolen**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/crypto-crime-report-2025) from crypto exchanges/DeFi in 2022 more than any prior year. Notable fintech breaches included:
  + **Revolut UK** A payments/ATM glitch allowed [**$20M+**](https://cybermagazine.com/cyber-security/revolut-hacked-as-cyber-criminals-steal-us-20m#:~:text=resulting%20in%20Revolut%20losing%20nearly,US%2423m) fraud and exposed 50,150 user records names, emails, etc.
  + **Cash App USA** Insider leak of investing account data: [**8.2 million**](https://www.upguard.com/blog/how-did-the-cash-app-data-breach-happen#:~:text=Cash%20App%20notified%20approximately%208,and%20its%20parent%20company%2C%20Block) customers had names, account numbers, portfolio info exposed.
  + **PayPal** Credential stuffing attack on [**35K accounts**](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/paypal-credential-stuffing-attack/640804/#:~:text=,birth%2C%20the%20company%20said%20Wednesday) exposed names, addresses, SSNs.
* Regulators noted finance remained the 2nd most breached sector 19% of incidents in one Kroll study. Overall, fintech was in the crosshairs of both targeted hacks and insider exploits.
* **2023:** Finance became the #1 breached industry. Kroll’s data breach outlook reports finance at **27% of breaches** handled in 2023. Crypto thefts continued: Chainalysis recorded **$1.7B** stolen from crypto platforms down 54% from 2022’s [**$3.7B**](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2024/#:~:text=year%E2%80%99s%20Crypto%20Crime%20Report%20go,2022%20to%20231%20in%202023), including the Ronin Network hack [**$625M**](https://www.coinbase.com/bytes/archive/axie-infinity-625-million-dollar-hack-explained#:~:text=Last%20week%2C%20in%20what%E2%80%99s%20being,Let%E2%80%99s%20take%20a%20closer%20look) loss. Traditional fintech firms also suffered:
  + **Finastra UK** Early signs in Nov 2024 reported by some sources of a massive data leak [**400 GB**](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2024/11/fintech-giant-finastra-investigating-data-breach/#:~:text=has%20learned,purportedly%20stolen%20from%20the%20company) of bank client records.
  + **Lemonade USA** Auto insurtech glitch exposed [**190K**](https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/breaking-news/lemonade-attributes-data-breach-to-technical-issue-in-auto-insurance-quote-system-532588.aspx#:~:text=Insurtech%20firm%20Lemonade%20Inc,of%20approximately%20190%2C000%20insurance%20applicants) driver’s license numbers in 2025.
  + **Coinbase USA** In May 2025, bribed agents leaked limited customer data names, masked SSNs, balances; no funds stolen, but a $20M ransom demand ensued.
* DeepStrike consultants note 2023 saw [**social engineering surge**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/social-engineering-statistics-2025) Kroll saw BEC increase 21% YoY and [**supply chain attacks**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/supply-chain-attack-statistics-2025) MOVEit, vendor hacks cause many fintech breaches.
* **2024:** Crypto theft hit [**$2.2B**](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2025/#:~:text=In%202024%2C%20funds%20stolen%20increased,2023%20to%20303%20in%202024) up 21% from 2023, driven by large exchange hacks e.g. DMM Bitcoin $305M. Fintech continues seeing diverse attacks from ransomware on banks to data leaks at insurers e.g. Lemonade. SecurityScorecard finds [**18.4%**](https://securityscorecard.com/company/press/securityscorecard-report-links-41-8-of-breaches-impacting-leading-fintech-companies-to-third-party-vendors/#:~:text=,more%20than%20double%20the%20global) of top fintechs had public breaches, and nearly half of those had repeat incidents. In short, 2024 kept fintech in the breach headlines.
* **2025 so far:** Early incidents include the Coinbase breach and regulatory fines e.g. PayPal’s $2M settlement in NY for 2022 phishing lapses. Security analysts expect continued pressure on fintech as regulators tighten oversight.

### **Global Distribution**

![Digital illustration of a holographic world map showing fintech breach intensity by region (red zones in U.S., U.K., and APAC) with blue-gold defense networks representing DeepStrike’s global cybersecurity coverage.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2Fedc573ef41d2bf5c0c4740bcc92093bfc74db56d-1536x1024.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

Fintech breaches are **global**. The US leads with many incidents Coinbase, PayPal, Lemonade, Root, Cash App. The UK/EU have high profile cases Revolut, Finastra and strict GDPR fines. Asia Pacific sees frequent crypto exchange hacks Coincheck, WazirX, KuCoin, DPRK linked attacks accounted for $660M in 2023, $1.34B in 2024. Emerging markets are also targeted: data leaks affect millions in Brazil, India, etc. Essentially, any country with active digital finance is at risk.

### **What Data Gets Stolen?**

![Digital illustration of a transparent data vault revealing five layers of stolen fintech data (PII, financial, credentials, IDs, crypto) intercepted by DeepStrike’s blue-gold shield network.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2F017ad88d396fef70ddf8b9e3d35b1c2a539ef728-1536x1024.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

Typical fintech breaches leak:

* **Personal Data PII:** Names, addresses, emails, phone numbers are common. Revolut’s 2022 breach leaked names, addresses and emails for [**50K+**](https://cybermagazine.com/cyber-security/revolut-hacked-as-cyber-criminals-steal-us-20m#:~:text=resulting%20in%20Revolut%20losing%20nearly,US%2423m) users. Lemonade’s 2025 leak exposed driver’s license numbers for [**190K**](https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/breaking-news/lemonade-attributes-data-breach-to-technical-issue-in-auto-insurance-quote-system-532588.aspx#:~:text=Insurtech%20firm%20Lemonade%20Inc,of%20approximately%20190%2C000%20insurance%20applicants) applicants.
* **Financial Data:** Account numbers, card details, balances. Example: Slim CD UK payment processor leaked [**1.7M**](https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/hotforsecurity/hackers-breach-payment-service-provider-slim-cd-credit-card-data-of-1-7-million-people-exposed#:~:text=A%20recent%20data%20breach%20affecting,7%20million%20credit%20card%20owners) credit cards numbers, expiry dates. Cash App insiders took account IDs and portfolio info of [**8.2M**](https://www.upguard.com/blog/how-did-the-cash-app-data-breach-happen#:~:text=Cash%20App%20notified%20approximately%208,and%20its%20parent%20company%2C%20Block) users.
* **Credentials:** Less common, but highly damaging. The PayPal attack obtained logins via credential stuffing affecting [**35K**](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/paypal-credential-stuffing-attack/640804/#:~:text=,birth%2C%20the%20company%20said%20Wednesday) accounts. In crypto, stolen private keys can instantly drain wallets e.g. Ronin, Wormhole.
* **Specialized Data:** Insurers often leak SSNs/licenses Root, Noblr, Lemonade have all paid fines for such leaks. Crypto breaches often don’t expose user data they just lose funds.

### **Financial Impact**

![Infographic showing a financial “risk waterfall” from direct losses to reputational impact, with DeepStrike’s blue-gold defense line reversing breach costs through proactive security testing.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2F23c4cabd6b7653ebd6e8469980192a01d7cea85e-1536x1024.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

The costs are **staggering**. Direct theft in crypto reached **billions per year**: Chainalysis tallies [**$3.7B**](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2024/#:~:text=year%E2%80%99s%20Crypto%20Crime%20Report%20go,2022%20to%20231%20in%202023) stolen in 2022, $1.7B in 2023, $2.2B in 2024. Meanwhile, remediation costs for companies are millions. IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach reports show finance firms averaging [**$5.90M**](https://www.idquantique.com/random-number-generation/applications/banking/#:~:text=In%20parallel%2C%20IBM%20and%20Ponemon%E2%80%99s,number%20two%20after%20healthcare) per breach versus $4.45M overall. And breaches linger: over 50% of [**breach costs**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/data-breach-statistics-2025) occur after one year.

Beyond direct losses, regulators are punishing breaches. For example, PayPal paid [**$2.0M**](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/paypal-credential-stuffing-attack/640804/#:~:text=,birth%2C%20the%20company%20said%20Wednesday) in 2025 for a 2022 credential stuffing failure, and insurers Root/Noblr paid $975K/$500K for quote data leaks affecting tens of thousands.

Customers also bear costs: identity theft, fraud, leaked crypto funds unsurprisingly, victims of Lazarus Group hacks have lost millions.

Finance sector breaches rose sharply [**27%**](https://www.kroll.com/en/publications/cyber/data-breach-outlook-2024#:~:text=In%202023%2C%20finance%20was%20the,of%20breaches) of Kroll cases in 2023. IBM says [**$5.90M**](https://www.idquantique.com/random-number-generation/applications/banking/#:~:text=In%20parallel%2C%20IBM%20and%20Ponemon%E2%80%99s,number%20two%20after%20healthcare) average breach cost for finance. Chainalysis: $7+ billion in crypto stolen 2022- 2024. SecurityScorecard: [**41.8%**](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2025/#:~:text=In%202024%2C%20funds%20stolen%20increased,2023%20to%20303%20in%202024) of fintech breaches via third parties. These figures highlight why fintech security is now mission critical.

## **Breach Incidents by Fintech Subsector**

The table below compares example breaches across fintech industries:

| Subsector | Example Breach Year | Data Compromised | Impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Crypto Exchanges & DeFi | Ronin Network Mar 2023 | None just funds stolen | $625M stolen |
| Neobanks/Digital Banks | Revolut 2022 | PII names, addresses, emails, partial card data | 50,150 users; $23M lost |
| Payments & Wallet Apps | Cash App/Block Dec 2022 | PII & financials names, brokerage account IDs, portfolio data | 8.2M users |
| Payments/Cards | SlimCD Jun 2024 | Card data names, card numbers, expiry dates, addresses | 1.7M credit cards |
| Payment Providers | PayPal Dec 2022 | Account credentials/PII names, SSNs, etc. | 35K accounts |
| Insurtech | Lemonade Apr 2025 | PII 190K driver’s license numbers | 190K applicants |
| Fintech Service Provider | Finastra Nov 2024 | Client financial data 400 GB from banks | Enterprise clients; unknown cost |

This mix of examples illustrates that **everyone is at risk**. Crypto bridges see multi million thefts of coins. Challenger banks suffer both fraud and data leaks. Payment apps face insider leaks and credential stuffing. And even service providers like Finastra can spill sensitive files for top banks. The stolen data ranges from basic PII to massive sums of money.

## **Why Fintech Breaches Are Rising**

![Infographic showing four rising red curves (value, connectivity, insider risk, and legacy systems) converging toward a breach epicenter, surrounded by DeepStrike’s glowing blue-gold containment ring.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2F6ce80bf903ce15236b5230a3780fffb214b50e80-1536x1024.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

Several factors fuel fintech breach stats:

* **High Value Targets:** Fintech holds both data and money, so criminals are incentivized. Attackers seek quick profit stealing crypto or funds or juicy PII for resale.
* **Complex Attack Surface:** Fintech often involves many systems: web/mobile apps, APIs, cloud services, third party integrations, IoT devices, ATMs, PoS terminals. This complexity creates vulnerabilities: in fact, SecurityScorecard finds the weakest spots are **application security** and exposed supply chain tools.
* **Third Party Risk:** Fintechs rely on vendors, cloud platforms, payment processors, data brokers. A single partner breach can cascade: [**41.8%**](https://securityscorecard.com/company/press/securityscorecard-report-links-41-8-of-breaches-impacting-leading-fintech-companies-to-third-party-vendors/#:~:text=NEW%20YORK%20%E2%80%94%20May%2021%2C,Based%20on%20a%20comprehensive) of fintech breaches originated via third party vendors. DeepStrike’s experience underscores that supply chain attacks like MOVEit based ransomware have repeatedly hit banks and fintech clients.
* **Insider Threats:** As seen with Cash App, a rogue employee can cause huge leaks. Fintech insiders have access to critical data and should be monitored.
* **Legacy Security Gaps:** New fintech startups may push features faster than security. Common coding flaws SQL injection, SSRF, etc. and misconfigurations remain. For example, API bugs have led to breaches Revolut’s refund flaw.
* **Social Engineering:** Financial users are targets for phishing. Kroll reports a 21% jump in BEC/phishing in 2023, and banks often see credential stuffing PayPal or phishing induced account takeovers. See our [**account takeover case study**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/full-account-takeover-through-deeplink-vulnerability) for PayPal’s breach.
* **Crypto Specific Risks:** Crypto and DeFi use smart contracts and private keys. Bugs or poor key management lead to multi million hacks. Chain bridges like Ronin have repeatedly failed security audits.

In short, fintech firms are rich targets with hard problems. Attackers adapt rapidly, so **continuous vigilance** is needed.

## **Mitigations: Security Best Practices**

![Infographic of an eight-segment cyber defense wheel labeled with fintech best practices (testing, coding, red teaming, MFA, vendor risk, encryption, response, awareness) orbiting around the DeepStrike shield logo.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2Ff4757cf2237d5ed9a01d4232a0d2959cd9c1a334-1536x1024.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

The good news: knowing these stats guides defenses. Fintech security teams can take action:

1. **Penetration Testing** Regularly simulate attacks on fintech apps and networks. DeepStrike recommends investing in robust penetration testing services and continuous penetration testing platforms to uncover flaws before attackers do. For example, testing payment APIs, mobile apps, and cloud configurations can find the OWASP Top 10 issues that fintech breaches often exploit. [**PTaaS** Penetration Testing as a Service provides](https://deepstrike.io/blog/penetration-testing-as-a-service-ptaas) ongoing pen tests, ideal for dynamic fintech environments.
2. **Secure Coding & Reviews** Follow OAuth security best practices for authorizing transactions and use token audits to avoid JWT exploits. Enforce strong input validation to prevent common web vulnerabilities like SQL injection or SSRF. Use automated tools SAST/DAST alongside manual code reviews.
3. **Threat Modeling & Red Teaming** Think like an attacker. Conduct red team exercises to test phishing resilience see our [**phishing attack trends and statistics**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/Phishing-Statistics-2025) and incident response. Simulate supply chain attacks to see if vendors could bring you down.
4. **Strong Authentication** Enforce MFA everywhere. Phishing and credential reuse still drive many breaches. Use identity solutions e.g. device based login, behavioral analytics. DeepStrike has helped fintech clients deploy MFA and bot mitigation to cut account takeover risk.
5. **Third Party Risk Management** Vet and monitor all vendors. Since [**42%**](https://securityscorecard.com/company/press/securityscorecard-report-links-41-8-of-breaches-impacting-leading-fintech-companies-to-third-party-vendors/#:~:text=NEW%20YORK%20%E2%80%94%20May%2021%2C,Based%20on%20a%20comprehensive) of breaches came via partners, fintechs must implement strict vendor security reviews and require breach notifications/contracts. If a key provider shows vulnerabilities, isolate or replace it quickly. This ties to broader supply chain attack statistics concerns.
6. **Data Encryption & Tokenization** Store PII and financial data encrypted at rest and in transit. If credentials or files are stolen, encryption can prevent misuse. Tokenize card data PCI standards so breaches leak useless tokens instead of raw numbers.
7. **Backup & Incident Response** Keep immutable backups to resist ransomware and regularly test incident plans. This helps limit downtime and costs after a breach. For compliance, recall**: [PCI DSS section 11.3](https://deepstrike.io/blog/pci-dss-penetration-testing-2025-guide)**, [**SOC 2**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/soc-2-penetration-testing-2025), and [**HIPAA**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/hipaa-penetration-testing-2025-guide) require such exercises.
8. **Employee Training** Teach staff to spot phishing, secure development, and proper data handling. Many breaches exploit human error. This ties into phishing trends and statistics and human factor mitigation.

As one DeepStrike consultant puts it: Fintech security is not a one off checkbox; it’s an ongoing practice. Leveraging Penetration Testing Services and secure engineering is not just ideal but necessary. Even simple fixes patching servers, closing idle ports, [**DDoS protection**](https://deepstrike.io/blog/ddos-attack-statistics) add up. Given the stakes, fintechs should budget for continuous testing and advanced monitoring tools like XDR or CSPM. In short, **secure by design** must be a priority.

Fintech breach statistics show one thing clearly: **the threat is real and escalating**. From massive crypto thefts to sneaky API vulnerabilities, the attacks of 2025 demand more than just awareness they require action. DeepStrike’s hands-on experience affirms that breaches in fintech cost millions and erode trust. The solutions are proactive: **regular [Penetration Testing Services](https://deepstrike.io/blog/penetration-testing-services)**, vigilant monitoring, and strong security culture.

**Ready to Strengthen Your Defenses?** The threats of 2025 demand readiness. If you need to validate your security posture, identify hidden risks, or build a resilient defense, DeepStrike can help. Our team of expert penetration testers and red teamers provides clear, actionable guidance to protect your fintech business.

![Digital illustration of a cybersecurity professional activating a holographic blue-gold shield labeled with DeepStrike’s fintech testing and defense services, protecting a digital financial skyline from red attack vectors.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2Fa3jopls3%2Ftestdataset%2F97e1b365ea6ff1f133a395366bf3c087c6073bb7-1536x1024.jpg&w=3840&q=80)

Explore our [**penetration testing services**](https://deepstrike.io/penetration-testing-services) to see how we uncover vulnerabilities before attackers do. [**Drop us a line**](https://deepstrike.io/contact) we’re always ready to dive in.

**About the Author**Mohammed Khalil is a Cybersecurity Architect at DeepStrike, specializing in advanced penetration testing and offensive security operations. With certifications including CISSP, OSCP, and OSWE, he has led numerous red team engagements for Fortune 500 companies, focusing on cloud security, application vulnerabilities, and adversary emulation. His work involves dissecting complex attack chains and developing resilient defense strategies for clients in the finance, healthcare, and technology sectors.

## **FAQs**

* **How common are fintech data breaches?**

Very common. Breaches in the financial sector have surged in 2023, finance topped breach counts 27% of Kroll cases. SecurityScorecard found 18.4% of top fintechs had public breaches by 2024. With many high profile incidents each year, assume any fintech is at risk without proper security.

* **What data is most often stolen in fintech breaches?**

Mostly customer **PII and financial info**. Attackers grab names, emails, addresses, SSNs, and credit card details. Crypto hacks typically steal funds, not personal info. Insurtech breaches often leak SSNs/licenses from quote forms. Any stored credentials or tokens are especially valuable if compromised.

* **How much does a fintech breach cost?**

Extremely costly. IBM’s 2023 report says average **$5.90M** for financial breaches, higher than most industries. Those costs include remediation, fines, legal fees, and customer churn. Crypto losses dwarf that billions stolen, but even a single data leak can force regulatory fines in the millions e.g. fines against PayPal, Lemonade.

* **Are crypto exchanges targeted more than banks?**

Crypto platforms see larger heists due to stored funds on chain. For example, over $7B was stolen from crypto in 2022- 2024. Traditional banks generally deal more in data leaks PII, account takeover. Both face threats: crypto = big money hacks, banks = third party attacks and fraud. In practice, both must secure smart contract code, keys, and customer data.

* **How do phishing and social engineering affect fintech security?**

Greatly. Phishing is a top entry point. Kroll noted a 21% rise in business email compromises in 2023. Many fintech users fall for scams that lead to credential theft. Fintech firms train employees and clients on these threats. We link to phishing attack trends and statistics for more context.

* **Can small fintech startups afford these protections?**

They must try. Breaches at startups can be catastrophic. Solutions like cloud penetration testing or managed security services SOC as a service scale to budget. Regulators also push smaller firms to follow frameworks NIST, ISO 27001. Our advice: prioritize security early it’s cheaper than cleaning up a breach later.

args.summary:
This article from DeepStrike (published Nov 4, 2025, updated July 28, 2026, by cybersecurity architect Mohammed Khalil) analyzes fintech breach statistics. Key findings: finance accounted for 27% of all global data breaches in 2023 (up from 19-22% in prior years), making it the #1 most breached industry, with an average cost of $5.90M per incident (vs. $4.45M global average per IBM). Crypto platforms have lost over $7 billion total: $3.7B in 2022, $1.7B in 2023 (down 54%), and $2.2B in 2024 (up 21%). A SecurityScorecard study found 41.8% of fintech breaches originate from third-party vendors, and only 18.4% of top fintechs had public breaches by 2024.

Notable incidents chronologically include: Revolut UK (2022) — $20-23M fraud via payments/ATM glitch, 50,150 user records exposed; Cash App (Dec 2022) — insider leak of 8.2M customers' data; PayPal (Dec 2022) — credential stuffing affecting 35K accounts; Ronin Network (Mar 2023) — $625M stolen; Finastra (Nov 2024) — 400GB of bank client records leaked; Lemonade (Apr 2025) — 190K driver's license numbers exposed; Coinbase (May 2025) — bribed agents leaked customer data with $20M ransom demand; DMM Bitcoin (2024) — $305M hack.

Affected subsectors span crypto exchanges/DeFi, neobanks, payment apps, card processors (SlimCD leaked 1.7M cards), payment providers, insurtech, and fintech service providers. Stolen data includes customer PII (names, addresses, SSNs, driver's licenses), financial data (account numbers, card details, balances), and credentials.

Factors driving the rise: high-value targets, complex attack surfaces, third-party risk, insider threats, legacy security gaps, social engineering (21% increase in BEC in 2023 per Kroll), and crypto-specific risks (smart contract/private key vulnerabilities).

Mitigation recommendations: regular penetration testing/PTaaS, secure coding and code reviews, threat modeling and red teaming, strong authentication (MFA), third-party risk management, data encryption and tokenization, backup and incident response planning (aligned with PCI DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA), and employee training on phishing.

The article concludes fintech security requires continuous, proactive "secure by design" practices rather than one-time checks, given escalating threats. Factual data in the article contains some internal inconsistencies (e.g., incidents dated 2025 listed under 2023, and Ronin hack listed both as 2022 and out meaning supply via distributed records).

# Cyber Breaches in Banking: Key Risks for Financial Institutions

![Manisha Martin](https://www.atlassystems.com/hubfs/Manisha%20Profile.png)

[Manisha Martin](https://www.atlassystems.com/blog/author/manisha-martin)

![](https://www.atlassystems.com/hubfs/ChatGPT%20Image%20Nov%2027%2c%202025%2c%2003_41_42%20PM.png)

9 min read  |  Last Updated: 14 Aug, 2026

![bolt 1](https://www.atlassystems.com/hubfs/bolt%201.svg)

#### TL;DR

* **$9.36 million average breach cost:** US financial industry data breaches in 2024 cost $9.36 million on average as cybercriminals target valuable customer financial and personal data
* **Six common attack vectors:** Malware and ransomware, phishing schemes, insider threats, third-party vendor vulnerabilities, payment card system breaches, and API exploits threaten bank security
* **Real breaches demonstrate risks:** Capital One's 100 million records stolen through cloud misconfiguration, Flagstar Bank's 837,000 customers affected through MOVEit vendor breach illustrate serious threats
* **Prevention requires multiple layers:** Employee phishing simulations, AI-powered threat detection, zero trust architecture, regular security audits, and continuous third-party assessments reduce breach risk

Financial institutions store highly valuable data, and cybercriminals constantly target them to disrupt services, steal sensitive information, or extort money. Because of this, information security in the financial industry has become a top priority.

A cybersecurity breach in banking occurs when an unauthorized party gains access to computer systems, networks, or data containing sensitive financial information. A cybercriminal may hack a bank’s website and steal valuable customer information (like personal details or account numbers) or hold systems hostage for ransom. Digitalization, advanced hacking techniques, and the high value of financial and personal data all make banks prime targets for cybercriminals.

According to Statista, the average cost of a financial industry data breach in the US in 2024 was [$9.36 million](https://www.statista.com/statistics/463714/cost-data-breach-by-country-or-region/). This blog post explores cybersecurity breaches in banking to help you know how to keep your systems and data safe.

## Common Cybersecurity Breaches in Banking

Malicious actors use different tactics to breach networks and wreak havoc from within your bank systems. Here are the top ones:

### Malware and ransomware

Malware is any program built to disrupt, damage, or expose a computer system. It’s usually distributed through malicious emails, websites, and text messages. Malware’s popular attack methods include viruses, worms, and trojans. Ransomware, a popular type of malware, is often used by cybercriminals to steal data or even shut down operations. They use malicious software to lock users out of their own systems or data until a ransom is paid to restore access.

### Phishing

In this type of attack, cybercriminals use fraudulent emails, websites, or text messages that look legitimate to trick customers or employees into revealing sensitive information like bank account numbers or passwords. Once they gain access, they may infiltrate a bank’s internal systems, steal money, or commit identity theft. In many cases, the target doesn’t realize they’ve been compromised, and the hacker may launch several attacks without anyone suspecting malicious activity.

### Insider threats

Some cybersecurity breaches in banking come from within a bank. Insiders with access to critical data may intentionally or unintentionally give away information or provide an entry point for hackers. They may be disgruntled employees, contractors, business partners, or anyone with physical or remote access to a financial institution. Negligent employees can also give cybercriminals access by leaving devices unlocked or falling for a phishing scheme.

### Third-party vendor vulnerabilities

Hackers love supply chain attacks as they provide high impact for low effort. By compromising one supplier or service provider, attackers can trigger a [third-party data breach](/blog/third-party-data-breach) that exposes multiple financial institutions at once. They can compromise many targets by breaching one supplier or inserting malicious code into a software update. They also use threats like zero‑day exploits, dependency confusion, and typosquatting. According to a report by Cybersecurity Ventures, software supply chain attacks will cost businesses a massive [$138 billion by 2031](https://world.einnews.com/pr_news/659375862/software-supply-chain-attacks-to-cost-the-world-60-billion-by-2025).

The image below shows the sequence of a third-party breach.

### Payment card system breaches

These cybersecurity breaches happen when malicious actors gain unauthorized access to systems storing sensitive payment card information, like credit card numbers and expiration dates. Hackers can steal and misuse this data, causing financial and reputational damage to a bank and its customers.

### API exploits

Here, unauthorized entities exploit vulnerabilities in the API to gain access to a bank’s system or data. This can happen if an API’s security is compromised or insufficient. An API exploit can lead to unauthorized data access, data theft, or even system manipulation to control integral parts.

## Major Real-World Bank Data Breaches

### Case 1: Capital One (2019) - cloud misconfiguration

A former software engineer for Amazon Web Services hacked a server storing Capital One's data and stole [100 million credit card applications](https://www.cnn.com/2019/07/29/business/capital-one-data-breach). Data stolen included social security numbers, bank account numbers, and Canadian social insurance numbers. The data breach affected about 100 million people in the U.S. and over 6 million in Canada.

### Case 2: Flagstar Bank (2023) - third-party breach (MOVEit)

In 2023, cybercriminals breached Flagstar Bank's security and accessed the addresses, phone numbers, Social Security numbers, and tax records of [837,390 Flagstar customers](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/flagstar-sec-fine-cyberattack/736070/). The cause was a third-party vendor, Fiserv, which experienced a breach via the MOVEit Transfer vulnerability. Hackers exploited vulnerabilities in the MOVEit transfer software and used stolen contractor login credentials to gain access.

### Case 3: First Horizon (2021) - credentials compromise

In 2021, an unauthorized party obtained login credentials and exploited a vulnerability in third-party security software to access First Horizon customer accounts. The hackers accessed fewer than 200 online accounts, stole personal information, and withdrew [under $1 million](https://www.americanbanker.com/news/first-horizon-discloses-data-security-breach).

### Federal government institution - US Treasury Department (2024)

In late 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department was the victim of [a supply chain attack](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/feature/Treasury-Department-hacked-Explaining-how-it-happened). The hackers compromised a third-party vendor, BeyondTrust, and exploited vulnerabilities in the remote support software, which the Treasury Department used for technical assistance. They stole a cryptographic key, accessed the Treasury's network, and compromised over 400 computers and thousands of unclassified documents.

### Lessons to learn from these incidents

The following lessons can be learned from these four breaches:

* It’s crucial to secure all cloud technology and all firewall configurations with attack surface monitoring software
* Third-party monitoring is vital in preventing breaches, as it helps organizations identify and address security vulnerabilities in their vendors' systems
* The importance of implementing multi-factor authentication (MFA) by default, using behavioral analytics for login monitoring, and adopting a zero-trust architecture

## Why Banks Are Prime Targets for Cybersecurity Attacks

Banks are custodians of not only money, but also sensitive personal and financial information. Here’s why they are high targets for cybersecurity attacks.

### They hold highly valuable data (Social Security numbers, account numbers)

Banks store confidential financial data, like customer account details and credit card information, and any attack on their systems can cripple operations. Cybercriminals often target the financial sector for monetary gain, and over [17.5 million credit card numbers](https://socradar.io/finance-threat-landscape-report-17-5m-credit-card-numbers-sold-on-blackmarket/) were sold in the black market in 2022. Cybercriminals use this data for identity theft, unauthorised transactions, and financial fraud.

### Banks still use legacy systems and have digital transformation challenges

Legacy operating systems no longer receive security enhancements or patches from vendors. But despite their obsolescence, they remain in active use in some financial organizations because they support crucial hardware or applications that might be costly to replace or upgrade. Digital transformation challenges also increase banks’ attack surface. If new technologies like cloud computing are implemented faster than they can be secured, they can expose banks to cybersecurity breaches.

### Gaps in vendor and endpoint security

Banks today are increasingly reliant on third parties to help them run their operations, but these introduce new security risks, such as unpatched servers and software, and unprotected web assets. Remote work has also introduced distributed endpoints, giving cybercriminals the opportunity to focus their attacks on endpoint devices.

## Best Practices for Prevention and Risk Management

While comprehensive security solutions can help financial organizations defend themselves against cybersecurity breaches, implementing best practices is equally important for long-term security.

Here are some top strategies:

### Employee training and phishing simulations

Employees are often the first line of defense against cyber threats. Conduct proper training, and include phishing simulations to provide a realistic environment for employees to practice identifying and responding to phishing attacks.

### Advanced threat detection and endpoint monitoring (EDR/XDR)

Advanced threat detection tools use AI, ML, and behavioural analytics to spot possible threats and suspicious activities. They perform real-time monitoring to detect anomalies that security teams can investigate. Threat intelligence integration also makes bank security teams aware of attack trends and newly exploited weaknesses.

Endpoint monitoring focuses on protecting individual devices that connect to a network, like laptops, smartphones, and IoT devices. These devices are prime targets for cybercriminals as they are gateways to corporate systems. Banks must secure every endpoint, ensuring each device can detect and block cyber threats before they cause serious problems.

 Atlas Systems' [cybersecurity risk management software](https://www.atlassystems.com/complyscore/platform/cybersecurity-risk-management) combines this kind of AI-driven threat detection with continuous monitoring across your IT environment .

### Implementing Zero Trust architecture and performing regular security audits

Zero Trust architecture operates on the principle of "Never trust, always verify." Users and devices undergo strict identity verification before being granted access to resources. This is contrary to the traditional security model that trusts everything within a defined network perimeter.

Regular security audits are also crucial in preventing cybersecurity breaches in banking, as they help your institution identify vulnerabilities in systems and processes and address them before attackers exploit them. Audits also help banks to ensure compliance with industry regulations.

### Regular third-party security assessments

Third parties supply the resources your bank needs to run smoothly, but if their security is compromised, they can cause your organization to suffer a data breach. To stay a step ahead of third-party breaches, be vigilant during vendor selection. Perform [cyber risk](/blog/third-party-cyber-risk) assessments on prospective vendors to quantify the level of risk. Continuous monitoring of vendor environments can also help your bank detect risky activity before it fully impacts the institution.

[A good TPRM solution](/complyscore) can help your organization to proactively identify, assess, and mitigate risks posed by vendors and partners.

## Role of AI, ML, Automation, and Tech in Breach Prevention

### AI and ML are used for anomaly detection and real-time response

As new threat variants escalate and mutate, it becomes harder for financial institutions to detect the latest security breaches. AI tools have powerful analytical and computing capabilities. They use machine learning to identify unusual patterns in financial data within minutes and detect a wide range of issues, from fraud to cyberattacks.

Banking systems that use AI can also perform real-time incident response automatically, like separating threats from other data, isolating compromised machines, and alerting security teams. They analyze data and make decisions instantaneously, which is critical in the banking industry where delays can have serious consequences.

### Blockchain streamlines audit trails and supports predictive threat intelligence

Blockchain records each transaction as a "block" of data, cryptographically linking it to the previous block to form an unbreakable chain. Recorded transactions can’t be altered or deleted, and any change is instantly visible as it breaks the cryptographic link in the chain.

Blockchain streamlines audits by providing a transparent and tamper-resistant ledger. There’s no need for complex reconciliation processes as all transactions are securely recorded in real time.

Blockchain also provides a highly reliable and secure data source for AI and machine learning, enabling more reliable threat detection and faster response times. AI and ML models can analyze the secure blockchain data to identify patterns and anomalies that indicate a potential threat.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### **1. What is the biggest cybersecurity breach in banking history?**

The biggest cybersecurity breach was the First American Financial Corp data breach, which exposed more than 885 million financial and personal records linked to real estate transactions.

### **2. How do banks prevent cyberattacks?**

Banks prevent cyberattacks by enforcing the use of secure access controls (like multi-factor authentication), encrypting data, implementing logging and monitoring, and installing firewalls.

### **3. What are examples of data breaches in banks?**

Examples of [data breaches](/blog/third-party-data-breach) in banks include malware attacks, phishing and social engineering attacks, third-party and supply chain attacks, and cloud infrastructure attacks.

### **4. How do fintech breaches differ from cyberattacks on traditional banks?**

Fintech breaches exploit newer, rapidly deployed technologies like APIs and cloud services, as well as third-party integrations. Attacks on traditional banks, on the other hand, usually target legacy systems and outdated infrastructure.

This blog post, authored by Manisha Martin for Atlas Systems (updated Aug 14, 2026), examines cybersecurity breaches in banking, which occur when unauthorized parties gain access to systems containing sensitive financial information. Key data point: the average cost of a US financial industry data breach in 2024 was $9.36 million (Statista). Banks are prime targets due to the high value of financial data (over 17.5 million credit card numbers were sold on the black market in 2022), reliance on legacy systems that no longer receive security patches, and gaps in vendor/endpoint security exacerbated by remote work and third-party supply chain dependencies.

The article outlines six common attack vectors: malware and ransomware, phishing, insider threats, third-party vendor vulnerabilities, payment card system breaches, and API exploits. Software supply chain attacks are projected to cost businesses $138 billion by 2031.

Key real-world breach case studies:
1. Capital One (2019) - cloud misconfiguration; a former AWS engineer stole 100 million credit card applications, affecting ~100 million people in the US and 6+ million in Canada.
2. Flagstar Bank (2023) - third-party breach via MOVEit; 837,390 customers' data exposed through vendor Fiserv's MOVEit Transfer vulnerability.
3. First Horizon (2021) - credentials compromise; fewer than 200 accounts accessed with under $1 million withdrawn.
4. US Treasury Department (2024) - supply chain attack via BeyondTrust; attackers stole a cryptographic key and compromised over 400 computers.

Lessons learned include securing cloud/firewall configurations with attack surface monitoring, continuous third-party monitoring, and implementing MFA by default, behavioral analytics, and zero-trust architecture.

Best practices for prevention: employee training with phishing simulations; advanced threat detection and endpoint monitoring (EDR/XDR) using AI/ML; Zero Trust architecture and regular security audits; and continuous third-party security assessments. The roles of AI/ML (anomaly detection and real-time response), blockchain (tamper-resistant audit trails and threat intelligence), and automation are discussed. The article concludes by promoting Atlas Systems' ComplyScore® AI-powered TPRM platform for vendor risk monitoring and breach prevention.

The FAQ notes the biggest banking breach was First American Financial Corp (885+ million records exposed), and distinguishes fintech breaches (exploiting new APIs, cloud, third-party integrations) from attacks on traditional banks (targeting legacy systems).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from FortifyData provides an updated tracker of the biggest third-party data breaches of 2025 and 2026, highlighting lessons learned and mitigation strategies. The article notes that Verizon reported nearly 30% of data breaches in 2025 involved third-party suppliers, and the average cost to remediate a third-party-originated breach is now nearly $4.8 million.

The page details 14 major third-party breaches, including:
1. **Chain IQ Group AG (June 2025)** – Ransomware attack exposed 130,000+ employee records from clients including UBS and Pictet, including UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti's direct phone number.
2. **Toronto District School Board / PowerSchool (Dec 2024–2025)** – Student and staff data dating back to 1985 exposed, including SSNs; attackers continued extortion even after ransom was paid.
3. **Kellogg's and Adidas / Cleo Vendor (Dec 2024)** – Clop ransomware group exploited two zero-day flaws in Cleo's file-transfer platform; over 66 companies breached via same vulnerabilities.
4. **Qantas / Offshore Contact-Centre Platform (June 2025)** – Up to 5.7–6 million customer records compromised; facing class-action claims and criminal investigation.
5. **Episource Healthcare Billing (Jan–Jun 2025)** – Medical billing firm owned by Optum; over 5.4 million individuals affected.
6. **Hy-Vee / Atlassian (June 2025)** – Stormous group extracted ~53 GB of internal documents via stolen credentials and infostealer malware.
7. **Insight Partners (Jan 2025)** – Social engineering attack on third-party cloud CRM; $90+ billion AUM firm exposed sensitive fund data.
8. **UK Co-op & Marks & Spencer via Delivery Partner (Apr–May 2025)** – 6.5+ million customer records compromised via phishing on vendor employees; linked to Scattered Spider using DragonForce tools.
9. **Community Health Center (Feb 2025)** – Undisclosed vendor breach affecting patient data.
10. **Change Healthcare / UnitedHealth (Feb 2024–2025)** – Largest healthcare breach ever, ~190 million individuals affected; UnitedHealth spent over $2–2.45 billion responding and reimbursed providers $4.7+ billion.
11. **Sam's Club / Cleo (Mar–Apr 2025)** – Clop exploited zero-day CVE-2024-50623; class-action lawsuit filed but lead plaintiff later dropped.
12. **Harrods via Supplier Portal (May 2025)** – Outdated access controls and lack of real-time monitoring enabled access to supplier records.
13. **Ascension via MOVEit Transfer (May 2025)** – 437,329 patients exposed; two years of credit monitoring offered across multiple states.
14. **Multiple Enterprises via Salesforce (Aug 2025)** – UNC6395 campaign tricked employees into approving malicious OAuth apps; Allianz Life alone exposed 1.1 billion personal records; 700+ organizations targeted including Adidas, Google, Cartier, Louis Vuitton, and others.

The article concludes with four tips to reduce third-party breach risk: (1) continuous auditing, (2) API/SaaS security controls, (3) employee and vendor training (human error responsible for 44%–95% of incidents), and (4) strong TPRM processes. SUMMARY:
<summary>
NYC Health + Hospitals (NYC H+H) disclosed a major data breach affecting at least 1.8 million people, making it one of the largest healthcare breaches of 2026 so far. The breach was attributed to an unnamed third-party vendor with access to NYC H+H systems, fitting the pattern of supply-chain compromises. NYC H+H detected suspicious activity on February 2, 2026, and confirmed an unauthorized actor had access to parts of its network from roughly late November 2025 through February 2026. The incident was reported to the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on March 24, 2026.

The exposed data falls into three layers: (1) Classical PII including full names, contact details, Social Security Numbers, driver's license and passport numbers, taxpayer IDs, IRS identity protection PINs, billing/payment records, and bank and card data; (2) Medical and insurance data including detailed diagnoses, medication lists, test results, insurance and claims data that could enable blackmail, targeted scams, discrimination, and fraudulent claims; and (3) Biometrics including fingerprint and palm-print data, which are especially sensitive because they stay with a person for life and cannot be easily erased or replaced.

The breach is part of a broader pattern, as the FBI's IC3 reported healthcare was the most targeted critical infrastructure sector for ransomware in 2025, with 460 ransomware incidents and 182 reported healthcare data breaches. The Change Healthcare ransomware attack alone exposed medical and billing data for more than 190 million Americans.

For those affected, NYC Health + Hospitals is offering identity theft prevention and mitigation services, including credit monitoring, through Kroll Information Assurance, LLC for 24 months at no cost to all individuals who have worked for or been a patient of NYC H+H. Recommended protective steps include: checking the company's advice, changing passwords, enabling FIDO2-compliant two-factor authentication, watching for impersonators, taking time to verify urgent communications, considering not storing card details, and setting up identity monitoring.
</summary>

2. **Anthem Inc.** - 78.8M records. Spear phishing by Chinese state-linked actors. $115M class action settlement + $16M HIPAA penalty.
3. **Conduent Business Services LLC** - 62.2M records. Network intrusion with 3 months undetected access. Concentration risk in healthcare supply chain.
4. **Viamedis and Almerys (France)** - ~33M combined. Compromised healthcare professional credentials. Largest breach in French history.
5. **Welltok, Inc.** - 14.8M records. MOVEit Transfer zero-day exploited by Cl0p ransomware group.

8. **MediSecure (Australia)** - ~12.9M records. Ransomware via compromised third-party vendor. Company entered voluntary administration.
9. **Optum360/Quest Diagnostics (via AMCA)** - 11.5M records. Fourth-party risk case via debt collector's web payment portal.
10. **HCA Healthcare** - 11.3M records. Theft from external storage for email formatting.

The page continues through #34, covering breaches at Premera Blue Cross, LabCorp, Medibank (Australia), Excellus, Episource, Community Health Systems, Yale New Haven, Ascension, TRICARE/SAIC, Blue Shield of California, Advocate, TriZetto, Trinity Health, QualDerm, Advocate Aurora, PIH Health, DaVita, and others. **Industry Targeting Statistics:** A data table shows that the Medical (MED) sector was by far the most targeted, with 3,912 breaches (61.55%) between 2005-2019 and 1,587 breaches (76.59%) between 2015-2019. --- SOURCE 8: 2026 Data Breaches: Cybersecurity Incidents Explained - PKWARE ---
URL: https://www.pkware.com/blog/2026-data-breaches

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## PKWARE 2026 Data Breach Report (July 2026 Edition)

This is a monthly data breach report published by PKWARE (a data protection/encryption vendor) on August 10, 2026, by Bob Cristello. The report analyzes the five largest data breaches of July 2026, highlighting that most breaches did not result from broken perimeters but rather from attackers using access that already worked (phished employees, vishing, vendor credentials).

### Key July 2026 Statistics:
- 4 of 5 incidents involved attackers using access that already worked
- 3 of 5 exposed identifiers that cannot be reissued (SSNs, driver's licenses, biometrics)
- 6,998,886 individuals affected (largest known U.S. driver's license exposure in 2026)
- IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report (July 29): global average $4.99M, U.S. average $11.5M
- Phishing led all initial attack vectors for the 4th consecutive year
- Two incidents drew proposed class actions within 11 days of notification

### The Five July 2026 Breaches:

**1. AssuranceAmerica (Insurance, Atlanta-based MGA)** — Largest known exposure of U.S. driver's license numbers in 2026, affecting 6,998,886 individuals. Malicious activity targeted a single employee on March 16, 2026; detected March 17. Exposed data included names, contact info, auto insurance policy info, driver/vehicle info, claims info, driver's license numbers, Tax ID info, and SSNs. Offering 12 months of credit monitoring through IDX. Filed with Maine and Indiana AGs, first reported by TechCrunch.

**2. Ernst & Young (Professional services)** — Unauthorized access to a third-party IT service management platform (March 28–April 12, 2026) used for internal support workflows. Downloaded client documents containing tax filings with SSNs, financial account and payment card information. Detected April 23, notifications July 13, proposed class action July 20. ShinyHunters claimed responsibility on July 27, also claiming supply-chain credentials gave access to EY's Jira, GitHub, and Azure. State filings list 873 Texas, 480 Massachusetts, and 13 Vermont residents. Offering 24 months of credit/identity monitoring.

**3. Craneware (Healthcare software, Edinburgh)** — Disclosed incident to London Stock Exchange July 20, 2026. Trisus platform supports 2,000+ U.S. hospitals/health systems and nearly 10,000 clinics/retail pharmacies. Exfiltrated file names, a percentage of employee data, and a subset of customer/partner records. Vector, threat actor, and duration not disclosed. Contained, external forensic specialists confirmed no residual indicators of compromise.

**4. Abbott (Medical devices & diagnostics)** — Confirmed July 16, 2026 unauthorized access to legacy Exact Sciences systems in Cancer Diagnostics business, ~12 weeks after its $21 billion acquisition closed March 23, 2026. ShinyHunters claims 30 million customer records including ~1 million SSNs, 22M+ doctor/patient notes, 20M+ medical orders (unverified). Claimed access via vishing compromising a Microsoft Entra SSO account. Separate unverified claim by ShadowByt3$ about LabCentral customer portal access. Proposed federal class action filed July 24.

**5. NYC Health + Hospitals (Public health system)** — Largest U.S. public health system. Access from late Nov 2025 through Feb 2026 following third-party vendor compromise; detected Feb 2, 2026. At least 1.8 million affected (reported to HHS). Data included medical records, health insurance info, biometrics (fingerprints and palm prints), SSNs, driver's license numbers, geolocation, financial account info. LeakNet published preview July 27 of claimed 11-terabyte archive linked to 12M+ people (unverified). Offering 24 months of credit monitoring through Kroll.

### Key Takeaways for Security Teams:
- Valid credentials do not trigger alarms; the only variable is what state the data was in when the attacker reached it
- Sensitive data drifts to support tickets, acquired legacy environments, and vendor-reachable systems — automated discovery and field-level encryption/tokenization are essential
- One vendor's incident becomes many disclosures (Craneware, EY's platform, NYC H+H vendor)

### Report's Core Message:
The recurring theme is that a breach is not finished while stolen data remains readable. PKWARE advocates for data-layer protection (encryption, tokenization, automated discovery), data minimization, and protecting data at rest rather than relying on perimeter defenses.

### Archive of 2026 Editions:
The report also includes summaries of prior monthly editions:

URL: https://compliancehub.wiki/citizens-frost-bank-everest-ransomware-glba-vendor-risk

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On April 20, 2026, the Everest ransomware gang listed Citizens Financial Group and Frost Bank on its dark web leak site, claiming to hold 3.4 million Citizens customer records (names, addresses, account numbers, document identifiers) and 250,000 Frost Bank records (Social Security numbers, tax IDs, mortgage rates, investment data, income). Both banks confirmed the breaches originated at third-party vendors — a statement printing provider for Citizens and a tax document fulfillment firm for Frost — with their own networks not directly compromised. Class actions were filed by April 24, including two against Citizens in U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island, and law firms announced investigations into Frost Bank claims.

The article distinguishes Everest (a RaaS operation active since 2020 focused on data exfiltration/extortion targeting vendors with high-value customer data but weaker security) from ShinyHunters (credential theft and cloud misconfigurations, as seen in the April 2026 Salesforce/Snowflake supply chain attacks). Regulatory context includes the GLBA Safeguards Rule (amended 2023), which requires financial institutions to select capable service providers, contractually require safeguards, and oversee service providers. The 2023 OCC/Fed/FDIC interagency third-party risk management guidance establishes a lifecycle model (due diligence, contracts, ongoing monitoring, concentration risk). The 2021 OCC rule requires banking organizations to notify their primary federal regulator within 36 hours of a "notification incident," with service providers contractually obligated to notify banks promptly. NYDFS Part 500 (with 2023 amendments) imposes third-party obligations on Citizens given its New York operations.

Key distinctions: Frost Bank's data (SSNs, tax IDs) carries materially higher identity fraud risk than Citizens' data, giving Frost plaintiffs stronger Article III standing post-Spokeo. The article provides actionable recommendations: tier vendor risk programs by data sensitivity, audit vendor contracts for 36-hour notification obligations, assess concentration risk in statement/document fulfillment (a small number of specialized vendors serve large portions of the industry), exercise third-party incident response procedures, and build multi-state breach notification capability. The central thesis is that in 2026, vendor breaches no longer absolve financial institutions — regulators now hold banks accountable for vendor oversight failures regardless of who technically owned the compromised systems.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Citizens/Frost Breach: 3.65M Records via One Vendor ---
URL: https://blog.cybelesoft.com/citizens-frost-breach-vendor-access-vdi

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Cybele Software blog post (by Leonardo Laurencio, CSO) analyzes the April 2026 Everest ransomware breach involving Citizens Bank and Frost Bank, where up to 3.65 million records (roughly 3.4M Citizens + ~250K Frost records including SSNs) were claimed stolen. Critically, neither bank's network was breached—the data was taken from a shared third-party statement-printing and tax-document vendor. Within weeks, six class-action lawsuits were filed against the banks, not the vendor, because liability flows upstream regardless of where the compromise occurred.

Core argument: The root cause is data location—data is stolen from vendor environments because data lives on vendor systems. Every file shipped to a vendor inherits that vendor's security posture. The proposed durable fix is to invert the model: host vendor working environments inside the bank's tenancy as virtual desktops behind a Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) gateway, so only pixels leave the datacenter and no data reaches the vendor's endpoint.

Key architectural details: The post identifies four problematic vendor access patterns (standing VPN credentials, network-level reach, local copies as workflow, no session evidence) and contrasts VPN/network access with a virtual desktop behind ZTNA gateway (scope, data location, credentials, duration, endpoint risk, exfiltration paths, audit, revocation). It recommends hosting vendor desktop pools on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) using private subnets with no public IPs, in-region data residency for GLBA/DORA/LGPD compliance, elastic per-engagement capacity, and cost savings. Regulatory drivers include FFIEC third-party risk guidance, GLBA Safeguards Rule, and DORA (fines up to 2% of worldwide turnover).

The post includes a 30-day remediation plan: Week 1 inventory of third parties, Week 2 kill standing access, Week 3 stand up a vendor desktop pool in a private OCI subnet with Thinfinity, Week 4 run evidence-based tabletop exercises. A YAML-style declarative vendor profile configuration example is provided using Thinfinity Workspace with MFA, time-boxed access windows, full session recording, disabled clipboard/file transfer/drive mapping/printing, and instant revocation. End-of-project deprovisioning leaves nothing to claw back from vendor laptops because nothing was ever on them.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Liability flows upstream regardless of where the compromise happened. And here's the architectural lesson buried in the incident: the data was stolen from the vendor's environment because the data was in the vendor's environment. Every file you transfer to a vendor's endpoint inherits that vendor's security posture, forever.

<summary>
This article examines the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario's (IPC) investigation into the PowerSchool cyberattack, which affected approximately 3.86 million Ontarians and over 5.2 million Canadians. The breach, reported in January 2025, targeted the Student Information System (SIS) and PowerSource support portal used by 20 Ontario school boards and the Ministry of Education. The IPC concluded that reasonable safeguards were NOT in place due to systemic weaknesses including elevated user privileges contrary to "least privilege" principles, no multi-factor authentication on PowerSource, continuous remote access, short log retention, and inconsistent/outdated contractual agreements lacking key provisions (confidential information, subcontracting restrictions, security obligations, retention schedules, audit rights, governing law). The IPC also found the institutions' breach response inadequate due to gaps in breach planning, data retention, and oversight. Key deficiencies included lack of robust breach response plans, absence of clear retention schedules, weak monitoring, over-collection of highly sensitive data (health card numbers, SINs, insurance policy details) collected without legal authority or necessity, and limited direct reporting to local law enforcement (only three boards reported directly to Ontario police). PowerSchool refused to share full forensic reports despite contractual obligations. Notable positive steps included removal of unauthorized data fields, revocation of credentials, and clear notifications.

The IPC issued recommendations including: restricting remote SIS access to "as needed" only, amending agreements to include essential privacy/security clauses, requiring annual security audits and certifications (ISO, SOC 2), stopping collection of unnecessary sensitive data, implementing retention schedules, updating breach-response plans for third-party risks, and conducting Privacy Impact Assessments (now mandatory for FIPPA institutions as of July 1, 2025). ## 2026 Mexican Government Data Breach Analysis: Chronus Group Attack

In January 2026, a major data breach targeting the Mexican government resulted in the alleged exfiltration of 2.3 terabytes of sensitive data from at least 25 government institutions. The incident, attributed to the **Chronus Group** (a loosely organized hacktivist collective active since at least 2021), exposed personal information of up to 36 million Mexican citizens, including names, addresses, dates of birth, and healthcare registration records (IMSS Bienestar enrollment proof).

### Key Technical Details
The breach was facilitated by multiple attack vectors:
- **Legacy system exploitation** - obsolete platforms not properly decommissioned or segmented from active networks
- **Third-party vendor compromise** - platforms developed and administered by private entities for state-level government bodies (nearly 30% of government agencies exchanged data with over 5,000 third parties; vendor-related breaches surged 68%)
- **Credential abuse** involving unrevoked credentials and lack of centralized oversight
- **Phishing and infostealers** - notably **LummaC2** and **Vidar** (Lumma Stealer S1213 is documented in MITRE ATT&CK framework)

Attack methods mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques including phishing (T1566), supply chain compromise (T1195), credential harvesting (T1555.003), and exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041). Attribution to Chronus Group is assessed with medium-high confidence; use of LummaC2 and Vidar confirmed with high confidence.

### Timeline
- **January 30, 2026**: Chronus Group posted documents/datasets allegedly exfiltrated from Mexican government systems
- Mexico's Agencia de Transformación Digital y Telecomunicaciones (ATDT) downplayed the incident, claiming data appeared to be compiled from previous breaches rather than a new compromise; however, technical analysis and threat intelligence confirmed exposure of sensitive citizen data

### Threat Landscape
Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina are the most targeted countries in Latin America. In 2025, there were 452 ransomware incidents in Latin America and the Caribbean (28 targeting government, 36 healthcare, 16 finance). The government sector's risk score surged 95% between 2019 and 2023. Exposed data enables identity theft, synthetic identity fraud, SIM swaps, and account takeovers via dark web marketplaces.

### Mitigation Recommendations
- **High priority**: Immediate decommissioning of obsolete systems, centralized third-party vendor oversight, MFA for all remote/privileged access, credential review and revocation
- **Medium priority**: Regular penetration testing focused on legacy infrastructure, phishing security awareness training
- **Low priority**: Dark web monitoring, updated incident response plans for supply chain threats
- Establishment of unified data governance frameworks across federal, state, and third-party systems

Sources include Kiteworks (Feb 2026), Recorded Future (2025), CSIS (May 2026), and MITRE ATT&CK.

Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina were the most targeted countries, likely due to being LAC's largest economies, with critical industries (healthcare, finance, government) being common targets because they hold high-value data and often rely on vulnerable legacy systems.

Key findings include: DarkForums and Telegram are the primary forums and communication platforms used by threat actors; threat actors are primarily financially motivated and leverage social engineering, ransomware, and mobile malware; 452 ransomware incidents impacted the LAC region in 2025 (just over 6% of global attacks), with top affected industries being healthcare (36), manufacturing (49), government (28), IT (21), and education (20); banking trojans were used in smishing campaigns targeting WhatsApp users; and LummaC2 was the most prolific infostealer in the first half of 2025, replaced by Vidar in the second half following a law enforcement disruption of LummaC2 (which took down ~2,300 malicious domains).

Background factors driving cybercrime include post-COVID digital development outpacing security maturity, reliance on legacy infrastructure, economic instability, high youth unemployment, and inequality. Only 13% of LAC respondents expressed confidence in national cyber incident preparedness. Only seven LAC countries have critical infrastructure protection plans, and only twenty have CSIRTs. The region has the world's fastest-growing rate of disclosed cyber incidents.

Cybercriminal tactics observed include phishing via email, SMS, and WhatsApp; exploitation of RDP, VPNs, and web admin panels; and ~29,000 exposed LAC-related credentials on Russian Market. Novel NFC-based malware emerged, including PhantomCard and RelayNFC (targeting Brazilian banking customers). Cryptocurrency wallet-targeting malware (drainers, clippers, miners) is growing, with Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, Venezuela, and Colombia dominating the crypto ecosystem. APT activity increased, including Dark Caracal (Poco RAT), TAG-144/Blind Eagle (targeting Colombia), TAG-141/FamousSparrow (SparrowDoor), and Storm-2603/Gold Salem (ransomware). Hacktivism also rose, with groups like Chronus Team (Mexico) and FiveFamilies transitioning to ransomware-as-a-service.

Botnet activity (including Kimwolf/AISURU and Horabot) grew using compromised SOHO/IoT devices. Payment terminal malware rose, with ATM malware attacks spiking 46% in LAC, including Ploutus (linked to a December 2025 DOJ indictment of 54 individuals from Tren de Aragua) and MajikPOS. Top ransomware groups impacting LAC included Qilin, LockBit, Safepay, The Gentlemen, and Kazu. Top five countries impacted by ransomware: Brazil (128 attacks), Mexico (78), Argentina (63), Colombia (51), and Peru (27).

Mitigations recommended include using Recorded Future's Global Ransomware Landscape Dashboard, configuring threat monitoring alerts, updating legacy systems, engaging in public-private information sharing, and generating awareness through education. The outlook anticipates LAC will remain a popular ransomware target and hotspot for mobile malware in 2026, particularly given SMEs constitute over 95% of all businesses in the region. This article from Bridgeforce examines the evolving Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM) landscape for 2026, positioning TPRM as a core component of operational resilience, customer trust, and strategic growth rather than merely a compliance requirement. 

**Key Risk Areas for 2026:**
- **Cyber + Non-Cyber Risk Convergence:** Institutions must assess vendors holistically across cybersecurity, operational resilience, financial viability, data governance, and geopolitical exposure. Regulators expect end-to-end risk evaluation across the full vendor lifecycle rather than point-in-time assessments.
- **Fraud Evolution:** While digital fraud evolves, traditional methods persist—check washing (chemically removing ink to alter payee/amount fields) has resurged. Vendors supporting payments, item processing, or exception handling need advanced fraud analytics and image validation capabilities.

**Regulatory and Political Shifts:**
- The 2025 Executive Order "Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans" prohibited financial institutions from denying services based on political or religious beliefs and removed "reputation risk" from regulatory exams. This pushes institutions toward objective, quantifiable risk criteria, clearer risk taxonomies, and consistent scoring models.
- The anticipated re-proposal of Basel III Endgame rules, combined with increasing global regulatory divergence, adds complexity—especially for institutions with international vendors or cross-border data flows. TPRM frameworks must be designed to scale with regulatory change.

**Technology-Driven Transformation:**
- Annual reviews and static vendor questionnaires are no longer sufficient. Leading institutions are adopting AI-enabled continuous monitoring tools for real-time risk scoring, anomaly detection, predictive analytics, and ongoing risk signals (cyber posture changes, financial distress, adverse events).
- Zero-trust security models are becoming standard requirements for vendors with privileged access, including least-privilege access, continuous authentication, and strict identity controls.
- Location-aware, real-time risk alert tools are essential given geopolitical instability and climate-related disruptions, providing visibility into vendor geography and location-specific risks.

**Fourth-Party and Supply Chain Risk:**
Regulators expect oversight of vendors' vendors—a subcontractor failure can create as much exposure as a primary relationship. Many institutions still lack visibility beyond first-tier providers, making extended supply chain mapping and monitoring critical.

**Seven Recommended Steps for 2026:**
1. Build a risk-tiered vendor inventory (based on services, data access, geography, automation exposure)
2. Perform tailored due diligence and contracting matched to vendor risk
3. Implement continuous monitoring with AI and automation using real-time dashboards
4. Audit third- and fourth-party relationships (regulators expect oversight of vendors' vendors per FINRA)
5. Institutionalize regulatory alignment and governance with transparent oversight from planning to termination
6. Centralize reporting and leadership engagement (regulators expect board-level awareness and transparency)
7. Prepare for disruption before it happens

The article concludes that institutions treating TPRM as a living, strategic capability—rather than a static checklist—will thrive in 2026 by navigating complexity with the right tools, frameworks, and partners. --- SOURCE 1: Canada Life Data Breach: What Canadians and Canadian Businesses Need to Know | Cybersecurity Canada ---
URL: https://cybersecuritycanada.ca/news/posts/canada-life-data-breach-what-canadians-need-to-know

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Canada Life data breach, disclosed publicly on April 23, 2026, exposed the personal information of up to 70,000 people (less than 0.5% of Canada Life's customer base), most belonging to one large corporate group plan. The criminal extortion group ShinyHunters gained access through a single compromised employee account and used it to query data in Canada Life's Salesforce CRM environment. ShinyHunters set a ransom deadline of April 21, 2026 with a "pay or leak" demand.

Two figures circulate but answer different questions: 70,000 is Canada Life's verified count of individuals whose data was actually accessed, while 5.6 million is ShinyHunters' unverified claim for records it could reach in the broader Salesforce environment—a number Canada Life has not confirmed.

**Data exposed:** Full name, date of birth, mailing address, gender, and annual income level. Canada Life stated that Social Insurance Numbers, banking details, and medical information were NOT part of the accessed data. This combination is sufficient for targeted phishing, identity verification fraud, and benefits-related social engineering.

**About the attacker:** ShinyHunters is a long-running cybercriminal extortion group linked to a series of 2025–2026 intrusions targeting cloud-hosted CRM platforms, particularly Salesforce. The group typically compromises employee credentials (via phishing, credential reuse, or help-desk social engineering), authenticates to the Salesforce tenant, bulk-exports customer records, and issues a ransom demand. This is not a flaw in Salesforce itself; the weak point is the human account and absence of controls to catch unusual bulk exports.

**Actions for affected Canadians:** Watch for official notification (navigate directly to canadalife.com, don't click email links); enrol in free credit monitoring; place free fraud alerts with Equifax Canada and TransUnion Canada; be sceptical of "Canada Life" calls and emails for several months; never give out passwords, MFA codes, or banking details to inbound callers.

**Lessons and actions for Canadian businesses (next 7 days):** 1) Audit who can bulk-export from your CRM; 2) Turn on phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 keys or passkeys) for privileged accounts; 3) Enable anomaly alerts on bulk data access; 4) Train help desk against social engineering (require verified callbacks before resetting credentials); 5) Confirm incident response plans cover SaaS compromise.

**Bigger picture:** The incident demonstrates that "identity is the new perimeter"—a single employee's identity is now frequently the entire security perimeter. The defensive response: treat every employee identity as a potential breach point, make MFA strong and required, limit what any single account can do, and watch for bulk-export/mass-query/impossible-travel signals. Canada's privacy regulators expect reasonable security measures under PIPEDA, and federal obligations are tightening under Bill C-26—"reasonable" now includes configuring SaaS platforms properly.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The two numbers circulating in coverage do not contradict each other, but they answer different questions. 70,000 is Canada Life's verified count of individuals whose personal data was actually accessed. 5.6 million is the figure ShinyHunters has claimed for the records it could reach in the broader Salesforce environment—a number Canada Life has not confirmed."
