--- SOURCE 1: Analysis of Enforcement Action by the ICO in 2025 | URM Consulting ---
URL: https://www.urmconsulting.com/blog/analysis-of-enforcement-action-by-the-ico-in-2025-actions-way-down-security-data-breach-fines-way-up

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog by Stuart Skelly, a Senior Consultant at URM, analyzes the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) enforcement activity in the UK for the calendar year 2025, comparing trends against 2024. The central theme is a marked drop-off in the number of enforcement actions combined with a significant increase in the value of fines issued.

Key findings:
- The ICO took only 31 enforcement actions in 2025, half the frequency of 2024 (which saw 62 actions against 47 organisations). Of the 7 public sector organisations, 3 were police forces (with Greater Manchester Police receiving two reprimands in 6 months).
- 17 of the 31 actions were for breaches of the DPA and UK GDPR. Private sector organisations comprised nearly half of those enforced against under UK GDPR/DPA in 2025, versus only about one-eighth in 2024.
- The ICO issued or supported the courts in issuing 15 fines. Only one fine was applied to a public body: an £18,000 penalty against the charity Birthlink for the unnecessary destruction of thousands of adoption records.
- The largest fines of 2025 were security-related breaches following cyber attacks: £14m against Capita plc and Capita Pension Solutions Limited (combined), £3.07m against Advanced Computer Software Group Ltd, £2.31m against 23andMe Inc, and £1.23m against LastPass UK Ltd. A £60,000 fine was also issued to law firm DPP Law for data loss from a cyber attack, plus two smaller court-issued fines against individuals.
- PECR fines totalled only £1.025m in 2025 versus about £20.68m for UK GDPR violations—a reversal from 2024 when PECR breaches dominated.
- The average fine rocketed nearly tenfold from approximately £150K in 2024 to £1.45 million in 2025. The 15 fines brought in around £21.7m to the Treasury, eight times the 2024 yield. Just over half (8) of the fines exceeded £100,000.
- Six of the seven UK GDPR-related reprimands went to public sector bodies, consistent with the ICO's stated policy of not fining public authorities since it is ultimately taxpayers who pay. Two enforcement notices were issued to public bodies for failures in dealing with subject access requests; all other 7 enforcement notices went to private companies for PECR breaches.
- Enforcement activity declined sharply despite, not because of, a drop in complaints—the ICO received over 42,300 data protection complaints in 2024/25, up ~2,500 from the prior year. Civil society groups, academics, and lawyers wrote to the parliamentary Science, Innovation and Technology Committee calling for an inquiry into what they called a 'collapse' in ICO enforcement, prompted in part by the ICO's decision not to investigate the Ministry of Defence after a severe data breach leaking details of over 19,000 Afghans fleeing the Taliban.
- In contrast to earlier concerns, the ICO took no enforcement action in 2025 related to cookies, suggesting its verbal crackdown on top websites' cookie compliance has worked as intended.
- The planned increase of the PECR penalty cap to £17.5 million in 2026 (aligning it with the UK GDPR maximum) is unlikely to have an immediate impact since no PECR fines approached the current £500,000 statutory maximum.

The article concludes with URM's promotional content offering GDPR consultancy services (gap analysis, DSAR support, vDPO, and training courses including BCS CDP certification) to help organisations avoid ICO enforcement action.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"there were only 31 occasions on which the ICO took enforcement action in 2025, half of the frequency compared to the previous year", "The average fine in the UK rocketed nearly tenfold from approximately £150K in 2024 to a whopping £1.45 million in 2025", "The largest fines of 2025 were the £14m, £3.07m, £2.31m and £1.23m monetary penalties imposed on 2 companies in the Capita group (Capita plc and Capita Pension Solutions Limited totalling £14m), the UK company Advanced Computer Software Group Ltd, the US genealogy company 23andMe Inc, and LastPass UK Ltd respectively", "in 2024/25 the ICO received over 42,300 data protection-related complaints, which represents an actual increase of around 2,500 complaints on the previous year", "In 2025, just over half (8) have been over that 100K figure... In total, these 15 fines brought in around £21.7m to the Treasury, which is eight times the fine yield for 2024"

--- SOURCE 2: Recent ICO Data Breach Enforcement Emphasizes ... ---
URL: https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/2026/02/recent-ico-data-breach-enforcement

SUMMARY:
<summary>
In the final quarter of 2025, the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) issued GDPR fines totaling £15 million against Capita (including Capita Pension Solutions Limited) and LastPass UK Limited for data breaches resulting from cyberattacks. The fines provide insight into the ICO's current enforcement approach.

Key themes from the decisions:
1. Proactive cybersecurity risk assessment is essential. The ICO fined Capita £14 million on 15 October 2025, finding that inadequate security penetration testing, insufficient security operations center staffing, and poor administrator access controls created a "foreseeable and avoidable risk" exploited by the threat actor. The ICO did not accept cost or time as excuses for security shortcomings and extensively cited UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) guidance in determining "appropriate" security measures.

2. Companies should consider using privilege to protect internal documents. The Capita decision cited internal security documents (e.g., penetration tests) that highlighted weaknesses, so companies should consider conducting testing under privilege where appropriate.

3. There is a high bar for mitigating factors. The ICO fined LastPass £1.2 million on 20 November 2025, noting that despite "good" cooperation, it did not go "beyond what is reasonably to be expected." In Capita, prompt GDPR notification within 14 hours (well before the 72-hour deadline) was not considered a mitigating factor.

4. Fines can be assessed on holding or investment companies' revenue. The ICO based its LastPass fine on the global revenue of its holding company (consistent with EU case law), resulting in a fine of approximately 8.5% of LastPass' turnover. Private equity sponsors and investment companies should note this when budgeting compliance plans and framing corporate "group" entities.

Immediate actions recommended for companies: benchmark cybersecurity against NCSC guidance, review privacy policies/security testing/incident response plans, consider internal records wording and privilege utilization, establish effective ICO engagement models, and conduct tabletop data breach simulations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
These fines underscore the ICO’s emphasis on data breach enforcement and provide insight into the ICO’s approach to investigations and enforcement., "Companies should consider benchmarking cybersecurity against NCSC guidance, reviewing and updating incident response policies, and weighing the use of privilege in internal security documentation.", The ICO based its fine calculation on the global revenue of the holding company (not just the revenue of LastPass), resulting in a significant fine representing approximately 8.5% of LastPass’ turnover.

--- SOURCE 3: The LastPass ICO £1.2M Privacy Fine - Captain Compliance ---
URL: https://captaincompliance.com/education/the-lastpass-ico-1-2m-privacy-fine

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Captain Compliance analyzes the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) £1.2 million fine issued to LastPass for the 2022 data breach that affected 1.6 million British users. The author argues the penalty is inadequate compared to the actual harm, noting cryptocurrency thefts exceeding $438 million directly attributed to cracked LastPass vaults.

The breach unfolded in two stages in August 2022. Stage One involved attackers compromising a LastPass developer's corporate MacBook Pro, gaining access to the development environment and exfiltrating 14 of approximately 200 source code repositories containing production credentials. Stage Two exploited CVE-2020-5741, a known Plex Media Server vulnerability on a senior DevOps engineer's personal laptop. This allowed attackers to install a keylogger, capture the engineer's master password (shared between personal and business vaults), and gain access to AWS keys and decryption keys for LastPass's backup database, stealing encrypted vault data and personal information of millions of users.

Key timeline of cryptocurrency thefts attributed to the breach: October 2023 ($4.4 million), January 2024 ($150 million from Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen), February 2024 ($6.2 million), May 2024 (over $250 million total), December 2024 ($12.38 million), and April 2025 (over $50 million). Blockchain investigator ZachXBT tracked stolen funds; in March 2025, US authorities seized ~$24 million, with the FBI and Secret Service confirming the thefts stem from cracked LastPass vaults.

The article highlights legal failures including inadequate risk assessments, poor third-party risk management, insufficient privileged access controls, and misleading breach communications. Comparative penalties noted: British Airways fined £20 million (400,000 customers), Marriott £18.4 million (339 million customers), versus LastPass's £0.75 per affected user.

For privacy counsel, the article offers eight lessons: security theater kills; privileged access demands special treatment; personal device policies need enforcement; incident communications create legal exposure; "no evidence of decryption" isn't "no risk"; zero-knowledge architecture failed its promise; regulatory penalties don't reflect actual harm; and third-party software on employee devices is organizational risk. The breach continues generating new victims into 2025, creating an unusual situation where harm escalates over time rather than diminishing. LastPass faces ongoing US class action litigation that could dwarf the ICO fine.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Your passwords and notes vault have been copied by hackers in an attempt to decrypt your vault and steal ALL of its contents. It is only a matter of time and effort before they are able to access your data… Even if you do that, if you stored anything of value in there that you can't change, you are still screwed." - Security researcher Taylor Monahan
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Public listed company, Capita, fined £14m by the ICO for a data breach | Trowers & Hamlins law firm ---
URL: https://www.trowers.com/insights/2025/october/public-listed-company-capita-fined-14m-by-the-ico-for-a-data-breach

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Trowers & Hamlins (a law firm) reports that publicly listed company Capita plc and its subsidiary Capita Pension Solutions Limited (CPSL) were fined a total of £14 million by the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) in October 2025 for a data breach.

**The Breach:** In March 2023, Capita suffered a significant cyberattack that led to personal data of approximately 6.6 million individuals being stolen. The breach began when a malicious file was downloaded onto a Capita employee's device. Although a high security alert was triggered within 10 minutes, Capita failed to shut down the device for another 58 hours, allowing the attacker unrestricted access. The attacker later deployed ransomware and reset all user passwords, locking employees out of the network. Compromised data included names, addresses, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, bank details, passport scans, biometric data, and special category data (health records, racial/ethnic origin, political/religious beliefs, trade union membership, criminal record checks, and sexual orientation). The ICO received numerous complaints, and Capita faces a multi-party High Court claim involving nearly 4,000 claimants.

**Capita's Response:** Capita took remedial actions including restricting administrator access, deploying a more robust asset management system, and doubling Security Operations Centre analysts. However, the ICO found systemic failures including: failure to implement appropriate technical measures to prevent lateral movement and privilege escalation; failure to respond promptly to alerts (a critical alert left unaddressed for 58 hours); negligent oversight of penetration testing results that flagged high-risk vulnerabilities months before the incident; and inadequate resourcing/alert handling.

**The Fine:** Capita accepted the findings and entered a voluntary settlement, agreeing not to appeal. Penalties were reduced from an initial £58 million to £14 million (£8 million payable by Capita PLC, £6 million by CPSL). Information Commissioner John Edwards stated "the scale of this breach and its impact could have been prevented had sufficient security measures been in place."

**Key Takeaways:**
- Security measures must be proportionate to the sensitivity and volume of data processed.
- Timely responses to security alerts are critical.

URL: https://www.hlc.com/en/publications/the-uks-proposed-cyber-security-and-resilience-bill

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Hogan Lovells publication analyzes the UK's proposed Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, introduced to Parliament on 12 November 2025. It is the first major overhaul of UK cybersecurity legislation in almost a decade, designed to strengthen essential and digital services against cyber attacks with a strong emphasis on national security. The Bill amends the existing UK NIS Regulations in three primary ways:

**Expanded Scope:** UK NIS currently applies to operators of essential services (utilities, transportation, healthcare) and certain digital services providers (cloud computing, online search, online marketplaces). The Bill extends coverage to data centres, managed service providers, large electrical load controllers, and entities designated as "critical suppliers" — allowing regulators to designate companies in any sector as critical if they supply goods/services to UK NIS organizations where disruption could significantly impact the economy or society.

**Reporting Requirements:** The Bill lowers the threshold for notifiable incidents (now requiring incidents capable of having an adverse effect on network/Information system security). Organisations must make an initial notification within 24 hours of becoming aware of an incident, followed by a full notification within 72 hours, aligning the UK with EU NIS2 requirements. Reportable incidents must also be notified in parallel to the National Cyber Security Centre (part of GCHQ). Regulators can share incident information with relevant international authorities and inform the public when necessary.

**Expanded Regulatory and Government Powers:** Regulators gain power to charge fees (both periodic charges for oversight and specific charges for individual organisations). The maximum financial penalty will change from £17m to the greater of £17m or 4% of an undertaking's global turnover — aligned with UK GDPR. The Bill grants the Secretary of State the discretionary power to direct regulated entities to take steps mitigating imminent/live threats to UK national security, with enforcement fines of 10% of turnover or £17m for contravening such directions, and allows directors to forgo consultation if delay would harm national security.

**Comparison to EU NIS 2:** While the Bill aligns with NIS 2 on expansion of scope and stricter reporting, it diverges by: applying to fewer sectors; not imposing personal liability for management; allowing designation of critical suppliers; providing significant new powers to the SoS; introducing cost recovery through fees; and setting maximum fines at £17m or 4% global turnover (vs. €10M or 2% under NIS 2).

**Timeline:** No public timeline has been set, but the Government is anticipated to pass the legislation by the end of the current Parliamentary session in Spring 2026, with detailed compliance requirements expected via future secondary legislation. - DORA, alongside MiCAR, is a key component of the EU's Digital Finance Package aimed at harmonizing ICT risk management and strengthening EU financial market resilience
- DORA was first proposed in September 2020, formally adopted in December 2022 (Regulation EU 2022/2554), with a two-year transition period. The first package of RTS/ITS technical standards was published in January 2023, the second in July 2024, and DORA became fully applicable in January 2025
- The ESAs completed a feasibility study in January 2025 on further centralizing major ICT-related incident reporting, evaluating three models: the Baseline (decentralized, already in development), a Data Sharing model (feasible, 3+ years to develop), and a fully Centralized EU Hub (feasible, 5+ years to develop, would require amending DORA Art. 19)

**The Five Key Areas of DORA:**
1. **ICT Risk Management** (Art. 5-11): Requires internal governance frameworks, comprehensive ICT risk management frameworks, and operational resilience. The RTS adopted January 2024 establishes requirements for both the ICT Risk Management Framework and a Simplified ICT Risk Management Framework (SICTRMF)
2. **Incident Management, Classification & Reporting**: Significant incidents must be reported with specific timelines - initial notification within 4 hours of classification (no later than 24 hours after incident), intermediate report within 72 hours, and final report within 1 month
3. **Digital Operational Resilience Testing**: Includes vulnerability scans, penetration tests, and TLPT (Threat-Led Penetration Testing) for systemically important institutions at least every three years. TLPT follows a three-phase approach (Preparation, Test, Closure) and must be validated by supervisory authorities
4. **Third-Party Risk Management**: Requires due diligence on ICT providers, maintaining a register of all ICT contracts (including subcontractors), and annual communication to authorities. ESMA published a cross-sectoral third-party risk framework in June 2025. Notably, the European Commission rejected the initial RTS proposal on procurement of critical ICT services on January 21, 2025
5. **Information-Sharing Arrangements** (Art. 45): Financial entities may exchange threat intelligence within trusted communities, must notify NCAs of participation, and must protect data availability, authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality

**Regulatory Enforcement:**
- The supervisory framework divides responsibilities between ESAs (overseeing CTPPs, developing technical standards) and NCAs (national supervision). An Oversight Forum (Art. 32) coordinates among ESAs, NCAs, and EU bodies
- The Lead Overseer is a centralized EU authority monitoring systemic ICT risks posed by Critical Third-Party ICT Providers (CTPPs), addressing concentration risk from large providers like cloud platforms
- DORA uses a two-tiered enforcement approach: common principles at EU level (Art. 50-54), with Member States defining specific penalties. Italy aligned through D.Lgs. 23/2025 (March 2025), distinguishing severe violations (e.g., banks: €30K to 10% of annual turnover) and less severe violations (e.g., banks: €30K to 7% of turnover)

**DORA and AI Act Considerations:**
- Financial entities using AI systems must ensure compliance with both the AI Act and DORA. High-risk AI systems must be integrated into the ICT Risk Management framework, AI-related incidents reported under DORA, and AI providers subject to third-party risk assessments. Both regulations require robust testing and auditability (TLPT under DORA; pre-deployment checks and monitoring under AI Act Art. 73)

**Final Remarks:** DORA aims to harmonize ICT risk management across EU states, strengthen digital resilience, and safeguard customer trust. Compliance requires establishing strong ICT governance, developing comprehensive risk management frameworks, ensuring incident detection and reporting capabilities, conducting regular resilience testing, and managing third-party risks through contractual safeguards and continuous oversight.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Biggest Data Breaches in France (Updated July 2026) ---
URL: https://www.upguard.com/blog/biggest-data-breaches-france

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This UpGuard blog article (August 5, 2026, written by Kyle Chin and reviewed by Kaushik Sen) provides a comprehensive ranking of the 20 biggest data breaches in France, current as of July 2026. France has become the most heavily breached large jurisdiction in Europe by volume of exposed records, with the CNIL logging 6,167 personal data breach notifications in 2025 (up from 5,629 in 2024), around half involving hacking.

KEY TRENDS: The common thread across France's biggest breaches is abuse of legitimate access (compromised partner accounts, phished portals, poorly secured supplier systems) rather than exotic exploits. Concentration risk is critical—mid-sized intermediaries like Viamedis, Almerys, and Harvest hold data on behalf of hundreds of controllers, so one intrusion cascades into dozens of downstream notifications. At least seven separate incidents between 2024-2026 each affected more than five million people.

CNIL ENFORCEMENT: 2025 saw record fines of approximately €487 million (highest in history, ~9x the 2024 figure), including €325M against Google and €150M against Shein. Cumulatively the CNIL has issued more than €1 billion in fines since GDPR. Landmark breach-related decisions: France Travail fined €5M (Jan 22, 2026, Article 32 GDPR); Free Mobile fined €27M and Free €15M (€42M total, Jan 13, 2026).

TOP BREACHES (ranked):
1. FRANCE TRAVAIL: Up to 43 million people (largest in France/Europe by headcount), Feb-March 2024. Attackers impersonated Cap Emploi advisers to abuse legitimate credentials. Exposed names, birth data, social security numbers, contact info. No technical exploitation involved. Fined €5M in 2026; three suspects arrested.
2. VIAMEDIS & ALMERYS: Over 33 million people combined (largest French health breach), early 2024. Phished healthcare professional portals. CNIL confirmed combined figure; no fine as of July 2026.
3. FREE & FREE MOBILE (Iliad): ~19.2 million accounts, ~5.11M with IBANs, October 2024. Compromised subscriber management tool; data auctioned. Fined €42M total in 2026.
4. ANTS/FRANCE TITRES: 11.7 million accounts, April 2026. IDOR flaw in public portal. A 15-year-old suspect arrested; services disrupted into May 2026.
5. BOUYGUES TELECOM: 6.4 million customers, August 2025, including IBANs.
6. BOULANGER: Up to 27M records claimed by attacker (disputed/unverified), September 2024, via shared retail delivery vendor.
7. SFR: ~1.4 million customers (Sept 2024), with data including banking details resold November 2024 by a single actor who also hit Direct Assurance, Le Point, and Mediboard.
8. ORANGE: Ransomware (Warlock group), July 2025, ~4GB published (unquantified). Note: its separate €50M fine in 2024 was for unrelated advertising/cookie violations.
9. CULTURA: 1.5-2.6M accounts (unverified), same September 2024 retail campaign.
10. TRUFFAUT: ~270,000 accounts, same campaign.
11. AUCHAN: Several hundred thousand loyalty customers, November 2024.
12. PICARD: Tens of thousands of loyalty customers, November 2024.
13. DIRECT ASSURANCE (AXA): Tens of thousands (unverified), late 2024.
14. HARVEST: Wealth management software vendor serving ~4,600 clients (banks, insurers); breach via hosting provider (fourth-party), Feb 2025; MAIF and BPCE confirmed downstream exposure.
15. DEDALUS BIOLOGIE: 491,840 patients (most sensitive health data in French history - HIV status, genetic data, cancer diagnoses), 2021. Fined €1.5M in 2022 (processor fined directly, one of first significant European processor fines).
16. DEEZER: ~229 million user records (largest French dataset by record count) from third-party partner copy dated 2019, leaked November 2022.
17. DOCTOLIB: 6,128 appointments, July 2020; metadata alone revealed sensitive health info.
18. LE SLIP FRANÇAIS: ~1.5M email addresses, ~696K customer records, April 2024.
19. MANOMANO: Up to 37.8M records claimed by attacker (unverified, February 2026).
20. REPORTED 2026 PUBLIC SECTOR INCIDENTS (all unverified): OFII (2.1M claimed), Urssaf (12M claimed), Ministry of Education EduConnect (3.5M minors claimed), INSEE (12,800 agents).

RECOMMENDED CONTROLS: phishing-resistant authentication, strict third-party access governance, continuous dark web/attack surface monitoring, and CNIL 72-hour notification readiness. The article promotes UpGuard's Breach Risk and Vendor Risk products. FAQs confirm France Travail is the biggest breach (43M people) and that Free, Bouygues (2025), SFR, and Orange (2025) telecoms have all been breached.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: France's massive ID breach just exposed a bigger problem. ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fC1Vr5yymjg

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This video summary covers a major data breach at France's ANTS (National Agency for Secure Titles), the government agency responsible for issuing all passports, national ID cards, and driver's licenses in France. On April 15, 2026, the agency was breached, exposing up to 18 million personal records (later officially confirmed at 11.7 million accounts), affecting roughly a quarter to a third of French adults. The stolen data—including full names, email addresses, dates and places of birth, postal addresses, phone numbers, and unique account identifiers—was offered for sale on hacker forums within 48 hours (April 16). The agency disclosed the breach on April 22, a week after detection, and the Paris Prosecutor's Office later confirmed the number was between 12 and 18 million records.

The suspect arrested on May 4, 2026 was a 15-year-old operating under the "Breach 3D" alias on hacker forums—not a state actor or sophisticated criminal organization. This was at least the fourth significant compromise of French government identity infrastructure in under 12 months, following a September 2025 breach of roughly 12-13 million records (never confirmed), a December 2025 Interior Ministry email server compromise, and a January 2026 Immigration Office data theft via subcontractors.

The video's central argument is that this is a structural problem, not a one-off failure. France is preparing to integrate into the European Union Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI) rollout scheduled for 2027, and the same agency that was breached is part of that infrastructure. The EU wallet itself was previously demonstrated to have vulnerabilities: in April 2026, a security researcher bypassed its biometric locks and PIN codes in under 2 minutes using a free text file explorer. The video also cites similar patterns globally: India's Aadhaar system has been breached repeatedly affecting hundreds of millions of records; the UK is rolling out age verification under the Online Safety Act with verification vendors getting breached; and the US is implementing state-level mandates, with Discord losing 70,000 government ID photos through a third-party vendor in October 2025.

The video concludes that citizens have limited ability to opt out of mandatory digital identity infrastructure, and recommends pushing back on mandates while still being debated, supporting privacy organizations litigating these issues, and monitoring politicians' voting on these rollouts. The key message is that the French breach is a preview of what mandatory digital identification at scale looks like worldwide.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: French Government Agency Data Breach Hits Up to 19 Million Citizens ---
URL: https://www.safestate.com/post/french-government-agency-data-breach-hits-up-to-19-million-citizens

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A French government agency, the Agence nationale des titres sécurisés (ANTS or France Titres), has confirmed a data breach discovered on April 15, 2026, that may be one of the largest administrative leaks in the country's history. ANTS, which operates under the French Ministry of the Interior, is responsible for issuing passports, national ID cards, driver's licenses, and vehicle registration documents. The breach potentially exposed data from up to 19 million citizens' individual and professional accounts on the ants.gouv.fr portal. Confirmed exposed fields include full names, dates and places of birth, email addresses, login identifiers, and unique account IDs, with some cases also exposing home addresses and phone numbers. Uploaded documents (like scanned ID copies) were not affected, and the exposed data alone would not allow direct account access or document reissuance.

On April 16, a threat actor known as "breach3d" posted a claim on criminal forums offering between 18 and 19 million records for sale at an undisclosed price. The claimed dataset reportedly includes full names, contact details, birth data, home addresses, account metadata, gender, and civil status—fields extending beyond what ANTS officially confirmed. The attacker described the vulnerability as "elementary" and "really stupid," with technical analysis pointing to an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability on the ANTS API that required no sophisticated tooling—just manipulating a parameter in a request. The data has not been publicly leaked yet but remains a private criminal listing.

Authorities' response includes notification of CNIL (France's data protection authority) per GDPR Article 33, a report to the Paris Public Prosecutor, alerting ANSSI (France's national cybersecurity agency), and the Office anti-cybercriminalité (OFAC) leading the technical investigation. ANTS is notifying directly affected users and warning them to exercise extreme caution with SMS, calls, or emails appearing to come from ANTS, as fraudsters exploit breaches for impersonation campaigns.

The exposed data creates a ready-made profile for social engineering and targeted phishing, particularly for messages impersonating French administrative services. Professional account data also raises concerns for businesses like vehicle dealers and administrative service providers. This breach follows a pattern of French incidents including a breach of the FICOBA banking data registry earlier this year and an attack on parcel firm Relais Colis affecting tens of millions of records. The permanent nature of government-issued identity data (citizens cannot change dates of birth or national ID numbers) makes this data useful for identity fraud for years. Investigations remain active with no arrest reported.

Ceva confirmed the cyberattack in a statement to TechCrunch: "On Aug. 1, CEVA Logistics confirmed to affected customers that a cyber intrusion was impacting part of its European contract logistics operations." The company stated operational impact is limited to eight warehouses with no other global systems affected. Ceva said some affected applications and services are back online and that it is working with authorities. The company reported $18.3 billion in revenue in 2025 and operates over a thousand warehouses worldwide.

Ceva spokesperson Ryan Fisher declined to answer questions about how much data was taken or whether a ransom demand was received. The Dutch data protection authority has received breach reports from 10 organizations related to the incident, and Dutch authorities are investigating. FreightWaves reported the hack began on July 29. Shipping and logistics giants have become growing targets for cybercriminals due to their ability to access and hijack trucks and containers to get goods to real-world gangs.
</summary>

URL: https://www.regulation-dora.eu/blog/dora-enforcement-2026-end-grace-period

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published April 1, 2026 (updated April 16, 2026), outlines the shift from the DORA "grace period" of 2025 to an active enforcement reality in 2026. After DORA became fully applicable on January 17, 2025, regulators initially focused on education and accepted "good-faith" compliance efforts. Since Q1 2026, national competent authorities (NCAs) across the EU have moved to an interventionist supervisory posture, marked by three developments: (1) the Register of Information (RoI) xBRL-CSV submission deadline (the first hard compliance test), (2) expanded NCA supervisory capacity (BaFin, ECB, FCA, AMF/ACPR, DNB, Banca d'Italia), and (3) first formal measures—with DNB (Netherlands) issuing the first supervisory letters in early 2026.

NCAs now run automated analyses on RoI data, including concentration mapping (which fed designation of 19 CTPPs in November 2025), completeness scoring, cross-referencing with incident reports, and sub-outsourcing chain depth checks. The penalty framework distinguishes between financial institutions (Article 50) subject to national penalties (administrative fines, periodic penalty payments, public censure, cease-and-desist orders, and prohibition of management body members) and designated Critical ICT Third-Party Providers (Articles 35, 42) under EU-level oversight (periodic penalty payments up to 1% of average daily global turnover per day for up to six months, mandatory remediation notices, and requests to terminate contracts). Article 52 establishes personal liability for executives where infringements are attributable to natural persons.

Penalties vary by jurisdiction: Italy up to EUR 20M (wilful/gross negligence), Germany up to EUR 5M with EUR 1M personal liability, while France, Ireland, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands apply proportionate or EU-maximum thresholds. The article notes NCAs now treat zero incident reports as statistically anomalous—viewing it as evidence of a non-functional incident classification process. Priority audit areas in 2026 include RoI quality, board-approved ICT risk frameworks, Article 30 contract compliance, incident classification methodology, and resilience testing (with TLPT required by January 2028 for designated entities).

The enforcement ladder progresses from desk review/data request to supervisory letter, on-site inspection, formal remediation order, compulsion payment notice, and finally administrative fine/public censure. The article provides seven recommended actions: audit RoI submission, verify board documentation, run contract clause review, test incident classification, document testing programmes, assess TLPT applicability, and prepare management body evidence files. The bottom line: supervisors measure the quality of response to gaps, and active engagement with documented remediation and board-level ownership differentiates successful institutions from enforcement case studies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 18: DORA Enforcement: What Regulators Are Checking in 2026 | ComplyOne ---
URL: https://www.complyone.io/guides/dora/dora-enforcement-2026

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (updated 1 July 2026) provides an overview of DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act) enforcement one year after it became fully applicable on 17 January 2025. Regulatory focus has shifted from guidance to active supervision by national competent authorities, the ECB, EBA, and sector supervisors (ESMA for securities, EIOPA for insurance).

ENFORCEMENT BODIES: The ECB/SSM directly supervises significant credit institutions (first DORA-focused reviews began H2 2025); the EBA sets regulatory technical standards and directly oversees critical ICT third-party providers; NCAs supervise less significant institutions, payment institutions, e-money institutions, and investment firms (enforcement varies by member state, with some NCAs active since H1 2025 and others still building capacity).

COMMON NON-COMPLIANCE FINDINGS FROM EARLY EXAMINATIONS:
1. Register of Information deficiencies (most common): incomplete provider coverage, missing LEI codes, undocumented criticality assessments, missing/inaccurate data residency, absent sub-contractor information.
2. Contract gaps (Article 30): missing audit rights, incident notification obligations, and exit assistance provisions in legacy contracts with critical providers.
3. Incident reporting failures: no pre-established authority contacts/channels, undefined classification criteria causing slow major-incident determination, no pre-built notification templates. The 4-hour initial notification requirement proves difficult.
4. Testing documentation gaps: pen tests and vulnerability scans conducted but not formally documented, remediation not tracked, production systems not covered.
5. Management body engagement: ICT risk frameworks lack evidence of board approval; board-level ICT risk reporting is absent or only one-way IT reporting.

ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS AS OF EARLY 2026:
- Register of Information penalties: multiple NCAs in Germany, Netherlands, and France issued formal findings and remediation orders; fines of €100,000–€500,000 for mid-size entities.
- Contract compliance orders: authorities ordered renegotiation of critical provider contracts to include Article 30 provisions within defined remediation periods.
- Incident reporting: two ECB supervisory actions for delayed notifications — one 6-hour delay (exceeding the 4-hour window) and one failure to notify at all; both resulted in formal supervisory letters and enhanced monitoring.
- No significant financial fines for small entities yet; 2026 enforcement has focused on remediation orders, expected to change as remediation compliance windows close.

WHAT EXAMINERS WILL REQUEST: (1) Register of Information in ESA standard format with line-by-line review; (2) 2–3 sample critical provider contracts reviewed for Article 30; (3) incident logs from past 24 months including classification rationale and notification records; (4) board minutes evidencing ICT risk discussion and framework approval; (5) testing documentation (pen tests, vulnerability scans, resilience exercises) from past 12–24 months; (6) the documented ICT risk management framework and latest risk assessment.

PRIORITIES FOR COMPLIANCE: 1) Complete/validate the Register of Information (most examined document); 2) Audit contracts against Article 30 and build a contract amendment programme targeting completion within 90 days; 3) Document and test incident notification (pre-populate contacts/templates, run tabletop exercise to verify 4-hour window); 4) Organize testing documentation from past 12 months with remediation tracking; 5) Evidence board engagement — a single board agenda item is insufficient, establish quarterly board-level ICT risk reporting.

The article is presented by ComplyOne, which offers DORA compliance tools. Related guides cover DORA fintech checklists, ICT third-party risk management, and incident reporting requirements.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 19: Supervisory priorities 2026-28 ---
URL: https://www.bankingsupervision.europa.eu/framework/priorities/html/ssm.supervisory_priorities202511.en.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document from ECB Banking Supervision presents the supervisory priorities for the period 2026-28, reflecting the medium-term strategy set by the ECB's Supervisory Board based on a comprehensive assessment of main risks and vulnerabilities in the European banking sector.

**Context and Risk Assessment:**
- The European banking system has a sound risk profile with strong capital and liquidity positions, low non-performing loans, and resilient profitability despite falling interest rates.
- Global uncertainties have surged to exceptional levels due to geopolitical tensions, shifting trade policies, climate crises, demographic change, and technological disruptions, making tail risks unprecedently high.
- The 2026-28 priorities were developed amid an escalation in global trade tensions (including US import tariffs announced in April 2025) and broader geopolitical risks.
- Euro area real GDP growth is projected to strengthen over the projection horizon, with inflation stabilizing around the 2% target.

**Priority 1: Strengthening banks' resilience to geopolitical risks and macro-financial uncertainties**
This priority addresses three key vulnerabilities:
1. **Ensure prudent risk-taking and sound credit standards** - To prevent accumulation of new non-performing loans, with a thematic review of credit underwriting standards, targeted review of loan pricing, and credit risk on-site inspections. Supervisors identified weaknesses in provisioning and IFRS 9 frameworks, including arbitrary overlays and inadequate risk capture.
2. **Ensure adequate capitalisation and consistent implementation of CRR III** - Focuses on implementing the new standardised approach under the CRR III/CRD VI package (in force since 1 January 2025), covering credit risk (targeted reviews and OSIs on risk-weighted assets), operational risk (review of business indicator component), and market risk. The 2026 thematic stress test will assess institution-specific geopolitical risk scenarios.
3. **Ensure prudent management of climate and nature-related (C&N) risks** - Global temperatures have surpassed 1.5°C above pre-industrial average, only ~25% of natural hazard losses are insured, and 90% of surveyed banks consider themselves materially exposed to C&N risks (up from ~50% in 2021). Activities include thematic review of transition planning (in line with CRD VI), monitoring of Pillar 3 ESG disclosures, and targeted OSIs.

**Priority 2: Strengthening banks' operational resilience and fostering robust ICT capabilities**

1. **Implement robust and resilient operational risk management frameworks** - With the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) in force since early 2025, activities include targeted follow-up on material shortcomings in ICT security/cyber resilience, two OSI campaigns on cybersecurity and third-party risk management, threat-led penetration testing, targeted review of ICT change management, and deep dive into cloud service provider dependency. The oversight of critical third-party providers under DORA will launch in January 2026. Reported significant cyber incidents have doubled in recent years.
2. **Remedy deficiencies in risk reporting capabilities (RDARR)** - Progress remains slow with no improvement in SREP scores; a system-wide strategy was approved in December 2024 covering all supervised entities, focusing on management bodies' accountability and remediation strategies. Weaknesses include data governance frameworks, data infrastructure/IT architecture, and data accuracy/integrity (gaps against BCBS 239 principles).
3. **Medium to long-term priority strategy on digital and AI-related strategies** - Focuses on banks' AI strategies, governance and risk management, with particular attention on generative AI applications. ECB Banking Supervision will conduct targeted horizontal workshops with selected banks on generative AI, cooperate with market surveillance authorities on the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, and continue horizon scanning (including monitoring stablecoins).

**Supervisory Cycle (Box 1):** The priorities inform integrated planning including horizontal activities, on-site missions, and JST initiatives, summarized in Supervisory Examination Programmes (SEPs) communicated to banks annually at the start of the supervisory cycle. Tools include thematic reviews, targeted reviews, deep dives, and on-site inspections, following a "risk identification-risk remediation" approach.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The supervisory priorities for 2026-28 reflect ECB Banking Supervision's medium-term strategy for the next three years. Global uncertainties have surged to exceptional levels, creating an environment of heightened fragility, where risks once considered remote are becoming more likely.

--- SOURCE 20: What Is DORA? What Financial Institutions Need to Know in 2026 | Mitratech ---
URL: https://mitratech.com/resource-hub/blog/what-is-dora

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Mitratech is an educational article titled "What Is DORA? What Financial Institutions Need to Know in 2026." The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) is an EU regulation requiring financial institutions to withstand, respond to, and recover from ICT-related disruptions and threats. It entered into application on January 17, 2025, and applies to banks, credit institutions, insurers, investment firms, payment and e-money institutions, crypto-asset service providers, central counterparties, trading venues, credit rating agencies, and their ICT third-party providers—including non-EU firms with EU operations or EU-facing services.

DORA is organized around five key domains (pillars): 1) ICT Risk Management and Governance (management body owns the ICT risk framework with board-level oversight that must be evidenceable); 2) Incident Response and Reporting (major ICT incidents reported to NCA in three stages—initial notification within 4 hours of classification, intermediate report within 72 hours, and final report within one month, per RTS 2025/301); 3) Digital Operational Resilience Testing (including TIBER-EU-aligned Threat-Led Penetration Testing for significant entities under Article 26); 4) Third-Party Risk Management (maintaining a Register of Information, contract provisions including audit rights, exit strategies, and concentration risk management); and 5) Information and Intelligence Sharing (least prescriptive and least supervisory-attention-generating domain).

Enforcement has shifted from supervisory tolerance to active review in 2026. The ECB published its Guide on Outsourcing Cloud Services in July 2025, removing interpretive ambiguity. NCAs are now examining whether controls are working, continuously maintained, and evidenceable on demand—not just whether they exist.

Key details on the Register of Information: it is a mandatory, structured record of every third-party ICT contract, submitted annually to the NCA (structured around standardized ESA templates under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2956). The 2026 submission cycle covered data as at December 31, 2025, running through Q1 2026. Each entry must capture provider identity (including LEI or EU-ID), service descriptions with criticality classification, data locations, sub-outsourcing arrangements, contractual terms, and substitutability assessment. The register is a live supervisory instrument that NCAs may request outside the annual cycle without fixed lead time. Common failure points include incomplete LEI data, missing sub-outsourcing dependencies, and inaccurate criticality classifications.

Regarding Critical Third-Party Providers (CTPPs): as of October 2025, 19 ICT providers have been formally designated by the ESAs as systemically important. CTPPs face direct ESA oversight (by a Lead Overseer), including onsite inspections, audit access, and financial penalties for non-cooperation. However, CTPP designation does NOT replace financial entities' own compliance obligations—entities retain full DORA duties including due diligence and contractual protections.

Penalty framework is set out in Articles 50-54 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554. The article recommends organizations conduct gap assessments across the five domains, and advocates for continuous vendor monitoring, tested incident classification criteria, and continuously updated Register of Information, rather than annual point-in-time assessments. The article is published by Mitratech, a legal and compliance solutions provider, and includes related articles on AI third-party risk management under global AI regulations and the NIST Privacy Framework.
</summary>

# What is a Third-Party Data Breach? 7 Recent Examples

## Tags:

[Vulnerabilities & Incidents](/blog?field_topics_target_id=111)

[Third Party Risk Management](/blog?field_topics_target_id=211)

![prevent third party attacks](/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_xlarge/public/2023/01/20/Shutterstock_1357340402.jpg?itok=DjO8CC65)

Share:

* [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.bitsight.com/blog/third-party-data-breach "Facebook")
* [Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.bitsight.com/blog/third-party-data-breach "Twitter")
* [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.bitsight.com/blog/third-party-data-breach "LinkedIn")

Written by [Kaitlyn Graham](/our-team/kaitlyn-graham)

## What is a Third-Party Data Breach?

A **third-party data breach** is a security incident where an organization's sensitive data is compromised or stolen due to a vulnerability or cyber attack on one of its third party vendors. This type of breach happens outside the primary organization's own IT infrastructure but still impacts them, as the third-party vendor, contractor, or service provider has access to their data.

Stolen data may include sensitive, proprietary, or confidential information such as credit card numbers, trade secrets, customer, or patient data. Third party breaches cost millions of dollars every year to companies of all sizes. The average total [cost of a data breach](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/cost-of-data-breach) is $4.35 million, and in the United States, it rises to $9.44 million.

Because attackers target a member of the victim’s supply chain, a third party data breach might also be called a [supply chain attack](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/what-are-software-supply-chain-attacks). These attacks are often successful because third parties, including vendors, suppliers, contractors, or business partners, may have weaker security controls than the organizations they provide services to.

## 7 Recent Third-Party Data Breaches

Third-party vendors are critical to your business – but they also introduce cyber risk. Indeed, [supply chain attacks](https://www.bitsight.com/uses/supply-chain-cybersecurity-risk-management) are now the preferred method used by threat actors, and [62% of network intrusions](https://www.verizon.com/about/news/ransomware-threat-rises-verizon-2022-data-breach-investigations-report) originate with a third-party – often someone in your software supply chain.

The alarming aspect of a third-party data breach is the sheer scale of impact. Hackers have the potential to attack thousands of organizations in one fell swoop. According to a [study](https://assets.kpmg/content/dam/kpmg/xx/pdf/2022/01/third-party-risk-management-outlook-2022.pdf) by KPMG, 73% of organizations have experienced at least one significant disruption from a third-party cyber incident within the last three years.

Managing [third-party cyber](/glossary/third-party-cyber-risk) risk can be complex, but neglecting it poses substantial risks. Let’s look at five of the biggest third-party data breaches in recent years, how they happened, and their impact. We’ll also offer a step-based approach for maturing your third-party risk management (TPRM) program.

## 1. NotPetya (2017)

Although supply chain-based attacks have grown tremendously in the past year or two, one of the more notable ones happened in 2017. A Petya ransomware variant called NotPetya was used to target a Ukrainian accounting software package -- using a vulnerability previously exploited in the WannaCry supply chain attack as well as a credential-stealing technique for non-vulnerable machines -- before deploying ransomware.

### Impact

The malware quickly spread beyond Ukrainian targets, affecting numerous multinational corporations, resulting in extensive financial losses, operational disruptions, and data destruction.

## 2. SolarWinds (2020)

In December 2020, [SolarWinds](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/bitsight-analysis-of-solarwinds-orion-part-1-prevalence) (a provider of network and system monitoring software) confirmed that its network had been penetrated by a malicious actor and a complex malware program inserted into software updates of its technology platform – SolarWinds OrionⓇ. The program comprised a multistage process, scanning downstream customer networks to detect security tools it could avoid or disable, and stealthily connecting to the attacker’s command and control servers. The malware persisted for months before initial detection.

### Impact

Because SolarWinds owned “the keys to the kingdom” for many organizations, it was an ideal target for disseminating an attack. Even organizations who did not use SolarWinds products were exposed to risk due to the prevalence of the company’s solutions within the supply chain. It’s estimated that 18,000 customers (including government agencies and 14% of the Fortune 1000) were impacted.

The [financial fallout](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/financial-impact-cyber-attacks) was also significant. [Incident response](/blog/how-create-incident-response-plan-2026-5-step-template) and forensic services cost companies [11% of their annual revenue](https://heimdalsecurity.com/blog/solarwinds-attack-cost-impacted-companies-an-average-of-12-million/) (an average of $12 million). Moreover, [Bitsight’s analysis](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/the-financial-impact-of-solarwinds-a-cyber-catastrophe-but-insurance-disaster-avoided) quantified the insured losses from the attack at $90,000,000. The breach also set the stage for other supply chain attacks.

Read more about [The Future of Supply Chain Cyber Risk Management After SolarWinds](https://www.bitsight.com/sites/default/files/migration/documents/Good%2520Harbor_%2520SolarWinds%2520Salon%2520Discussion.pdf) and lessons learned from the failures that led to the attack.

## 3. Microsoft (2021)

Because most security tools trust anything implicitly signed by Microsoft, the tech giant is a frequent target of cyber attacks, and many of these exploit the interconnected supply chain. In March 2021, a series of breaches, known as the [HAFNIUM attacks](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/hafnium-observations), compromised the on-premises Microsoft Exchange Servers of 30,000 global organizations. The attacks allowed hackers to access employee email accounts and install malware to facilitate long-term access.

### Impact

Further demonstrating the surge in [software supply chain security hacks](/glossary/software-supply-chain-security), just months later, 38 million records were exposed due to a vulnerability in Microsoft Power Apps (a popular low-code business intelligence tool). Perpetrators gained access to COVID-19 testing, tracing, and vaccination records, as well as employee information for major organizations using the tool, such as Ford Motor Company, American Airlines, and the New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority.

## 4. Toyota (2022)

[According to McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/industrials-and-electronics/our-insights/reimagining-industrial-supply-chains), an auto manufacturer has around 250 tier-one suppliers, but the number proliferates to 18,000 across the full value chain – making these companies highly vulnerable to a third-party data breach.

For example, in March 2022, [Toyota](https://www.cpomagazine.com/cyber-security/toyotas-supply-chain-cyber-attack-stopped-production-cutting-down-a-third-of-its-global-output/) suspended production at 14 [manufacturing plants](https://www.bitsight.com/industries/cyber-risk-management-for-manufacturing) in Japan after a supplier of plastic parts – Kojima Industries – was hit by a cyber attack. Toyota subsequently suspended operations of “all 28 lines at 14 domestic plants,” according to a company statement. The impacted output accounted for a third of global Toyota production.

Per McKinsey, even a short disruption of 30 days or fewer can put three to five percent of EBITDA margin at stake.

## 5. Uber (2022)

In December 2022, ride hailing giant Uber experienced a third-party data breach as a result of a compromised vendor. Teqtivity, which helps Uber track, monitor, and manage IT assets, [confirmed](https://www.teqtivity.com/breach-notification-statement/) that a hacker breached its systems and gained access to email addresses and other information pertaining to more than 77,000 Uber employees.

The hack follows a similar incident [targeting DoorDash](https://www.itpro.co.uk/security/phishing/368905/doordash-data-breach-exposes-customer-details), where bad actors leveraged a connected vendor’s stolen credentials to access the food delivery giant’s internal systems and breach customer information, including credit card details.

## 6. U.S. School Districts (2022)

[School districts](https://www.bitsight.com/industries/cyber-risk-management-solutions-for-education) are a lucrative target for hackers due to the volume of PII on their networks and limited security resources. Moreover, as EdTech tools gain traction, software supply chains have become a favored [attack vector](/blog/attack-vector-vs-attack-surface-what-difference).

For example, a 2022 attack on [Illuminate Education](https://www.k12dive.com/news/following-high-profile-data-breach-illuminate-education-acquired-by-ed-tec/630927/), a leading provider of student-tracking software, resulted in data breaches at the nation’s two largest school systems – New York City Public Schools and Los Angeles Unified School District – and [countless more](https://thejournal.com/articles/2022/05/15/list-of-all-schools-confirmed-impacted-by-illuminate-education-data-breach.aspx). The same year, [495,000 student records at Chicago Public Schools](https://portswigger.net/daily-swig/chicago-public-schools-data-breach-blamed-on-third-party-ransomware-attack) were exposed as a result of an attack on a third-party provider.

## 7. MOVEit (2023)

File transfer solutions are frequent targets of cybercriminals, due to their role in facilitating the exchange of sensitive data across the supply chain. In June 2023, three critical SQL injection vulnerabilities were discovered in Progress Software’s MOVEit Transfer platform, a tool designed to securely transfer sensitive files used by close to 1,700 organizations. Zellis, a UK-based payroll and HR solutions provider, was affected by the MOVEit vulnerability and targeted by the Cl0p ransomware gang.

### Impact

This attack resulted in unauthorized access to sensitive personal information of both Zellis and its clients. The MOVEit supply chain attack also affected dozens of other organizations, including British Airways, the BBC, and the Minnesota Department of Education, and posed a significant risk to millions of individuals globally.

## How to Prevent a Third-Party Data Breach: VRM Best Practices

Third-party vendors are key to any business in today’s interconnected economy, providing critical services like billing, software development, or data storage. So how do you make sure your vendors do not create unnecessary risk?

The answer is not to avoid third party relationships, but to engage only with vendors who show a robust security posture. This can be easily accomplished by thorough [vendor risk assessments](https://www.bitsight.com/resources/40-questions-you-should-have-in-your-vendor-security-assessment) and [continuous monitoring](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/how-continuous-monitoring-revolutionizes-third-party-risk-management), as part of vendor risk management ([VRM](https://www.bitsight.com/vendor-risk-management)) and holistic third party risk management ([TPRM](https://www.bitsight.com/third-party-risk-management)) programs. Here are some ways in which a third party risk management program can help [secure your supply chain](https://www.bitsight.com/uses/supply-chain-cybersecurity-risk-management) and **prevent a third party data breach**:

* Streamlining due diligence and vendor risk assessments to [assess vendors](https://www.bitsight.com/resources/bitsight-vendor-risk-management-data-sheet) before onboarding
* Automating the onboarding and [reassessment](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/how-and-when-to-reassess-your-vendors-cybersecurity-posture) process for more agile risk mitigation
* Facilitating [continuous monitoring](https://www.bitsight.com/uses/continuous-monitoring) based on real-time data feeds and analytics
* Increasing visibility over risk from third party and [fourth party](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/what-fourth-party-risk-why-its-important-and-how-manage-it) relationships
* Customizing and updating security requirements upon newly discovered threats and vulnerabilities
* Identifying vendors who no longer meet security standards and facilitating their offboarding without causing business continuity issues

## Managing Third-Party Risk: TPRM

These and other third-party data breaches demonstrate the importance of managing third-party risks. Yet, the KPMG [study](https://assets.kpmg/content/dam/kpmg/xx/pdf/2022/01/third-party-risk-management-outlook-2022.pdf) found that 61% of businesses underestimate the importance of TRPM. They also struggle to maintain a fit for purpose operating model, citing two key reasons:

1. Technology investments fail to provide visibility into third-party risk.
2. The challenge of limited resources makes it hard to understand and [mitigate third-party risk](/node/8646) at scale – across hundreds, if not thousands, of vendors.

Indeed, most businesses accept that it was luck, not their TPRM programs, that helped them avoid a major third-party data breach in the past few years.

As your vendor portfolio grows (most businesses work with an average of 1,000 suppliers), you need a way to scale your TPRM program while reducing the burden on security and risk management teams. Below are some must-haves that can help you do this, regardless of the maturity of your TPRM program:

### **1. Tier vendors or suppliers**

It is not necessary to analyze each vendor in the same depth. Given limited time and resources, pay attention to those third parties that a) provide the most critical services, and b) have access to systems and [sensitive data](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/sensitive-data-examples-how-to-protect-it). Our [tier recommender service](https://www.bitsight.com/press-releases/new-bitsight-innovations-help-organizations-achieve-a-higher-standard-for-third-party-risk-management) can aid in grouping your vendors based on their risk and criticality to your business. As your TPRM program matures, you can expand its scope to cover a broader range of third parties and additional risk areas.

### **2. Set vendor risk tolerance thresholds**

Bitsight’s data insights make it easy to [establish an acceptable risk threshold](https://www.bitsight.com/security-ratings) a supplier must achieve to be considered a potential partner – and then measure them against it.

### **3. [Continuously and automatically monitor](https://www.bitsight.com/uses/continuous-monitoring) the security postures of third parties**

With [Bitsight for TPRM](https://www.bitsight.com/third-party-risk-management), you’ll get dashboard views into the cyber health of each supplier (during [due diligence](/blog/what-is-due-diligence-in-cyber-security) and over the lifetime of the contract) and automatic alerts the moment risk is discovered.

### **4. Collaborate with partners to reduce risk and exposure**

To ensure rapid triage, [share Bitsight’s findings with your vendors](https://www.bitsight.com/resources/enable-vendor-access-video) so they can view hidden risk in their networks.

### **5. Extend cyber risk insights to fourth parties**

Because risk can quickly cascade across the supply chain, use [Bitsight for Fourth-Party Risk Management](https://www.bitsight.com/fourth-party-risk-management) for an unprecedented view into security vulnerabilities across your entire vendor ecosystem.

### **6. Unify vendor data and assessments**

Organize vendor security and risk management data in a unified tool. For instance, [Bitsight Vendor Risk Management (VRM)](https://www.bitsight.com/vendor-risk-management) spans all aspects of VRM with one fully integrated solution. You can make informed decisions about where to prioritize resources without needing to jump between disparate tools.

These best practices don't have to be standalone. You can automate third-party assessment, validation, vulnerability detection, and reporting at scale with an [end-to-end TPRM solution](https://www.bitsight.com/third-party-risk-management) that [integrates with your existing vendor risk management tools](https://www.bitsight.com/tprm-integrations), so you always stay on top of threats.

This article from Bitsight (written by Kaitlyn Graham) explains third-party data breaches and provides seven notable recent examples, followed by best practices for preventing them through third-party risk management (TPRM) and vendor risk management (VRM).

**What is a Third-Party Data Breach?**
A third-party data breach is a security incident where an organization's sensitive data is compromised or stolen due to a vulnerability or cyber attack on one of its third-party vendors, contractors, or service providers. It occurs outside the primary organization's own IT infrastructure but impacts them because the vendor has access to their data. Such breaches may also be called supply chain attacks. Attackers often target third parties because they may have weaker security controls than the organizations they serve. Key statistics: the average total cost of a data breach is $4.35 million (rising to $9.44 million in the US); 62% of network intrusions originate with a third party; and 73% of organizations have experienced at least one significant disruption from a third-party cyber incident in the last three years (per a KPMG study).

**Seven Notable Third-Party Data Breaches:**
1. **NotPetya (2017):** A Petya ransomware variant targeted a Ukrainian accounting software package using a previously exploited WannaCry vulnerability, spreading globally to multinational corporations, causing extensive financial losses, operational disruptions, and data destruction.
2. **SolarWinds (2020):** Malicious actors inserted complex malware into SolarWinds Orion® software updates. The malware scanned downstream customer networks for months. An estimated 18,000 customers (including government agencies and 14% of the Fortune 1000) were impacted. The attack cost companies 11% of annual revenue (average $12 million), with insured losses of $90,000,000.
3. **Microsoft (2021):** The HAFNIUM attacks compromised on-premises Microsoft Exchange Servers of 30,000 global organizations. Months later, 38 million records were exposed due to a vulnerability in Microsoft Power Apps, including COVID-19 testing, tracing, vaccination records, and employee data for Ford Motor Company, American Airlines, and the NY Metropolitan Transportation Authority.
4. **Toyota (2022):** Production was suspended at 14 Japanese plants (a third of global output) after supplier Kojima Industries was hit by a cyber attack. Per McKinsey, auto manufacturers have ~250 tier-one suppliers but 18,000 across the full value chain; a short disruption of 30 days can put 3-5% of EBITDA margin at stake.
5. **Uber (2022):** Compromised vendor Teqtivity (which manages IT assets) leaked email addresses and information of more than 77,000 Uber employees. A similar incident targeted DoorDash with stolen vendor credentials.
6. **U.S. School Districts (2022):** A 2022 attack on Illuminate Education (student-tracking software) caused data breaches at New York City Public Schools and Los Angeles Unified School District. Also, 495,000 student records at Chicago Public Schools were exposed via a third-party ransomware attack.
7. **MOVEit (2023):** Three critical SQL injection vulnerabilities were found in Progress Software's MOVEit Transfer platform (used by ~1,700 organizations). The Cl0p ransomware gang targeted Zellis (UK payroll provider), affecting British Airways, the BBC, and the Minnesota Department of Education, risking millions of individuals globally.

**How to Prevent Third-Party Data Breaches (VRM/TPRM Best Practices):**
- Streamline due diligence and vendor risk assessments before onboarding
- Automate onboarding and reassessment processes
- Facilitate continuous monitoring with real-time data feeds
- Increase visibility over third- and fourth-party risk
- Customize security requirements upon new threats
- Identify and offboard vendors who no longer meet security standards

**Managing Third-Party Risk (TPRM):**
Per KPMG, 61% of businesses underestimate the importance of TPRM, citing technology investments failing to provide visibility and limited resources. Most businesses work with an average of 1,000 suppliers. Recommended practices include: (1) tiering vendors by criticality and risk, (2) setting vendor risk tolerance thresholds, (3) continuously and automatically monitoring third-party security postures, (4) collaborating with partners to reduce risk, (5) extending insights to fourth parties, and (6) unifying vendor data and assessments in one tool (e.g., Bitsight VRM/TPRM solutions).

# Data Breach Impacts Victorian Schools: Key Cybersecurity Lessons for 2026

![Teenage Girl Raising Hand While Attending Computer Class with Teacher Present | school data breach](https://netstrategy.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/teenage-girl-raising-hand-while-attending-computer-2026-01-08-08-20-43-utc-2000x977.jpg)

A single network intrusion has granted hackers access to the personal information of current and past Victorian government school students. 

The Victorian Department of Education confirmed in January 2026 that an ‘external third party’ obtained student names, email addresses, school names, year levels, and encrypted passwords through a school’s network.

The department has stated that no other personal data – such as dates of birth, phone numbers, or home addresses – was compromised, and there is currently no evidence the data has been released publicly. 

However, this breach is a stark reminder of the cybersecurity challenges facing Australian schools.

The department has since identified the point of breach and implemented a series of safeguards, including temporarily disabling systems to help prevent further unauthorised access. 

But here’s the real question: if it happened to them, could it happen to your school?

## **The consequences of data breaches for Australian schools**

[This data breach](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-01-14/student-data-breach-victorian-education-department/106230114) is not an isolated case. Schools across Australia are increasingly targeted because they hold valuable personal data but often lack the security resources of other sectors. 

This school’s data breach exposes what’s at stake:

## 

![](https://netstrategy.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/data-breach-schools-scaled.jpg)

## **7 critical actions to protect your school from a data breach**

### 1. Assume you are a target

Schools hold vast amounts of sensitive data. Cybercriminals know this. 

[Education is the number 3 most attractive sector to attack](https://securitybrief.com.au/story/education-remains-a-target-for-cyberattacks-says-microsoft). Every school should operate under the assumption that they’re a potential target, regardless of size or sector. 

### 2. Conduct regular cybersecurity assessments

When was the last time your school had a [comprehensive cybersecurity assessment](https://www.netstrategy.net/it-services/cybersecurity-services/)? Regular audits help identify vulnerabilities before attackers do. This includes reviewing:

### 3. Strengthen access controls

The Victorian breach occurred through a school’s network. Multi-factor authentication, strong password policies, and limiting system access to only what staff need can significantly reduce unauthorised entry points. 

Increasingly, we now see a growing trend to move towards student-based MFA, given new attack vectors we have detected in the last 12 months. 

### 4. Encrypt and protect sensitive data

While passwords in this breach were encrypted, not all data may receive the same protection. 

Schools should ensure that all sensitive information is encrypted both at rest and in transit. Encryption standards should be regularly reviewed and updated.

### 5. Train staff and students

[Human error remains a leading cause of breaches.](https://www.oaic.gov.au/news/blog/latest-notifiable-data-breach-statistics-for-january-to-june-2025) 

Regular cybersecurity awareness training helps staff and students recognise phishing attempts, understand safe data handling practices, and know how to report suspicious activity.

### 6. Have a Cyber Incident Response Plan

When a breach occurs, time is critical. 

Document who manages the response, containment steps, communication protocols, and regulatory reporting requirements before you need them. We believe that an optimised [Cyber Security Incident Response Plan](https://www.cyber.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-12/PROTECT%20-%20Cyber%20Security%20Incident%20Response%20Planning%20-%20Practitioner%20Guidance%20%28December%202024%29.pdf) (as opposed to a general school incident response plan) is more effective at guiding the appropriate response to a cyber incident. 

### 7. Partner with experts

Many schools lack internal resources to manage cybersecurity effectively. The right partner provides specialised knowledge, proactive monitoring, and rapid response when it matters most. 

Make sure your partner doesn’t just have cyber expertise but also the requisite education-specific knowledge to help detect blind spots and operational challenges that are unique to the education sector.

## **Preventing data breaches: what’s the first step for schools?**

In the wake of this breach, all Australian schools should take immediate steps to review and strengthen their cybersecurity posture:

## **Don’t wait for a data breach before protecting your school**

[Cybersecurity threats aren’t slowing down](https://www.cyber.gov.au/about-us/view-all-content/reports-and-statistics/annual-cyber-threat-report-2024-2025), and schools are increasingly in the crosshairs. The Victorian breach proves that no institution is immune. 

Everyone will be subject to a cyber incident at some point; it’s not a matter of *if* but *when*. How confident are you that you can quickly detect an incident and respond effectively? Currently, less than 1% of schools can meaningfully answer yes to both. 

Don’t wait for a breach to take action. Reach out for a confidential, no-obligation consultation with one of our security experts. [Contact NetStrategy](https://www.netstrategy.net/contact/) today to safeguard your school’s data and reputation

While the department reported there’s no evidence the data has been publicly released and more sensitive details (e.g. birth dates, home addresses, phone numbers) were not accessed, this event still highlights systemic challenges many organisations face in securing data, even where the immediate impact might seem limited. So is it time to revisit some of the simple things you can focus on to reduce your risk? Here are 3 simple things that can make a huge impact on your security: 1. Identity & Access Management Must Be Foundational Credential compromise and privilege creep are recurring root causes in many breaches. Strong identity hygiene — including multi-factor authentication, least-privilege access and regular access reviews — is crucial. Action: Conduct periodic audits of user privileges across all systems, especially for accounts with elevated access.   2. Segment and Limit Attack Surfaces Educational environments — like many enterprises — often accumulate access rights that aren’t consistently reviewed. This makes lateral movement easier for attackers and increases blast radius. Action: Implement network and segmentation controls that confine access to necessary resources only, and minimise exposure of sensitive systems from broader network compromise.   3. Educate Users — The Human Layer Still Matters Technical controls are critical, but user awareness is just as important. Individuals should be empowered to recognise phishing, report anomalies and maintain good cyber hygiene, especially around shared or school/organisation-issued accounts. Action: Invest in ongoing, role-based cybersecurity training — not just once-off modules.

  Dear Cyber Security Wannabe, Here are 10 Things You Can Teach People NOT to do. If you do, you will already have a head start in protecting the world's digital landscape. 1️⃣ Don't use weak passwords: Weak passwords are a major vulnerability that can be exploited by cyber criminals. Use strong, complex passwords and change them regularly. 2️⃣ Don't click on suspicious links: Clicking on links in emails or messages from unknown sources can lead to malware infections or phishing attacks. Be cautious and verify the source before clicking. 3️⃣ Don't ignore software updates: Software updates often include security patches that address known vulnerabilities. Keep your software up to date to stay protected. 4️⃣ Don't use public Wi-Fi without a VPN: Public Wi-Fi networks are often unsecured and can be used to steal sensitive information. Use a virtual private network (VPN) to encrypt your internet traffic and protect your data. 5️⃣ Don't share sensitive information: Be cautious about sharing sensitive information, such as personal or financial data, online. Only share this information with trusted sources. 6️⃣ Don't neglect backups: Regular backups can help you recover from a cyber attack or data loss. Make sure to back up your data regularly and store backups in a secure location. 7️⃣ Don't forget to use two-factor authentication: Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of security to your accounts. Use it wherever possible to protect your data. 8️⃣ Don't leave your devices unattended: Leaving your devices unattended in public places can make them vulnerable to theft or tampering. Keep them with you or secure them when not in use. 9️⃣ Don't download unauthorized software: Downloading unauthorized software, such as pirated software or software from untrusted sources, can introduce malware onto your device. 🔟 Don't ignore suspicious activity: If you notice any suspicious activity, such as unauthorized access to your accounts or unusual network traffic, report it to your IT department or security team immediately.   Day 5 of 100 Days of Cybersecurity. Today, I learned about Data Security Breaches. Data Security Breach is an incident that results in unauthorized access to data, thereby exposing private or personal information that hackers can use for financial gain or other advantages. It involves an incident when sensitive personal information has been stolen. The implication of Data Security Breaches is severe. There are consequences of Data breach A) Reputational damage- This is where security breaches can have a negative long term impact on an organization's reputation that has taken years to build. B) Vandalism - Hackers can vandalize an organization's website by posting untrue information. They can go as far as making a few minor edits or an organization's website. C) Theft - Cybercriminals can exploit or steal an individual's money or identity. D) Loss of Revenue - The financial impact of a security breach can be very devastating. Hackers can take down an organization's website, thereby preventing it from doing business online. E) Damaged Intellectual property - If hackers can lay their hands on confidential documents like intellectual properties, it will have an impact on the competitiveness of the organization. We must know that despite all the best intentions and efforts that we put in place to protect our organizations from cyber attacks, Cybercriminals will constantly find new ways to attack. Most times, they succeed. When they do this, it's up to you to respond quickly and minimize the impact. Learning Consistently.
