## B. Detailed APAC Third-Party Vendor Breaches (2025 – August 2026)

### B1. Japan

**Askul Corporation (October–December 2025)** — Major Japanese e-commerce and logistics provider supplying office products, stationery, IT equipment, and business consumables (part of the LOHACO/Yahoo Japan ecosystem). Ransomware attack attributed to **RansomHouse**, first detected October 19, 2025, causing significant operational disruption — suspending order processing and shipping for business and individual customers, as well as major partners like Muji (Ryohin Keikaku) and The Loft, which rely on Askul's logistics network; services began resuming in early December. [54][57][59]
- **Root cause:** compromise of an **outsourced partner's administrator account that lacked multi-factor authentication (MFA)**. The attacker used valid credentials to gain privileged access, disabled EDR and security software (MITRE T1562.001), moved laterally via remote services and valid accounts (T1021, T1078), deployed multiple ransomware variants simultaneously across servers, wiped backup files (T1490, T1485), and exfiltrated approximately 1.1 terabytes of data. [54]
- **Scale/impact:** approximately **740,000 customer records stolen** — ~590,000 business customer service records, 132,000 individual customer service records, 15,000 business partner records, and 2,700 employee records; exposed fields such as company names, user names, phone numbers, and email addresses. No credit card data compromise was confirmed (the LOHACO payment system does not store customer credit card information), and no ransom was paid. [54][56]
- **Timeline:** October 19, 2025 – attack detected and announced, operations suspended; October 29–31 – RansomHouse claimed responsibility; October 30 – public disclosure; November 10 and December 2 – data leaked in two stages; December 14–15 – Askul confirmed breach scope, notified Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC), and began contacting affected parties. Full system restoration still ongoing as of mid-December 2025. [54]
- **Response:** physically disconnecting infected networks, isolating devices, updating EDR signatures, applying MFA to all key systems, resetting administrator passwords, reinstalling or disposing of affected devices. CEO Akira Yoshioka stated the company would review and strengthen its BCP (Business Continuity Plan). RansomHouse, which emerged in March 2022, is known for extortion tactics rather than encryption and is linked to Russia-aligned threat actors including Alphv/BlackCat, LockBit 3.0, and RagnarLocker. [54][56][57]

**KDDI Email System Breach (June–July 2026)** — One of Japan's largest telecommunications providers (employing over 60,000 people; annual revenue roughly ¥5.9 trillion / ~US$40 billion) detected unauthorized access to its email system on June 17, 2026, affecting a system shared with five other Japanese ISPs: **STNet, Inc., JCOM Co., Ltd., Chubu Telecommunications C., Inc., NIFTY Corporation, and BIGLOBE Inc.** [74][75][77]
- **Root cause:** exploitation of a **vulnerability (reportedly a zero-day) in unnamed third-party software** used in the email system, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) — not caused by phishing, credential stuffing, or malware deployment. The vendor itself was reportedly unaware of the flaw until the same day KDDI cut off the attacker's access; as of July 9-10, 2026, no CVE had been issued and the vendor was still "developing a patch." [74][75]
- **Scale/impact:** up to **14.2 million email addresses and passwords** exposed across six ISPs (one later analysis put the figure at 12,231,954 email addresses and 7,616,173 passwords, with the platform serving up to 14.22 million accounts when inactive users are counted), including current, former, and inactive customers. Some passwords were hashed or encrypted, but KDDI did not disclose the encryption methods or the proportion stored in plaintext, creating uncertainty about credential abuse risk. No payment card data or My Number national ID equivalents were stored on the platform. [74][75][77]
- **Timeline:** May 16, 2026 – attacker exploits zero-day; June 17 – KDDI discovers intrusion and blocks attacker's access (52 days after initial exploit); June 23 – forensic audit confirms vulnerability patched; June 23–28 – public disclosure; July 6 – KDDI files incident report with Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications; July 7 – KDDI discloses breach publicly. Japan lacks a US-style 72-hour mandatory disclosure clock, which explains the slow disclosure pace. [74][75]
- **Business impact:** KDDI deployed EDR across affected systems, enforced mandatory password resets for active users, and used AI-assisted tools to review software design specifications across its infrastructure. This was KDDI's second major incident in four years, following the 2022 network outage affecting 39.15 million mobile connections. Analysts predicted phishing campaigns targeting the 12.2 million exposed addresses, tighter Japanese regulatory oversight of shared-infrastructure, and renegotiation of ISP reliance on KDDI's shared infrastructure. [74][75]

**Additional Japanese context:** Askul followed another major ransomware incident in Japan where threat actors hit **Asahi** in September 2025, stealing personal data on about 2 million customers and employees (disclosed October 2025, attributed to the Russian-speaking Qilin gang, disrupting production; Australian employee data was caught in the same attack, ~27 GB total per Webber Insurance). Auto parts manufacturer TEIN also reported ransomware crippling its headquarters network in October 2025. [44][56][59]

### B2. India

**Tata Electronics (June 2026)** — Indian electronics and semiconductor manufacturer (part of the Tata Group) and a key supplier to **Apple, Tesla, ASML, Intel, and Qualcomm**; entered iPhone manufacturing in 2023 by acquiring Wistron's India operations, acquired a 60% stake in Pegatron's Indian unit in 2025, signed a semiconductor supply deal with Tesla in 2024, employs more than 75,000 people. [65][67]
- **Timeline:** On June 12, 2026, the ransomware group **World Leaks** posted 204,341 files totaling **630.4 GB** on its dark web leak site. Tata Electronics confirmed the incident to Reuters and BleepingComputer on June 22, 2026, stating it identified the incident "a few weeks ago" (discovery placed in early-to-mid June 2026) and that response protocols were deployed immediately with no impact on operations. Tata reportedly received a ransom demand; amount and negotiation status undisclosed. [65][67][69]
- **Data exposed:** component design papers marked as Apple property (including detailed information on the **iPhone 18 Pro's** main circuit board chips, battery parts, camera modules, which suppliers provide each part, and which suppliers are competing for contracts), engineering drawings tied to a Tesla vehicle program (including Project Highland / revamped Model 3 and a Model Y charge-port controller marked "TRADE SECRET"), passport scans of Tata Electronics staff (including foreign nationals), manufacturing records, internal emails (including Outlook conversations), event logs spanning several years, SAP-related information, Standard Operating Procedure spreadsheets, and documents marked "proprietary and confidential" — including **cryptographic certificates and key files** that, if valid, could allow attackers to maintain access or impersonate systems. A search for "Apple" returned 181 files including a 52-page document on iPhone circuit board inspection standards bearing Apple's proprietary markings. [65][66][69]
- **Threat actor:** World Leaks emerged in early 2025 and is widely regarded as a rebrand of the Hunters International ransomware operation. Unlike traditional ransomware, World Leaks dropped encryption entirely and runs a pure data-extortion model: infiltrate quietly, exfiltrate data, then threaten public release. World Leaks has listed 169 victims, including Nike (claimed 188,347 files / 1.4 TB in January 2026) and Dell (1.3 TB claimed in July 2025). [65][69]
- **Root cause:** a **supply-chain attack** — not against Apple or Tesla directly, but against the company building their products. The attackers likely had access for weeks or months before detection (documents dated as late as May 2026), mapping the file system and identifying the most valuable data categories; "the breach response was activated after the damage was done, not before." Tata manufactures roughly one-third of Apple's iPhone production in India (Foxconn holds the remainder). India assembled about one in four iPhones worldwide in 2025 (roughly 55 million iPhones), up from just 6% four years ago. [65][66][69]
- **Downstream impacts:** reputational damage for both Tata Electronics and Apple (Apple was reportedly investigating internally and collaborating with Tata, enhancing security measures and initiating forensic audits); IP exposure giving rivals, suppliers, counterfeiters and bad actors a glimpse into Apple's supply chain structure; potential contract risk — "One ransomware group posting 630 GB of client trade secrets can end the relationship entirely." Neither Apple nor Tesla confirmed the authenticity of the files; no consumer payment or personal user data was compromised. This was Tata Group's second major breach within roughly ten months, following the JLR attack (below). [65][66][68][69]

**Jaguar Land Rover / Tata Motors ecosystem (August–October 2025)** — JLR, the UK-based automaker owned by Tata Motors, suffered a cyberattack beginning August 31, 2025, believed to be **the most damaging cyberattack in British history**, with estimated eventual total damage to the British economy of £1.9 billion (approximately $2.5 billion). JLR paused production on September 1, 2025; production lines ceased for three weeks, extended to October 1, 2025. The cost to the company was estimated at £50 million per week (some sources put daily losses at ~£5m/£6.8m in lost revenue, with typical daily turnover of ~£75m). JLR's three UK plants produce around 1,000 vehicles daily. The Bank of England (November 7, 2025) cited the cyberattack as a reason for slower GDP growth. [35][36][38][39]
- **Third-party dimension:** JLR depends on organizations within the Tata Group ecosystem for IT operations, including a March 2023 deal with **Tata Consultancy Services (TCS)** for IT services (application development, enterprise infrastructure management, cloud transition, cybersecurity — an £800 million cybersecurity and IT support contract) and a collaboration with **Tata Technologies** under the "Digital 2024" initiative. In March 2025, JLR was allegedly targeted by the HELLCAT ransomware group, which leaked ~350 GB of sensitive data including 700 internal documents from a compromise via Jira credentials (development logs, source code, a large employee dataset). Threat intelligence firm Cyfirma analyzed that the attackers likely retained network access from the March compromise, enabling them to time the 2025 outage for "New Plate Day," one of the busiest sales days of the year. [34][35][38][39]
- **Attribution:** a group calling itself "Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters" on Telegram claimed responsibility, suggesting collaboration between Scattered Spider, Lapsus$, and ShinyHunters; investigators later linked the attack to Russian hackers and investigated whether it was directed or tacitly supported by the Kremlin. Analyst Prayukth KV traced the attack to a social engineering/vishing campaign run by ShinyHunters weeks earlier, using data from prior attacks on CRM and database managers; the actor then moved across JLR's network, escalated privileges, deleted data-theft queries using TOR IP addresses, and possibly exfiltrated data via TOR exit nodes. [36][37][39]
- **Impact:** employee/supplier harm (supply chain staff "laid off in their hundreds," advised to apply for Universal Credit; MP Liam Byrne called it a "digital siege"), operational shutdown, data theft confirmed ("some data has been affected" per September 10 statement; JLR informed regulators including the UK ICO), suppliers across Europe forced to scale back or pause production, House of Commons debate, and a criminal investigation. Chris Gibson (FIRST) noted systems were not appropriately segmented and the attack hit both IT and OT; Dark Reading estimated $50–70 million revenue loss per week and total costs of $1.7–2.4 billion. Ncontracts reported the JLR attack impacted over 5,000 companies with an estimated £1.9 billion in losses, highlighting the need for vendor oversight and resiliency planning. [36][37][38][39][78]

**Star Health and Allied Insurance (September 2024 — note: pre-2025 but foundational Indian insurance-sector context)** — India's largest standalone health insurer (market cap exceeding $4 billion) had data of potentially over 31 million customers leaked via Telegram chatbots created by a hacker using the alias "xenZen," who offered 7.24 terabytes of data for sale. UK-based security researcher Jason Parker discovered the chatbots, operational since at least August 6, 2024. Stolen data included names, addresses, phone numbers, policy details, government ID numbers, and highly sensitive medical information (test results, diagnoses). Reuters downloaded over 1,500 files including policy and claims documents; two policyholders confirmed their leaked documents were genuine (Sandeep TS — whose one-year-old daughter's hospital records included diagnosis, blood test results, medical history, and a bill of nearly 15,000 rupees; and Pankaj Subhash Malhotra — ultrasound results, illness details, federal tax and national ID card copies). Star Health reported the matter to Tamil Nadu cybercrime authorities and CERT-In, and its initial investigation claimed "no widespread compromise" and that "sensitive customer data remains secure" — claims contradicted by media investigations. The company did not notify affected customers. NordVPN research showed India represented 12% of five million people whose data was sold via chatbots in late 2022. [58][60]

### B3. Australia

**Qantas (June–July 2025)** — Australia's flag carrier confirmed on June 30–July 2, 2025 that customer data of **approximately 5.67–6 million customers** (5.12 million Australians) was stolen from a **third-party customer servicing platform used by a Qantas airline contact centre**. [69][70][71][72]
- **Root cause (per OAIC's official report):** A vishing/social-engineering attack. On Saturday June 28, 2025, a Qantas contact-centre agent (employed at an overseas contact centre operated by a third-party provider) received a phone call from a threat actor impersonating "Qantas IT help." The threat actor directed the agent to connect their CRM Platform instance to a data extraction tool, which was used to extract data from customer contact profiles the agent had access to. The vulnerability arose from a default configuration (allowing end users to authorize third-party application connections) that has since been changed by the CRM provider. [70]
- **Timeline:** June 28 – vishing attack; June 30 – Qantas detected unusual login attempts and contained the threat the same day; July 2 – public disclosure; July 9 – all impacted customers notified of specific compromised data types; October 11, 2025 – hackers released personal data on the dark web despite an ongoing NSW Supreme Court injunction. [70][71][72]
- **Data compromised:** names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Qantas Frequent Flyer details (numbers, tiers, points balances, status credits) and for ~1.7 million records also addresses, gender, and meal preferences. Qantas confirmed NO credit card details, financial information, passport details, or identity documents were accessed, and no Frequent Flyer accounts/passwords/PINs. All Frequent Flyer accounts have MFA/2FA enabled by default. The attack came days after an FBI alert that the airline sector was a target of Scattered Spider; Hawaiian Airlines and WestJet were hit by similar attacks in the same period. Qantas notified the AFP, ACSC, OAIC, and the NZ Office of the Privacy Commissioner. [70][71][72][73]
- **Regulatory outcome:** The OAIC conducted preliminary inquiries (July 11, 2025 – June 1, 2026) and concluded there was nothing to suggest Qantas failed to take reasonable steps under APP 1.2, APP 8 (cross-border disclosure — the SLA required ISO 27001:2013, audit rights, Privacy Act and GDPR compliance), or APP 11 (security — role-based access controls, documented training verified via audits, incident management framework). Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind closed the inquiries without commencing a Commissioner-initiated investigation, stating "the evidence supports the likelihood that a breach of privacy law occurred" was not met, but individual and representative complaints remain under consideration. Maurice Blackburn Lawyers has filed a representative complaint with the OAIC alleging Qantas breached the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth); ClassActions.com.au is running a compensation registration for the 5.7 million affected. [69][70][71]

**Genea Fertility (February–March 2025)** — One of Australia's largest IVF and fertility providers (19 fertility clinics across Australia plus one in Thailand), attacked by the **Termite ransomware group**, which stole approximately **700 GB (reportedly 940.7 GB) of highly sensitive patient data** and published it on the dark web. [19][23][24]
- **Timeline:** attackers gained access around January 31, 2025; Genea detected suspicious activity on February 14, 2025 (same day phone lines went down and data was exfiltrated); publicly confirmed the incident February 19, 2025; threat actor began publishing stolen data around February 26; Australian Passport Office responded February 28; Genea confirmed further data leakage March 4, 2025. Termite was reportedly present in Genea's systems between January 31 and February 14 (over two weeks of undetected access). [19][22]
- **Data exposed:** full names, dates of birth, emails, addresses, phone numbers, Medicare card numbers, private health insurance details, medical histories, diagnoses, treatments, medications, pathology results, doctors' notes, appointment details, emergency contacts, and potentially Australian passport information — spanning around six years of records. Genea confirmed genetic testing data, embryo identification details, and account passwords were held on separate isolated systems and NOT exposed. [19][23]
- **Impacts:** significant operational disruption (downed phone lines, inaccessible MyGenea app, delayed urgent treatment matters); patient anxiety over exposure of deeply private medical information; court-ordered injunction (obtained via the Supreme Court) criminalising access to breached data — but the data was still published; National Cyber Security Coordinator Michelle McGuinness coordinated a whole-of-government response. No ransom was reportedly paid. Genae's response: systems taken offline, engagement of cybersecurity partners and PR firm Porter Novelli, notifications to OAIC, ACSC, AFP, and identity-protection support through IDCARE. [19][24]
- **Legal/regulatory follow-up:** Phi Finney McDonald lodged a **representative complaint with the OAIC** on October 20, 2025 under s 38(2) of the Privacy Act against Genea on behalf of affected individuals. [21]
- **Third-party dimension:** ClinicComply notes Genea's breach was "traced to third-party supplier failures, demonstrating that vendor breaches can trigger your legal obligations" under the NDB scheme. In 2022, one in 17 babies born in Australia involved assisted reproductive technologies, with 108,913 ART treatment cycles total. [10][24]

**MediSecure (April–June 2024 — preceding 2025, but central APAC third-party reference case)** — Australian digital prescription services provider confirmed personal and health information of **12.9 million individuals** was stolen in an April 2024 ransomware attack. Attackers stole **6.5 terabytes of data** before deploying file-encrypting ransomware; MediSecure restored it using a clean backup. MediSecure stated it could not identify specific impacted individuals "without incurring substantial cost that MediSecure was not in a financial position to meet." Potentially stolen information: names, dates of birth, gender, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, individual healthcare identifiers, Medicare card numbers, prescription medication details, and Pensioner Concession, Commonwealth Seniors, Healthcare Concession, and DVA card numbers and expiry dates. [39]
- **Root cause:** MediSecure stated the incident believed to have originated from **a third-party vendor**; Huntress analysis concluded attackers exploited vulnerabilities in MediSecure's infrastructure, moved laterally, exfiltrated data, then encrypted systems, with investigation revealing gaps in patch management and network segmentation. [41][42]
- **Timeline:** May 2024 – systems compromised, breach detected and government notified; the company's website was taken down; public disclosure May 16, 2024; May 23 – threat actor "Ansgar" offered the data on an underground forum for $50,000; Mid-2024 – third-party cybersecurity experts engaged; June 2024 – MediSecure entered **voluntary administration**. [39][41][42]
- **Downstream impacts:** Australians warned of higher likelihood of phishing, identity-related crime, and cyber scams. The national prescription delivery service eRx (Fred IT Group) was NOT affected; the Australian Government had already consolidated the national prescription service to eRx under a nearly $100 million, four-year agreement, leaving MediSecure only for private prescriptions. No current e-prescriptions were impacted. The Australian Federal Police launched an investigation; the national cyber security coordinator convened a whole-of-government response. [39][41][42][43]

**Victorian Department of Education (January 2026)** — An external third party gained access to a Department of Education database via **a school's network intrusion**, exposing personal information of current and former Victorian government school students across all approximately 1,700 government schools. Compromised data: student names, school-issued email addresses, encrypted passwords, school names, and year levels. No dates of birth, phone numbers, or home addresses were accessed, and there was no evidence the data was publicly released. The department identified the point of breach and temporarily disabled systems. [85][86][88][94]
- **Regulatory:** The **Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner (OVIC)** launched a formal investigation into whether privacy obligations under the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 were met. [86]
- **Context:** This is part of a broader pattern — Queensland's Department of Education was hit in May 2026 when the ShinyHunters breach of third-party cloud provider **Instructure** exposed student/staff names, emails, and school locations; the LexisNexis March 2026 cloud breach exposed legal and government client data as a "significant supply chain event." [44][85]

**Dymocks (September 2023 — vintage precedent)** — Book retailer's data breach was traced to the systems of an **external data partner**, with approximately 1.24 million customer records stolen and published on the dark web (names, gender, addresses, email addresses, dates of birth, mobile numbers, Dymocks membership details). Dymocks became aware of the breach on September 6, 2023 (discovering it more than 2 months after — UpGuard notes the breach was discovered late on the dark web). Gordon Legal filed a representative complaint with the OAIC on September 25, 2023, accepted as valid on May 28, 2024. [45][46][48]

**Australian Clinical Labs (Oct 2025 — landmark enforcement)** — **Australian Clinical Labs received the first-ever civil penalty under the Privacy Act** — **$5.8 million** — in October 2025, broken down as $4.2M for failing to take reasonable steps under APP 11, $800K for failing to assess the suspected breach promptly, and $800K for failing to notify the OAIC timely. Case: Australian Information Commissioner v Australian Clinical Labs (No 2) [2025] FCA 1224. The underlying breach (2022, Medlab Pathology) affected 223,000+ individuals including 28,000 credit card numbers. [10][45]

**2025–2026 Australian breach list (Webber Insurance + UpGuard compilations):**
- **2026:** Updoc (August 2026, customer contact info); Court Services Victoria (July 2026, ~30,000 lines of court data); **Origin Energy (July 2026, ~900,000 current and former customers)**; CubePilot (July 2026); GO2 Health (July 2026, DVA ID numbers); Partnered Health (July 2026, Medicare and DVA numbers across dozens of GP clinics); Generation Life (June 2026); NSW Rural Fire Service (June 2026); Mackay Sugar (June 2026, two sugar mills shut down); Melbourne International Film Festival (June 2026, claimed 340,000+ customers); **Queensland Department of Education (May 2026, via third-party cloud provider Instructure, ShinyHunters)**; **LexisNexis (March 2026, major cloud breach of legal/government client data — significant supply chain event)**; **Victorian Department of Education (January 2026, all 1,700 government schools)**; Prosura (January 2026, ~300,000 car rental insurance customers); Regis Resources (January 2026). [44][45]
- **2025:** University of Sydney (December 2025, 13,000 individuals); Western Sydney University (October 2025, passport details, TFNs, payroll, health info); Asahi (October 2025, Australian employee data in Qilin ransomware attack, ~27 GB); iiNet (August 2025, 200,000+ customers); Metricon Homes (July 2025, Qilin ransomware); Louis Vuitton (July 2025, Australian customers affected); Ingram Micro (July 2025); United Australia Party (July 2025, "impracticable to notify individuals"); IKAD Engineering (defence supply chain); BMW (third-party); VETtrak; several schools. [44]
- **Qantas (2025):** 5.7M customers via third-party Manila contact centre compromise (Salesforce-targeted); OAIC decided not to investigate (July 2026) — see above. [45]
- **Australian superannuation credential-stuffing wave (2025):** 20,000+ accounts across funds (Rest: ~8,000); first coordinated attack on the A$4T super system; 4 AustralianSuper members lost A$500K. [45]

### B4. Singapore

**PDPC enforcement against SaaS providers (2025–2026):**
- **People Central Pte Ltd** (decision January 8, 2026): SaaS provider of online HR solutions fined **SGD 17,500** for breaching its protection obligation under the PDPA. Breach resulted in deletion of databases and exfiltration of personal data of **95,000 individuals**, likely found for sale on the dark web; data of an additional 24,765 individuals (emergency contacts and/or children of employees) also put at risk. On April 29, 2024, the company received an extortion email from a threat actor. Lapses: **lack of two-factor authentication and insufficient security testing**; failure to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews/multiple layers of security, and failure to conduct periodic vulnerability assessments and penetration testing. [49]
- **Singapore Data Hub Pte Ltd** (decision April 7, 2025): SaaS provider handling high volumes of personal data fined **SGD 17,500**. Breach resulted in exfiltration of personal data of **689,000 individuals**, likely posted on a web hacking forum on May 6, 2024. Unauthorized access occurred twice (April 28, 2024 and June 14, 2024) by at least two threat actors. Contributing factors: publicly accessible web servers running **outdated operating systems, lack of security testing, absence of access controls (firewalls, monitoring tools, MFA, encryption, network segmentation)**, weak password policy, no regular patching/upgrades. [49]
- **Air Sino-Euro Associates Travel Pte Ltd** (decision October 31, 2025): travel agency fined **SGD 47,000** for breaching accountability and protection obligations under the PDPA; breach resulted in exfiltration of personal data of **336,759 individuals**, first reported in an online news article on December 21, 2023. PDPC found the company failed to implement internal processes/policies and communicate them to employees, failed to appoint a data protection officer until after the cyberattack, failed to conduct regular security reviews (no contractual clauses with IT vendors on scope of responsibilities), failed to update an outdated operating system that the threat actor exploited, and failed to employ MFA or require sufficient password complexity for privileged accounts. [24]

**2023 precedent — healthcare provider + vendor both fined:** A Singapore-based healthcare services provider and its vendor were fined a total of **SGD 68,000** (provider SGD 58,000, vendor SGD 10,000) following a 2021 breach in which customer data of more than 150,000 patients and employees was offered for sale on a dark web forum (identity numbers, bank account numbers and codes, health information, surgical procedure codes). The provider had exacerbated the situation by inadvertently disclosing unnecessary sensitive data onto an online drive shared with the vendor. Key PDPC principle: "Even if a data intermediary or vendor is engaged to implement necessary data protection measures, the data controller bears the responsibility of exercising reasonable oversight of the vendor. A data controller may be found in breach of the PDPA even if its data intermediary or vendor is not." Under the PDPA, the maximum fine is 10% of annual Singapore turnover (for companies with turnover exceeding SGD 10 million) or SGD 1 million. [50]

**Thailand:** The Office of the Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) of Thailand levied fines totaling **B15 million (15 million Thai Baht) across 5 data breach cases**, announced August 4, 2025. [25]

## C. APAC Regulatory Frameworks and Enforcement Actions

### C1. Australia (OAIC / NDB scheme)

- **OAIC NDB statistics (January–June 2025):** 532 data breach notifications received (10% decrease vs. previous 6 months). Malicious or criminal attacks were the largest source (59%, 308 notifications), with cyber security incidents the predominant cause; average number of individuals affected by cyber incidents just over 10,000. The health sector had the most reported breaches (18%), followed by finance (14%) and Australian Government agencies (13%). **Human error accounted for 37% of all breaches (193 notifications), up from 29%** in the previous period. The OAIC published a case study about a government agency whose third-party software developer ran an unauthorized script that made private documents publicly available online on two separate occasions, highlighting that organizations are responsible for the actions of third-party providers when outsourcing personal information handling. [11]
- **2025 full-year figures:** OAIC received 1,205 data breach notifications in the 2025 calendar year — an 8% increase over 2024 (1,112) and the highest annual total since the NDB scheme commenced in February 2018. Of these, 59% (716) were attributed to malicious/criminal attacks; health service providers were the most affected sector (225 notifications, ~19%). In May 2025, OAIC reported 1,113 breaches during 2024 (25% increase over 2023's 893). [12][45]
- **Legislative/regulatory developments:** The Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 added new APP 11.3 requiring specific technical and organisational security measures. A single healthcare breach can trigger three separate reporting obligations: the NDB scheme (Privacy Act, 30-day assessment window), the My Health Record Act 2012 (immediate notification), and the **Cyber Security Act 2024** ransomware payment reporting rule (72 hours to report payments to ASD for entities with turnover above $3 million). Healthcare has been Australia's most-breached sector in every OAIC report since 2018, accounting for 18-20% of all notifications. The NDB scheme applies to ALL healthcare providers regardless of size or turnover — health information is excluded from the small business exemption. [10]
- **OAIC recommendations:** supplier risk management frameworks, contractual clauses on data retention/destruction, clear accountability arrangements for multi-party breaches (entity with most direct relationship typically notifies individuals), and regular cyber security assessments and audits of vendors. The OAIC noted IBM calculated the average cost of a data breach at $4.26 million in 2024. A 2023 OAIC report highlighted a significant rise in "secondary notifications" (multi-party breaches): 121 notifications vs. 29 in the prior period, most involving cloud or software providers impacting clients who outsourced personal information handling. [11][13]
- **Sector rankings 2024:** healthcare, government, financial services, legal/accounting/management services, and retail had the most breaches (along with liability of human error such as unlocked devices). [12]

### C2. Singapore (PDPA / PDPC)

- **Mandatory breach notification:** Organizations must conduct assessments when a breach may have occurred and notify the PDPC no later than **72 hours after determining a notifiable breach occurred**, plus notify affected individuals as soon as practicable. Guidelines suggest investigations should take no more than 30 calendar days. Breaches involving designated high-risk data (e.g., financial info combined with ID, medical info, account credentials, biometrics) or affecting 500+ Singapore residents require notification. [51][52]
- **Penalties:** Maximum financial penalty increased under the 2020 amendments to the greater of 10% of an organization's annual turnover in Singapore or SGD 1 million (effective October 1, 2022). Criminal prosecution (effective February 1, 2021) allows fines up to SGD 5,000 or up to two years imprisonment for knowingly/recklessly disclosing data, wrongful gain/loss use, or re-identification of anonymized data. Individuals also have a private right to civil action. [51][52]
- **Enforcement trends (Resguard, Feb 2026):** increasing penalty amounts (driven by the enhanced penalty framework from 2021); protection obligation is the most-cited basis; sector diversity (healthcare, financial services, retail, education, telecom, government-linked entities); growing scrutiny of organizational accountability (DPO oversight, board-level engagement). Most common violations: inadequate security measures (weak passwords, unpatched systems, poor access controls, lack of encryption), excessive data collection, failure to obtain proper consent, poor vendor management (organizations remain responsible for data processed by vendors), and delayed breach notification. Notable patterns: healthcare access control failures; financial services scrutiny from both PDPC and MAS; SME basic failures (leaving data publicly accessible, sending data to wrong emails, failing to appoint a DPO). Aggravating factors: no competent DPO, absence of policies, lack of training, repeated failures, delayed remediation, large data volumes. [26]
- **PDPC enforcement decisions portal** catalogs formal decisions when organizations breach the PDPA. [28]

### C3. Japan (APPI / PPC)

- **Framework:** The Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI), originally enacted 2003, last significantly amended effective April 1, 2022 (public sector integrated; local government laws after April 1, 2023). The Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) is the sole national regulator; it cannot conduct criminal investigations and the APPI imposes no administrative fines (introduction under discussion). Penalties: failure to submit reports — fine up to JPY 500,000; failure to follow PPC orders — up to 1 year imprisonment or fine up to JPY 1,000,000 (entity fine up to JPY 100,000,000); unauthorized disclosure — up to 1 year imprisonment or fine up to JPY 500,000 (entity fine up to JPY 100,000,000). [31][32][33]
- **Breach notification (Article 26):** Mandatory reporting to the PPC and affected data subjects in four categories: (1) leakage of sensitive personal information, (2) leakage involving property damage risk (credit card/bank data), (3) leakage likely caused by wrongful intent, (4) leakage affecting 1,000 or more individuals. Preliminary report within 3–5 days, final report within 30 days (60 days for unlawful-purpose incidents); notification may be unnecessary if data was encrypted. Unlike GDPR's fixed 72-hour window, APPI uses a "promptly" standard. [31][32][33]
- **Third-party/vendor obligations:** Article 25 requires supervision of entrusted persons (vendors); Article 28 requires prior consent for overseas transfers (with country name, protection system info, recipient measures); "appropriate and reasonable methodologies" include agreements and APEC CBPR. [31][33]
- **2026 reform:** A System Reform Policy under the Triennial Review of the APPI was decided on January 9, 2026, with four themes: promotion of appropriate data utilisation, regulation tailored to risk, prevention of improper use, and measures ensuring regulatory compliance effectiveness. Proposals include easing consent requirements for AI development (statistical creation), new regulations on children's personal data (under-12s consent from legal representatives), new regulations on biological data (e.g., facial features), and adjustment of the entrustment regulatory framework (e.g., cloud services). [30][31]
- **Notable enforcement:** In a June 2024 case, non-life insurance agents shared policyholder personal data without consent; the FSA issued a business improvement order (March 24, 2025) and the PPC issued administrative guidance (April 30, 2025). [31]
- **International cooperation:** The PPC has Memorandums of Cooperation with Singapore, the Philippines, Canada, the UK, and the EU; Japan-EU mutual adequacy in force since January 2019. [30]

### C4. India

- **CERT-In six-hour incident reporting requirement** (since April 2022) and India's **Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act** obligations for passport/employee data are the key regulatory levers referenced in coverage of Indian breaches (e.g., Tata Electronics). [65]
- DLA Piper's 2026 global handbook notes: "India has new data protection legislation taking effect." [27]

## D. Cross-Cutting Root Causes, Impact Patterns, and Emerging Best Practices

- **Dominant root causes documented across APAC 2025–2026 incidents:** compromised third-party/vendor credentials without MFA (Askul, Genea via Citrix server per UpGuard, Medibank via contractor credentials, JLR's prior HELLCAT compromise via Jira credentials), zero-day vulnerabilities in third-party software (KDDI), vishing/social engineering of vendor employees (Qantas, JLR/ShinyHunters, Salesforce UNC6395 campaign), outsourced partner/contact-centre access (Qantas Manila contact centre), pure data-extortion supply-chain infiltration (Tata Electronics), and human error at vendors (OAIC case study). [45][54][69][70][74]
- **Concentration risk:** UpGuard notes "the scale is structural, not accidental. Care delivery depends on a concentrated web of clearinghouses, insurers, and business associates, so one compromise can reach thousands of providers and payers at once." The same report ranks MediSecure (Australia, ~12.9M records) and Medibank (Australia) among the biggest healthcare breaches; Conduent's 62.2M-record breach is described as "concentration risk in the healthcare supply chain" with 3 months undetected network access. [5]
- **Statistics:** 2025 set a record for healthcare breach volume (772 large breaches, ~2.1 per day); between 2009–2025 over 1 billion Americans' records exposed across 7,418 large breaches; average healthcare breach cost USD 7.42 million with a 279-day lifecycle. Hacking/IT incidents account for 80%+ of large breaches. [5][7]
- **Financial-sector impact stats:** the IBM 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts average financial services breach at USD 5.56 million (~25% above the $4.44M global average); Verizon 2026 DBIR: vulnerability exploitation overtook stolen credentials as leading entry point (31%), ransomware in 48% of breaches, **supply chain involvement up 60% YoY, featured in 48% of breaches**. Vendors were the source of 41.8% of fintech breaches (SecurityScorecard); a 2025 Verizon DBIR figure cited by multiple sources: ~30% of all data breaches stem from third parties, nearly double the prior year. [18][81][82]
- **Financial fallout of third-party breaches:** third-party breaches cost an average of $4.9M vs. $4.4M for employee-caused breaches (+11%), take 98 days to detect vs. 81 days (+21% slower); supply chain attacks are 17 times more expensive to remediate than first-party breaches at an average $4.91 million per incident (IBM 2025); the average cost to remediate a third-party-originated breach is now nearly $4.8 million (FortifyData). [8][15][82]
- **Insider Risk Index findings (Jan 2025):** 60% of data breaches involve third-party access; 36% of organizations never assess vendor security before granting access; supply chain attacks up 300% since 2020; typical enterprise has 247 vendors with network access, 63% not assessed for security in 12+ months; 98% of organizations work with vendors that had breaches; 62% of breaches propagate from vendor to client. Taxonomy of vendor risk: malicious contractors, negligent vendors, compromised vendor infrastructure, over-privileged MSPs. [8]
- **Wikipedia supply-chain context (relevant APAC examples):** Notepad++ (2025) update infrastructure compromise attributed to Chinese state-sponsored Lotus Blossom/APT31, targeting telecom/financial sectors in East Asia; eScan (2026) regional update server breach deploying malware to South Asian customers (second eScan infrastructure breach); Toyota 2022 production suspension at 14 Japanese plants (a third of global output) after supplier Kojima Industries was attacked; 3CX (2023) attributed to North Korean Lazarus Group. [9][82]
- **Emerging TPRM best practices recommended by sources:**
  - **Continuous monitoring across every vendor tier**, not just tier-1; replace questionnaire-based evidence with intelligence-driven vendor engagement (Black Kite found questionnaires produced no useful signal in Cencora, Cleo, or HealthEC incidents); map concentration risk before attackers exploit it; build incident response for vendor-originated operational disruption, not just data breaches. [2]
  - **Bank of America seven-step TPRM framework:** create incident response plans; identify/track/govern most valuable data; measure third-party risks (full risk assessments); evaluate third-party security standards; bind security protocols to contracts/SLAs; maintain oversight with continuous monitoring, performance reviews, KPIs; refer to industry best practices and intelligence. [4]
  - **Healthcare-specific:** thorough due diligence before engaging vendors (security posture, HIPAA training, certifications, incident response protocols), ongoing monitoring, periodic security assessments, integrate vendors into incident response planning; proposed HIPAA Security Rule updates would require MFA, encryption, and proactive security testing across the vendor ecosystem; organizations cannot "outsource accountability." [6]
  - **Insider Risk Index TPRM 2025 framework (5 phases):** vendor discovery & inventory; risk assessment & tiering; contractual controls (6 essential clauses: security standards, right to audit, data protection, access management, breach notification/liability, termination/data return); continuous monitoring (monthly access reviews, BitSight/SecurityScorecard/SpyCloud); incident response playbook. Advanced controls: zero-trust for vendors, vendor security ratings, just-in-time access, data minimization. ROI of 145%-880% if prevents one breach. [8]
  - **Mitratech lifecycle best practices:** consider information security during sourcing/selection; clear contractual data expectations; continuous monitoring; independent verification (SOC 2, NIST CSF, CMMC); visibility into fourth- and Nth-party vendors; audit offboarding. [18][82]
  - **Bitsight:** tier vendors by criticality/risk; set risk tolerance thresholds; continuously and automatically monitor third-party security postures; extend insights to fourth parties; unify vendor data in one tool. [82]

# Third-Party Vendor Risk 2025–2026: Lessons from Major Breaches in Finance, Healthcare, and Technology

## Executive Summary

The 2025–2026 period marks a structural turning point in third-party risk. Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found third-party involvement in 30% of all breaches — double the prior year's 15%, the largest single-year shift in the report's history — and its 2026 edition shows supply chain involvement rising another 60% year-over-year to appear in 48% of breaches [2][16]. IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the average supply chain-originated breach at $4.91 million with a 267-day lifecycle, the longest of any vector tracked [2].

The breaches detailed in this report share a common geometry: attackers are no longer breaking into the headline organization. They are compromising a statement-printing vendor used by two banks (Citizens, Frost), a business-process outsourcer touching one in five Americans' health data (Conduent), a procurement firm serving Swiss banking giants (Chain IQ), an abandoned four-year-old integration credential (Klue), an outsourced contact-centre agent (Qantas), and an open-source security scanner trusted by the European Commission (Trivy). The data, the liability, and the reputational damage flow upstream to the client organization regardless of where the intrusion physically occurred.

Three cross-cutting lessons emerge for risk managers:

1. **Identity is the new perimeter.** Compromised third-party credentials — often lacking MFA, or consisting of OAuth tokens and "ghost" service accounts that were never revoked — were the entry point in a majority of the major breaches analyzed. Unit 42 found identity weaknesses played a material role in nearly 90% of its 750+ incident response investigations in 2025 [3].

2. **Concentration risk is now the defining systemic vulnerability.** One vendor serving hundreds of clients creates a single point of failure: Conduent (62.2 million people affected across dozens of health plans), Salesloft/Drift (700+ organizations), and CEVA Logistics (Valve, ING, Bol, De Bijenkorf simultaneously) demonstrate the cascading scale.

3. **Point-in-time due diligence is obsolete.** The vendor that passed its initial security review months earlier was breached in nearly every major case. Regulators in the EU (DORA), the US (SEC Regulation S-P, NYDFS), and Asia-Pacific (Singapore PDPC, Australia OAIC) are now demanding continuous monitoring, contractual risk allocation, and board-level accountability.

## 1. The 2025–2026 Third-Party Risk Landscape

### 1.1 Aggregated statistics

- **Verizon 2025 DBIR:** 30% of all breaches involved third-party suppliers (up from 15%); the average cost to remediate a third-party-originated breach is nearly $4.8 million [1][2].
- **Verizon 2026 DBIR:** vulnerability exploitation overtook stolen credentials as the leading breach entry point (31%); ransomware appears in 48% of breaches; supply chain involvement rose 60% year-over-year to feature in 48% of breaches [2][16].
- **IBM 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report:** supply chain breach average $4.91 million; 267-day mean lifecycle; 44% of zero-day attacks target managed file transfer systems [2].
- **Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (2026 IR Report):** analysis of 750+ engagements found identity weaknesses in ~90% of investigations; 65% of initial access is identity-driven; SaaS data was relevant to 23% of cases in 2025, up from 6% in 2022. In over 90% of breaches, preventable gaps (limited visibility, inconsistently applied controls, excessive identity trust) materially enabled the intrusion [3].
- **Kaspersky global study (March 2026):** 31% of enterprise businesses were impacted by a supply chain attack in the past year — more than any other threat type, yet only 9% ranked it their top concern [5].
- **ENISA Threat Landscape 2025:** 10.6% of EU cyber incidents map to supply chain risk; 66% of compromised suppliers either didn't know or failed to report they were breached [2][42].
- **Group-IB High-Tech Crime Trends 2026:** compromised OAuth tokens from Drift, Salesloft, and Salesforce cascaded into 700+ organizations; a ransomware attack on fintech firm Marquis exposed data from 70 financial institutions; the Shai-Hulud worm tore through ~800 npm packages [4].
- **Healthcare:** 772 large breaches were reported to the HHS OCR in 2025, exposing the PHI of 139.7 million individuals — the worst year ever by volume. Between 2009 and 2025, over one billion Americans' records were exposed across 7,418 large healthcare breaches [6][7]. The average healthcare breach cost $7.42 million, the highest of any industry, with a 279-day lifecycle [8][6].
- **Financial services:** the average financial-sector breach cost $5.56 million in 2025, ~25% above the global average; median ransomware demands against financial institutions reached a record $3 million in 2026 [16].
- **Asia-Pacific:** ThreatBook recorded 15,205 security incidents across APAC from June 2025 to June 2026, with data breaches at 39.9% of incidents; China, India, Australia, Japan and South Korea absorb 61.78% of all incidents [77]. HKCERT recorded a record 15,877 incidents in Hong Kong in 2025, up 27% [79].

### 1.2 Why third-party risk became systemic

Supply chain attacks have become "the go-to model for scalable cybercrime and state-aligned operations" [4]. The drivers: (1) an exploded attack surface — dozens of SaaS platforms, hundreds of open-source packages, multiple MSPs per enterprise; (2) industrialized access brokering — Group-IB identified 263 instances of corporate access from Asia-Pacific sold on dark web forums in 2025 alone [78]; (3) identity abuse replacing malware — OAuth tokens, API keys, and service accounts let attackers bypass MFA entirely; and (4) open-source ecosystems becoming prime targets — 454,600+ new malicious open-source packages were identified in 2025, a 75% year-over-year jump [2]. Unit 42 found the fastest 25% of intrusions reached data exfiltration in 72 minutes, down from 285 minutes the prior year, with AI compressing attack timelines from weeks to hours [3].

## 2. Americas: Documented Breaches

### 2.1 Conduent Business Services — 62.2 million individuals (Healthcare)

**Vendor:** Conduent, a New Jersey-based business process outsourcing company (~56,000 employees; $3.4 billion annual revenue) handling printing, mailing, document processing, payment integrity, and back-office services for health plans, government agencies, and large employers. It supports roughly 100 million residents across 46 states and processes about $85 billion in annual disbursements [9][10].

**Timeline:**
- **October 21, 2024:** SafePay ransomware group first accessed Conduent's network.
- **January 13, 2025:** intrusion detected — 84 days later — after several states reported service outages (notably Wisconsin child-support payments).
- **February 2025:** SafePay claimed responsibility, alleging theft of multiple terabytes.
- **October 2025:** notifications began, nearly one year after initial access; initial count 10.5 million.
- **February 2026:** victim count surpassed 25 million; Texas AG Ken Paxton opened an investigation.
- **June 4, 2026:** updated HHS filing confirmed at least 62,224,658 individuals affected — the third-largest healthcare breach of all time, behind only Change Healthcare (192.7 million) and Anthem (78.8 million) [9][10].

**Scale:** roughly one in five Americans. Affected clients include Humana, Premera Blue Cross, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Texas, Montana, Illinois, and New Mexico, Volvo Group North America, Gold Coast Health Plan, Wisconsin Department of Children and Families, and Oklahoma Human Services. Data exposed: names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, treatment information, medical records, and health insurance policy numbers [9][10].

**Root cause:** network intrusion by SafePay ransomware with approximately three months of undetected access — a business-process-outsourcing supply chain compromise. The ballooning victim count "proves the intricacy of determining breach scope when a single vendor serves hundreds of covered entity clients simultaneously" [9].

**Impacts:** direct breach costs of ~$9 million through September 2025, with another $16 million anticipated by Q1 2026 (partly covered by cyber insurance); more than 10 consolidated federal class actions in New Jersey; a Texas AG investigation; and sharp criticism from Missouri regulators over perceived non-cooperation. Conduent faced severe backlash for waiting nearly nine months before notifying affected individuals [9][10][8].

### 2.2 NYC Health + Hospitals — 1.8 million+ (Healthcare)

**Vendor/sector:** NYC Health + Hospitals, the largest US public health system, disclosed a major breach attributed to an "unnamed third-party vendor with access to NYC H+H systems" [11].

**Timeline:** suspicious activity detected February 2, 2026; unauthorized access ran from roughly late November 2025 through February 2026; reported to HHS March 24, 2026 [11].

**Scale/impact:** at least 1.8 million people affected. Exposed data included three layers: (1) classical PII (names, SSNs, driver's license and passport numbers, taxpayer IDs, bank and card data); (2) medical and insurance data (diagnoses, medications, test results, claims) capable of enabling blackmail and fraudulent claims; and (3) biometrics — fingerprint and palm-print data that "stay with a person for life and cannot be easily erased or replaced" [11]. In July 2026, LeakNet published a preview of a claimed 11-terabyte archive linked to 12M+ people (unverified). Response included 24 months of free Kroll credit/identity monitoring [11].

### 2.3 Citizens Financial Group / Frost Bank / TSYS — single shared vendor (Finance)

**Vendor:** a single third-party vendor providing statement printing for Citizens Financial Group and tax-document fulfillment for Frost Bank. Neither bank's own network was directly breached [12][13][14].

**Timeline:** April 20, 2026, the Everest ransomware gang listed both banks on its dark-web extortion portal with a six-day ultimatum. Class actions were filed within four days; on May 2, Everest listed TSYS (a Global Payments subsidiary) on its leak site [12][13].

**Scale:** 3.65 million bank records across both institutions — ~3.4 million Citizens records (names, addresses, account numbers; reportedly no SSNs) and ~250,000 Frost records including Social Security numbers, tax IDs, mortgage rates, income, and investment data capable of enabling full identity theft [12][13][14].

**Root cause:** a shared vendor with weaker security holding high-value customer data. Everest combined data exfiltration with ransom demands and a weeks-long dwell time. Analysts identified four problematic vendor-access patterns: standing VPN credentials, network-level reach, local copies as workflow, and no session evidence [14].

**Impacts:** six class-action lawsuits were filed against the banks — not the vendor — "because liability flows upstream regardless of where the compromise occurred" [12]. Regulatory framing shifted: "Our vendor was breached, not us" describes where the intrusion occurred, but does not answer whether the bank met its GLBA/OCC oversight obligations. Regulators now hold financial institutions accountable for vendor oversight failures regardless of who technically owned the compromised systems [12][13].

### 2.4 Marquis Software — 70+ financial institutions (Finance)

**Vendor:** Marquis Software, a Texas fintech providing customer relationship tools for banks and credit unions, tracking accounts, SSNs, account numbers, addresses, balances, and employee notes [15].

**Timeline:** breach occurred August 2025; detected August 14; company notified law enforcement and hired experts; warned 74+ institutions in November 2025; regulatory filings later revealed 672,075 people affected (law firms estimate up to 1.35 million) [15].

**Root cause:** a hack of vendor systems — UpGuard describes the vector as a SonicWall vulnerability — with a reported (but unconfirmed) ransom payment [15][16]. Group-IB classifies it as a ransomware attack on a fintech firm exposing data from 70 financial institutions [4].

**Impacts:** affected banks stressed that hackers never breached their own systems — yet the breach triggered notification obligations, legal exposure, and reputational damage across the client base. At least one affected company noted its bank was impacted but not among the 74 listed institutions, suggesting broader reach [15].

### 2.5 Allianz Life and Canada Life — Salesforce CRM campaigns (Insurance/Finance)

**Allianz Life (August 2025):** hackers linked to Scattered Spider and ShinyHunters exfiltrated over 2.8 million customer and partner records from Allianz Life's Salesforce CRM via advanced vishing attacks that bypassed technical defenses. UpGuard lists 1,497,063 affected individuals. The campaign targeted 700+ organizations, including Adidas, Google, Cartier, and Louis Vuitton [16][17].

**Canada Life (April 2026):** Canada's second-largest insurer disclosed that ShinyHunters gained access through a single compromised employee account and used it to query data in the insurer's Salesforce CRM environment. Canada Life's verified count was 70,000 individuals (less than 0.5% of ~14 million customers); ShinyHunters claimed 5.5 million records — described by analysts as "extortion inflation." Exposed data included names, dates of birth, addresses, gender, and income level; no SINs or banking details were confirmed. The vulnerability was "the human account and absence of controls to detect unusual bulk exports from a single user session — not a Salesforce flaw." Experts noted many large insurers still rely on basic passwords or easily phished MFA rather than phishing-resistant MFA, device checks, and conditional access [18][19].

### 2.6 PowerSchool — 62 million students, parents, and educators (Technology/Education)

**Vendor:** PowerSchool, a Folsom, California-based education technology provider serving over 18,000 school organizations across 90 countries and supporting 60+ million students [20].

**Timeline:** earliest unauthorized activity December 19, 2024; PowerSchool aware by December 28; communicated to customers January 7, 2025; DOJ court documents (May 2025) confirmed ~62 million individuals affected and a ransom demand of ~$2.85 million in bitcoin; Ontario Information and Privacy Commissioner (IPC) released its final report November 17, 2025 [20][21][22].

**Root cause:** a threat actor exploited credentials with elevated administrative privileges belonging to a PowerSchool subcontractor outside the US. Many institutions had enabled "always on" remote maintenance. CrowdStrike's investigation confirmed access via a single compromised credential to the PowerSource support portal, with data exfiltration via an export tool. The perpetrator — Matthew D. Lane, a 19-year-old US student — pleaded guilty [20][21].

**Ontario IPC findings:** Canada's most detailed regulatory response to a third-party breach concluded the institutions involved did NOT have reasonable safeguards. Systemic weaknesses included: elevated user privileges contrary to least-privilege principles; no MFA on PowerSource; continuous remote access; short log retention; inconsistent/outdated contracts lacking confidentiality, subcontracting, security, retention, and audit provisions; and over-collection of sensitive data (health card numbers, SINs, insurance details) without legal authority. The IPC ordered compliance proof within six months, emphasizing that "accountability cannot be outsourced" [21][22].

### 2.7 Salesloft/Drift → Salesforce OAuth supply-chain breach — 700+ organizations (Technology)

**Vendor:** Salesloft's Drift AI chat agent, which connects via OAuth to customers' Salesforce CRM systems. The intrusion cluster UNC6395 stole the OAuth tokens Drift uses to connect to customer Salesforce environments [23][24][25].

**Timeline (per Cloudflare's detailed reconstruction):** August 9 reconnaissance; August 12 initial compromise via stolen credential; August 17 bulk exfiltration via Salesforce Bulk API 2.0 (case text pulled in ~3 minutes, then the Bulk job entry was deleted to cover tracks); August 20 Salesloft revoked all Drift-to-Salesforce connections; August 25 Cloudflare disabled the Drift account and rotated 104 exposed API tokens; September 2 customers notified [23].

**Scale:** 700+ organizations impacted, including Cloudflare, Google, PagerDuty, Palo Alto Networks, Proofpoint, Zscaler, Tanium, BeyondTrust, CyberArk, Tenable, Qualys, Rubrik, Elastic, Workday, Workiva, Fastly, and Nutanix. Exposed data included business contacts, support case text, account information, and — in some cases — API keys and cloud credentials found in support cases [23][25].

**Root cause:** stolen OAuth tokens enabling attackers to impersonate the trusted Drift application and bypass MFA. Persistent OAuth access (non-expiring tokens), over-permissive app permissions, limited monitoring of SaaS logs, and unsecured secrets stored in Salesforce fields were the enabling blind spots. FINRA issued a member alert to all firms, recommending disconnection of integrations, credential rotation, forensic log review, and least-privilege controls [23][24][25].

### 2.8 Klue → Salesforce OAuth supply-chain breach — ~200 organizations (Technology)

**Vendor:** Klue, a market intelligence SaaS provider whose integration infrastructure connected customers' CRMs (Salesforce, HubSpot, Gong, Google Drive, Slack) [26][27][28].

**Timeline:** June 11–24, 2026. Attackers exploited a legacy dormant test credential created in 2022 for a prototype integration that was never shipped — "a ghost credential... that should have been revoked years ago." Klue detected the intrusion June 12, disclosed June 15, and engaged CrowdStrike. The Icarus extortion group listed Klue on its leak site June 19; a second hacking group then claimed access to the same stolen data and launched a separate extortion campaign — indicating the original attackers were themselves compromised [26][27][28].

**Scale:** ~195–200 organizations affected, including LastPass, Huntress, Recorded Future, Tanium, Jamf, HackerOne, Snyk, OneTrust, Sprout Social, Gong, Insurity, 8x8, ReliaQuest, Pendo, and BeyondTrust. Attackers queried the Salesforce environments of at least 12 organizations in one 24-hour exfiltration run: "a slow initial pull to blend with normal traffic, then a surge of nearly 1,000 queries in a 15-minute window — invisible to organizations without API-layer logging." Data exposed: customer names, emails, addresses, phone numbers, support case histories, sales records, and — critically — customer OAuth tokens [26][27][28].

**Impacts:** LastPass confirmed this was the eighth time customer data had been exposed since 2011 — the 2022 incident alone was linked to cryptocurrency thefts exceeding $150 million. FINRA issued a member alert despite Klue not being a financial services company. Icarus reportedly reached an agreement with Klue not to publish data, but a second group still holds a portion — "illustrating how ransom payments don't guarantee data disappearance." Analysts noted the breach "does not discriminate by security maturity": HackerOne and Recorded Future, both security companies, were victims [26][27][28][80].

### 2.9 Latin America — MedicSolution (Brazil) and the Mexican government

**MedicSolution (September 2025):** KillSec obtained more than 34 GB of data comprising 94,818 files — medical evaluations, lab results, unredacted patient photos, and records relating to minors — from a software provider serving Brazil's healthcare sector. "Notably, the data was not taken through a complex hack but was left exposed in misconfigured AWS cloud buckets, highlighting persistent gaps in incident response and monitoring across the sector." Despite outreach, MedicSolution issued no public response. Brazil's LGPD classifies health data as sensitive and requires breach reporting within three business days; the ANPD has issued fines totaling over BRL 98 million (~$20M) since 2023 [30].

**Mexican government (January 30, 2026):** the Chronus Group posted datasets allegedly exfiltrated from at least 25 government institutions — 2.3 terabytes affecting up to 36 million citizens, including healthcare registration records (IMSS Bienestar). Root causes: legacy system exploitation (obsolete platforms not decommissioned or segmented), third-party vendor compromise (nearly 30% of government agencies exchange data with over 5,000 third parties; vendor-related breaches surged 68%), and credential abuse with unrevoked credentials. Infostealers LummaC2 and Vidar were confirmed with high confidence [31]. Regional context: 452 ransomware incidents hit Latin America in 2025, with Brazil (128), Mexico (78), Argentina (63), Colombia (51), and Peru (27) hardest hit; healthcare, finance, and government are the most-targeted sectors [32].

## 3. Europe: Documented Breaches

### 3.1 Synnovis / NHS — ~900,000 patients (Healthcare)

**Vendor:** Synnovis, a pathology services provider in South-East London co-owned by Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, and SYNLAB [33].

**Timeline:** ransomware attack June 3, 2024; stolen data published June 20, 2024; notifications to affected patients began only in late 2025 because the investigation into the unstructured, fragmented stolen data took over a year [33].

**Scale/impact:** ~900,000 patients affected; 10,000+ outpatient and elective procedure appointments postponed. In June 2025, a hospital trust confirmed one patient's death was partly attributed to a delayed blood test result caused by the attack — the first publicly confirmed UK death linked to a cyber attack. Data could relate to any Synnovis service user across NHS hospitals, GP practices, and clinics in England [33][34].

### 3.2 DXS International — NHS clinical decision-support vendor (Healthcare)

**Vendor:** DXS International, a British company whose BestPathway and Next-Gen platforms serve ~2,000 GP practices and manage care for ~17 million registered patients — roughly 10% of all NHS referrals [35][36].

**Timeline:** unauthorized access detected December 14, 2025; DevMan ransomware group claimed the breach the same day, alleging theft of 300 GB; DXS disclosed in a London Stock Exchange filing December 18 and notified the ICO [35][36].

**Significance:** at ~£3.4 million annual revenue, DXS is small but strategically important given patient data exposure. UK cybersecurity regulations do not automatically cover third-party health IT suppliers like DXS — a gap the incoming Cyber Security and Resilience Bill is designed to close [35][36].

### 3.3 Miljödata — 1.5 million people (Sweden, Healthcare/Public Sector)

**Vendor:** Miljödata, a Swedish IT provider for sick-leave, rehabilitation, injury, and HR management software used by 80% of Sweden's municipalities (164+ municipalities and 4 regions affected) [81][82].

**Timeline:** attack detected August 24, 2025; DataCarry ransomware group published stolen data September 12–14, 2025; HIBP disclosed the breach September 16 [81][82].

**Scale:** personal data of 1.5 million people leaked, including Swedish personal identity numbers, medical certificates, rehabilitation plans, and work-injury reports. Affected organizations included the City of Stockholm (40,000+ employees), Scandinavian Airlines, Boliden, Volvo Group North America (16,991 current and former employees with SSNs and medical records), and multiple universities. Sweden's prosecution authority confirmed the leak; a GDPR investigation was launched [81][82].

### 3.4 Advanced Computer Software Group — ICO fine (Healthcare)

**Vendor:** Advanced Computer Software Group, a Birmingham-based NHS software supplier providing systems for NHS 111, GP records access, mental health trusts, and care organizations [37].

**Timeline:** LockBit ransomware attack in August 2022; ICO final fine £3,076,320 in March 2025 (reduced from a £6.09 million provisional fine) [37].

**Root cause:** LockBit accessed health and care systems via a customer account that lacked MFA — legitimate credentials used on a third-party account. The ICO determined Advanced "failed to keep its healthcare systems secure." The incident crippled NHS 111 services and forced staff to use pen and paper, prompting a COBR crisis meeting. Data of 79,404 people was exposed, including details of how to gain entry to the homes of 890 people receiving care at home [37][34].

### 3.5 Chain IQ Group — UBS and Pictet (Finance)

**Vendor:** Chain IQ, a Swiss-headquartered global indirect procurement service company serving more than 60 clients across 49 countries [38][39][40].

**Timeline:** attacked June 12, 2025, alongside 19 other companies; Worldleaks (formerly Hunters International) claimed the attack; Chain IQ contained it within 8 hours 45 minutes by revoking access; affected customers notified the same evening [38][39].

**Scale:** ~910 GB and more than 1.9 million files stolen, including personal data of 137,000 UBS employees (names, emails, phone numbers, job roles, and even the internal direct phone number of UBS's CEO) and 230,000 lines of Pictet internal billing data with highly detailed expenses. Other affected clients included Manor, Implenia, KPMG, Mizuho, FedEx, IBM, Swiss Life, AXA, and Swisscom. Chain IQ stated it holds no data relating to clients' core business, so no client financial data was stolen [38][39][40].

**Lesson:** "the procurement security paradox" — procurement systems contain vendor relationships, contractual details, financial transaction histories, and supply-chain dependencies, making them attractive targets; compromising a single provider unlocks access to dozens of client organizations [40].

### 3.6 CEVA Logistics — Valve, ING, Bol, De Bijenkorf, Ajax (Finance/Retail/Logistics)

**Vendor:** CEVA Logistics, a French-headquartered global logistics provider with 1,000+ warehouses, ~$18.3 billion 2025 revenue, and ~110,000 employees [44][45].

**Timeline:** attack affected CEVA's European contract logistics operation between July 29 and August 1, 2026; customers notified August 1; public reporting August 6–11 [44][46].

**Scale:** eight warehouses disrupted; air, ocean, ground, and rail operations continued. Affected organizations — none of which were themselves breached — included Valve (Steam hardware shipments in Europe), Bol, De Bijenkorf, Ajax, ING, and Ace & Tate. Exposed data: names, postal addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, order details, VAT numbers, and for Valve, the type and price of Steam hardware ordered. The Dutch Data Protection Authority received breach reports from 10 organizations and is investigating [44][45][46][47].

**Root cause:** unconfirmed, but the pattern — operational disruption plus confirmed data exfiltration — suggests ransomware or disruptive malware on public-facing applications. The incident demonstrates that "the organization suffering the original breach and the organization carrying the customer relationship are not the same. Contracts can transfer responsibilities, but they cannot transfer reputational impact." Valve warned customers to expect highly targeted fake messages referencing real order details, and Bol halted data exchange with CEVA [44][47].

### 3.7 European Commission — Trivy open-source supply-chain compromise (Technology/Government)

**Vendor:** Trivy, Aqua Security's open-source container and filesystem vulnerability scanner — among the most widely deployed security tools in modern CI/CD pipelines. Compromising Trivy was "not an attack against a single organization but against the security scanning layer of a large fraction of modern CI/CD pipelines simultaneously" [41][42][43].

**Timeline:** late February 2026, an automated bot exploited a `pull_request_target` GitHub Actions workflow, exfiltrating a PAT belonging to the aqua-bot service account; March 19, 2026, TeamPCP pushed a malicious tag (v0.69.4) and repointed 76 of 77 trivy-action tags and all 7 setup-trivy tags to malicious commits. The same day, the actor obtained a compromised AWS secret with management rights over European Commission AWS accounts. The Commission's CSOC received alerts March 24; CERT-EU was notified March 25; the Commission publicly disclosed March 27; ShinyHunters published the exfiltrated dataset March 28 [41][42][43].

**Scale:** ~91.7 GB compressed (340 GB uncompressed), relating to websites hosted for up to 71 clients of the Europa web hosting service (42 internal Commission clients and at least 29 other EU entities), including potentially the European Medicines Agency, European Banking Authority, ENISA, and Frontex. Personal data (names, usernames, email addresses) was confirmed; nearly 52,000 files of outbound email communications were included. No websites were taken offline or tampered with [41][43].

**Root cause:** a cascading supply-chain campaign by TeamPCP against open-source security infrastructure — Trivy, Checkmarx KICS, LiteLLM, and Telnyx — with a shared RSA-4096 key providing technical attribution. The payload exfiltrated CI/CD secrets, encrypted them, and used an ICP blockchain canister for C2 that "cannot be taken down via conventional means." CERT-EU recommendations: pin GitHub Actions to full SHA hashes, rotate all exposed credentials, audit CI/CD pipelines, and deploy behavioral monitoring for CI/CD environments [41][42][43].

### 3.8 Marks & Spencer and Co-op — Scattered Spider via third-party help desk (Retail)

**Vendor:** M&S and the Co-op were both breached in April–May 2025 via third-party help desks — Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) for M&S — using vishing and "MFA fatigue" social engineering [48][49][50][51].

**Timeline:** initial access believed to have begun as early as February 2025; attack launched over the Easter weekend (April 19–21) with contactless payment failures; M&S acknowledged the incident April 22; DragonForce ransomware encrypted VMware ESXi servers; online shopping suspended April 25; stolen customer data revealed May 13; M&S online orders only resumed June 10.

**Scale/impact:** M&S lost roughly £300 million in operating profit; up to £750 million wiped from market value; personal information of a portion of M&S's 9.4 million active online customers compromised. The Co-op lost £80 million operating profit, had contactless payments disabled in 200 of 2,300 stores, and exposed ~6.2–6.5 million member records. M&S reverted to paper-based tracking for fresh food and clothing. Four arrests were made by the NCA [48][49][50][51].

**Root cause:** SIM swapping to bypass MFA, then help-desk impersonation at TCS and other outsourced support providers to obtain credentials, then DragonForce ransomware deployment via Active Directory. CEO Stuart Machin called it "unlucky... through human error" [48][50].

### 3.9 Other notable European incidents

- **Kering (September 2025):** ~7.4 million customers of Gucci, Balenciaga, and Alexander McQueen had personal details and detailed spending data stolen via compromised Salesforce credentials — "one weak link = full compromise." Kering refused ransom negotiations [52].
- **France Titres / ANTS (April 2026):** 11.7 million accounts exposed via an "elementary" IDOR vulnerability on the government identity portal; a 15-year-old suspect arrested. At least the fourth significant French government identity-infrastructure breach in under 12 months [53][54].
- **Capita (ICO £14 million fine, October 2025):** the 2023 breach of the UK outsourcing giant hit councils, the NHS, and defence simultaneously through a single supplier, affecting ~6.6 million individuals — one of the largest UK security-failure fines on record [34].
- **Workday (August 2025):** vishing and malicious OAuth app approval exposed business contact data across up to 11,000 corporate customers and 70 million individual user records (unconfirmed figures); neither the core HR/payroll systems nor customer tenants were breached [16].
